### 3.8.2 Data Flow Architecture

The following diagram illustrates typical data flow patterns through the recommended technology stack:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App<br/>(React/React Native)
    participant ALB as Load Balancer
    participant Auth0
    participant API as Flask API
    participant Auth as Auth Middleware
    participant Service as Business Logic
    participant AI as Langchain Service
    participant LLM as LLM Provider<br/>(OpenAI/Anthropic)
    participant Vector as Vector DB
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant S3
    
    Note over User,S3: Authentication Flow
    User->>Client: Open Application
    Client->>Auth0: Initiate Login (OAuth 2.0)
    Auth0->>User: Present Login UI
    User->>Auth0: Enter Credentials
    Auth0->>Client: Return JWT Token
    Client->>Client: Store Token (Secure Storage)
    
    Note over User,S3: Typical API Request Flow
    User->>Client: Perform Action
    Client->>ALB: HTTP Request + JWT Token
    ALB->>API: Forward Request
    API->>Auth: Validate Request
    Auth->>Auth0: Verify JWT Signature
    Auth0->>Auth: Token Valid
    Auth->>Service: Authenticated Request
    
    Note over User,S3: Data Retrieval with Caching
    Service->>Cache: Check Cache
    alt Cache Hit
        Cache->>Service: Return Cached Data
    else Cache Miss
        Service->>DB: Query Database
        DB->>Service: Return Data
        Service->>Cache: Update Cache (TTL)
    end
    Service->>API: Response Data
    API->>Client: JSON Response
    Client->>User: Display Result
    
    Note over User,S3: AI/ML Processing Flow
    User->>Client: Ask Question (LLM)
    Client->>ALB: POST /api/chat + JWT
    ALB->>API: Forward Request
    API->>Auth: Validate JWT
    Auth->>Service: Authenticated Request
    Service->>AI: Process LLM Request
    AI->>Vector: Search Similar Documents
    Vector->>AI: Return Relevant Context
    AI->>LLM: Generate Completion<br/>(with context)
    LLM->>AI: LLM Response
    AI->>DB: Store Conversation
    AI->>Service: Return Response
    Service->>API: JSON Response
    API->>Client: Stream Response
    Client->>User: Display Answer
    
    Note over User,S3: File Upload Flow
    User->>Client: Upload File
    Client->>API: Request Pre-Signed URL
    API->>S3: Generate Pre-Signed URL
    S3->>API: Signed URL
    API->>Client: Return URL
    Client->>S3: Direct Upload (HTTPS)
    S3->>Client: Upload Complete
    Client->>API: Confirm Upload<br/>(Store Metadata)
    API->>DB: Store File Metadata
    DB->>API: Confirmation
    API->>Client: Success Response
    Client->>User: Upload Complete
```

### 3.8.3 Security and Compliance Considerations

**Security Architecture Principles**:

**Defense in Depth**:
- **Network Layer**: VPC isolation, security groups, NACLs
- **Application Layer**: Input validation, output encoding, CSRF protection
- **Authentication Layer**: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC via Auth0, MFA support
- **Authorization Layer**: JWT token validation, role-based access control
- **Data Layer**: Encryption at rest (database, S3), encryption in transit (TLS 1.3)

**Data Protection**:

**Encryption at Rest**:
- MongoDB: Native encryption or AWS encryption via DocumentDB
- S3: SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS encryption
- Redis: ElastiCache encryption enabled
- Container images: ECR encryption

**Encryption in Transit**:
- All external communication via HTTPS (TLS 1.3)
- Certificate management via AWS Certificate Manager
- Internal service-to-service communication within VPC can use TLS or rely on VPC security

**Secrets Management**:
- All API keys, database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager
- Automatic rotation for database passwords
- IAM roles for container access to secrets (no embedded credentials)
- Never commit secrets to version control (.env files in .gitignore)

**Input Validation and Output Encoding**:
- **Backend**: Pydantic models for request validation, sanitization of user inputs
- **Frontend**: React automatically escapes JSX content preventing XSS
- **Database**: Parameterized queries (ORM/driver handles escaping)
- **LLM**: Prompt injection protection through input sanitization and output validation

**API Security**:
- **Rate Limiting**: Per-user and per-IP rate limits (Flask-Limiter or API Gateway)
- **CORS Configuration**: Whitelist allowed origins, avoid wildcard in production
- **Request Size Limits**: Prevent DoS via large payloads
- **Timeout Configuration**: Prevent resource exhaustion from long-running requests

**Compliance Considerations** (Subject to Requirements):

**GDPR (if applicable)**:
- User consent management for data collection
- Right to access: API endpoints for data export
- Right to erasure: Data deletion workflows
- Data processing agreements with third-party services (Auth0, LLM providers)

**SOC 2 (if applicable)**:
- Audit logging of all data access and modifications
- Regular security assessments and penetration testing
- Incident response procedures
- Vendor security assessments (Auth0, AWS, LLM providers)

**HIPAA (if handling healthcare data)**:
- Business Associate Agreements (BAA) with all service providers
- Enhanced encryption and access controls
- Audit logging and monitoring
- Regular risk assessments

**Security Monitoring and Incident Response**:
- **Logging**: Centralized logging of authentication events, API calls, errors
- **Monitoring**: Alerts for unusual activity patterns, failed authentication attempts
- **Vulnerability Scanning**: Regular dependency updates, container image scanning
- **Penetration Testing**: Annual third-party security assessments (recommended)

## 3.9 Technology Selection Criteria and Decision Framework

### 3.9.1 Evaluation Criteria

As business requirements and technical constraints are defined during the requirements phase (per Section 1.6), the recommended technology stack should be validated against the following criteria:

**Functional Requirements Alignment**:
- Does the technology provide necessary capabilities for core features?
- Are required integrations supported with stable libraries/SDKs?
- Does the technology scale to projected user volumes and data sizes?

**Non-Functional Requirements**:
- **Performance**: Latency, throughput, response time requirements
- **Scalability**: Horizontal and vertical scaling capabilities
- **Availability**: High availability requirements (e.g., 99.9% uptime)
- **Reliability**: Error rates, fault tolerance, disaster recovery

**Technical Considerations**:
- **Maturity**: Production-ready with stable releases
- **Community Support**: Active development, large community, extensive documentation
- **Ecosystem**: Availability of complementary libraries and tools
- **Interoperability**: Compatibility with other selected technologies

**Operational Considerations**:
- **Ease of Deployment**: Container support, managed service availability
- **Monitoring and Debugging**: Observability tools, logging capabilities
- **Maintenance Burden**: Update frequency, breaking change frequency
- **Licensing**: Open-source license compatibility with product model

**Business Considerations**:
- **Cost**: Licensing costs, infrastructure costs, operational costs
- **Talent Availability**: Availability of developers with required skills
- **Vendor Lock-In**: Portability to other platforms if needed
- **Support Options**: Commercial support availability for critical components

**Security and Compliance**:
- **Security Track Record**: History of vulnerabilities, response time to security issues
- **Compliance Certifications**: SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA (if applicable)
- **Encryption Support**: Data encryption capabilities
- **Audit Trail**: Logging and monitoring capabilities for compliance

### 3.9.2 Alternative Technology Considerations

The recommended technology stack represents a balanced, modern approach suitable for a wide range of applications. However, alternative technologies may be more appropriate depending on specific requirements that emerge during planning:

**Backend Language Alternatives**:

**Node.js (TypeScript)**:
- **Advantage**: Unified language across frontend and backend (TypeScript)
- **Advantage**: Excellent for real-time applications (WebSocket support)
- **Disadvantage**: Less mature AI/ML ecosystem compared to Python
- **Use Case**: If real-time collaboration features are primary requirements

**Go (Golang)**:
- **Advantage**: Superior performance and lower memory footprint
- **Advantage**: Excellent for high-throughput, low-latency services
- **Disadvantage**: Smaller ecosystem, especially for AI/ML
- **Use Case**: If extreme performance is a primary requirement and AI features are secondary

**Backend Framework Alternatives**:

**FastAPI (Python)**:
- **Advantage**: Automatic API documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger)
- **Advantage**: Native async/await support for high-concurrency scenarios
- **Advantage**: Automatic request validation via Pydantic
- **Consideration**: Slightly less mature than Flask but rapidly gaining adoption
- **Use Case**: If API documentation and async support are priorities

**Django + Django REST Framework**:
- **Advantage**: Comprehensive framework with built-in admin, ORM, authentication
- **Advantage**: Excellent for rapid development of database-driven applications
- **Disadvantage**: More opinionated, potentially over-engineered for simple APIs
- **Use Case**: If extensive CRUD operations and admin interfaces are needed

**Database Alternatives**:

**PostgreSQL (Relational)**:
- **Advantage**: ACID compliance, complex query support, mature ecosystem
- **Advantage**: Better for structured data with complex relationships
- **Disadvantage**: Schema rigidity requires migrations for changes
- **Use Case**: If data has well-defined structure and complex relational queries are needed

**DynamoDB (AWS NoSQL)**:
- **Advantage**: Fully managed, serverless, infinite scalability
- **Advantage**: Tight AWS integration, pay-per-request pricing
- **Disadvantage**: More complex query patterns, potential vendor lock-in
- **Use Case**: If extreme scalability and AWS-native solution are priorities

**Frontend Framework Alternatives**:

**Vue.js**:
- **Advantage**: Gentler learning curve, progressive framework
- **Advantage**: Excellent documentation and tooling
- **Consideration**: Smaller ecosystem than React
- **Use Case**: If team has Vue.js expertise or prefers template-based approach

**Angular**:
- **Advantage**: Comprehensive framework with built-in routing, forms, HTTP client
- **Advantage**: Strong TypeScript integration (built with TypeScript)
- **Disadvantage**: Steeper learning curve, more opinionated
- **Use Case**: If building large enterprise application with team experienced in Angular

**Svelte/SvelteKit**:
- **Advantage**: Compile-time framework with no virtual DOM overhead
- **Advantage**: Smaller bundle sizes, excellent performance
- **Disadvantage**: Smaller ecosystem and community
- **Use Case**: If performance and small bundle size are critical priorities

**Cloud Platform Alternatives**:

**Google Cloud Platform (GCP)**:
- **Advantage**: Excellent AI/ML services (Vertex AI, BigQuery ML)
- **Advantage**: Competitive pricing for compute and storage
- **Consideration**: Smaller ecosystem than AWS

**Microsoft Azure**:
- **Advantage**: Best integration with Microsoft ecosystem (Active Directory, Office 365)
- **Advantage**: Hybrid cloud capabilities
- **Consideration**: Interface can be complex for new users

**Alternative Assessment Process**: When requirements are defined, conduct proof-of-concept (POC) implementations with the recommended stack and top alternatives to validate performance, development velocity, and operational characteristics against specific requirements.

### 3.9.3 Risk Assessment and Mitigation

**Technology Risk Assessment**:

**Vendor Lock-In Risks**:

**Risk: AWS Dependency**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (using AWS-specific services like ECS, DocumentDB)
- **Impact**: High (migration to another cloud provider requires significant effort)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Use AWS-compatible services where possible (MongoDB Atlas is cloud-agnostic)
  - Containerization (Docker) provides portability across cloud platforms
  - Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) can be adapted to other cloud providers
  - Avoid AWS-specific code in application layer; use abstraction layers

**Risk: Auth0 Dependency**
- **Likelihood**: Low (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC are standards)
- **Impact**: Medium (migration requires user re-authentication)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Standard protocols (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, JWT) enable migration to alternatives
  - Abstract authentication logic behind service interface
  - Export user data regularly for migration capability

**Risk: LLM Provider Dependency**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (OpenAI, Anthropic APIs are proprietary)
- **Impact**: Medium (API changes or pricing increases)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Langchain provides abstraction over multiple LLM providers
  - Design prompts and chains to be provider-agnostic where possible
  - Test with multiple providers during development
  - Implement fallback logic for provider unavailability

**Technical Debt Risks**:

**Risk: Rapid Framework Updates**
- **Likelihood**: High (JavaScript/React ecosystem evolves rapidly)
- **Impact**: Medium (outdated dependencies, security vulnerabilities)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Automated dependency updates via Dependabot or Renovate
  - Regular update cycles (monthly for minor versions)
  - Comprehensive test suite to catch breaking changes
  - Pin major versions until intentional migration

**Risk: Python Async Adoption**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (Flask is traditionally synchronous)
- **Impact**: Low to Medium (performance limitations for I/O-heavy workloads)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Use async libraries where available (aiohttp, motor for MongoDB)
  - Consider FastAPI migration if async becomes critical
  - Horizontal scaling addresses throughput needs initially
  - Asynchronous task queue (Celery) for background processing

**Operational Risks**:

**Risk: Monitoring Gaps**
- **Likelihood**: High (monitoring services not yet selected)
- **Impact**: High (blind spots in production issues)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Prioritize monitoring service selection before production deployment
  - Implement comprehensive logging from day one
  - Basic CloudWatch monitoring as minimum baseline
  - Gradual enhancement of observability as budget allows

**Risk: Cost Overruns**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (cloud costs, LLM API costs can escalate)
- **Impact**: High (budget constraints)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Cost monitoring and budget alerts from beginning
  - Implement caching to reduce redundant API calls
  - Use cost-effective LLM models for appropriate use cases (GPT-3.5 vs. GPT-4)
  - Right-size infrastructure (avoid over-provisioning)
  - Regular cost optimization reviews

**Security Risks**:

**Risk: API Key Exposure**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (developer error, misconfiguration)
- **Impact**: High (unauthorized access, data breach, cost exposure)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Secrets Manager for all sensitive credentials
  - Pre-commit hooks to prevent secret commits (git-secrets, trufflehog)
  - Regular secret rotation
  - Principle of least privilege for all IAM roles

**Risk: Prompt Injection Attacks**
- **Likelihood**: Medium (LLM-specific attack vector)
- **Impact**: Medium to High (unintended LLM behavior, data leakage)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Input sanitization and validation
  - Output validation and filtering
  - Prompt engineering with delimiters and instructions
  - LLM-specific security tools (e.g., NeMo Guardrails)

**Continuity Risks**:

**Risk: Third-Party Service Outages**
- **Likelihood**: Low to Medium (all services have occasional outages)
- **Impact**: High (application unavailability)
- **Mitigation**:
  - Implement circuit breakers and graceful degradation
  - Caching strategies to serve stale data during outages
  - Status page subscriptions for all critical services
  - Multi-region deployment for critical components

### 3.10.2 Technical Discovery Activities

Once prerequisites are established, conduct the following technical discovery activities to validate or refine the technology stack:

**Phase 1: Proof of Concept Development (Weeks 1-2)**

**Objective**: Validate that recommended technologies can implement core features with acceptable performance and development velocity.

**POC Scope**:
- Implement simplified version of one core feature end-to-end
- Frontend (React) → API (Flask) → Database (MongoDB) → AI (Langchain + LLM)
- Authentication flow with Auth0 integration
- Deploy to AWS with containerization (Docker + ECS)

**Success Criteria**:
- Feature functions correctly with all technology integrations
- Performance meets preliminary requirements
- Development team can productively work with selected technologies
- Deployment process is understood and documented

**Deliverables**:
- Working POC application (not production-quality)
- Performance benchmarks and metrics
- Developer experience feedback
- Cost estimates for projected usage
- Identified gaps or challenges

**Phase 2: Architecture Validation (Weeks 3-4)**

**Objective**: Validate that the technology stack can support full system architecture and scale.

**Activities**:
- **Load Testing**: Simulate expected user volumes to identify bottlenecks
- **Security Review**: Assess security posture against requirements
- **Cost Modeling**: Project operational costs at different usage scales
- **Integration Testing**: Validate all third-party service integrations
- **Disaster Recovery**: Test backup/restore and failover procedures

**Deliverables**:
- Load test results and capacity planning
- Security assessment report
- Detailed cost projections
- Integration architecture documentation
- Disaster recovery plan

**Phase 3: Alternative Evaluation (If Needed, Weeks 5-6)**

**Objective**: If POC reveals concerns, evaluate alternatives for problematic components.

**Scenarios**:
- Performance issues → Evaluate Go or Node.js backend alternatives
- Development velocity concerns → Evaluate FastAPI or Django alternatives
- Cost concerns → Evaluate different LLM providers or caching strategies
- AWS lock-in concerns → Evaluate multi-cloud or cloud-agnostic alternatives

**Process**:
- Spike implementation with alternative technology
- Comparative analysis: performance, cost, developer experience
- Migration effort assessment if switching after POC
- Final recommendation with trade-offs documented

### 3.10.3 Proof of Concept Recommendations

**POC Implementation Guidelines**:

**Development Environment Setup**:
1. Repository structure with frontend, backend, and infrastructure directories
2. Docker Compose for local development environment
3. Sample .env files with required environment variables (with placeholder values)
4. README with setup instructions

**Feature Selection for POC**:
- Select ONE core feature that exercises all technology stack components
- Recommended: User authentication + AI-powered query (if AI is core feature)
- Avoid complex business logic; focus on technology integration validation

**Code Quality Standards** (Even for POC):
- TypeScript strict mode for frontend
- Type hints for Python backend
- Basic linting configuration (ESLint, Flake8)
- Basic test coverage for critical paths (>50%)
- This establishes quality standards for production development

**Infrastructure as Code from Start**:
- Define all AWS resources in Terraform from POC phase
- Avoid manual console configuration (leads to drift and undocumented infrastructure)
- Use separate Terraform workspaces for dev and POC environments

**Documentation During POC**:
- Architecture decision records (ADRs) for technology choices
- Setup and deployment instructions
- Known issues and limitations
- API documentation (even if minimal)

**POC Evaluation Metrics**:

**Development Velocity**:
- Time to implement POC feature
- Developer satisfaction and confidence with technologies
- Ease of debugging and troubleshooting

**Technical Performance**:
- API response latency (target: <500ms for standard requests)
- LLM response time (target: <5 seconds for typical queries)
- Concurrent user handling (target: >100 simultaneous users on modest infrastructure)

**Operational Metrics**:
- Deployment time and complexity
- Infrastructure cost for POC usage
- Monitoring and debugging capabilities

**Risk Indicators**:
- Unresolved integration issues
- Performance bottlenecks that cannot be easily addressed
- Excessive complexity in any component
- Dependency conflicts or compatibility issues

**Post-POC Decision Gate**:

**Proceed with Recommended Stack If**:
- ✓ POC feature works with all integrations
- ✓ Performance meets preliminary requirements
- ✓ Team is productive and confident
- ✓ Cost projections are within budget
- ✓ No blocking security or compliance concerns

**Evaluate Alternatives If**:
- ✗ Significant performance concerns that cannot be resolved through optimization
- ✗ Team struggles with technologies despite adequate learning time
- ✗ Cost projections significantly exceed budget
- ✗ Integration challenges with critical third-party services
- ✗ Security or compliance gaps that selected technologies cannot address

**Finalize Stack and Proceed to Implementation If**:
- All prerequisites completed (Section 1.6)
- POC successfully validates technology choices
- Architecture review conducted and approved
- Team trained and ready to begin development
- Infrastructure provisioning plan documented
- CI/CD pipeline established

## 4.2 SYSTEM INTEGRATION WORKFLOWS

### 4.2.1 Authentication and Authorization Flow

#### 4.2.1.1 OAuth 2.0 Authentication Process

The system implements OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication via Auth0, providing secure, industry-standard user authentication across all client applications (web, mobile, and desktop).

**Authentication Workflow**:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client Application<br/>(React/React Native/Electron)
    participant Auth0 as Auth0<br/>Identity Provider
    participant SecureStorage as Secure Storage<br/>(Browser/Device)
    
    Note over User,SecureStorage: Initial Authentication Flow
    User->>Client: 1. Access Application
    Client->>Client: 2. Check for Valid Token
    
    alt No Valid Token
        Client->>Auth0: 3. Initiate OAuth 2.0 Flow<br/>(Authorization Code + PKCE)
        Auth0->>User: 4. Redirect to Auth0 Login UI
        User->>Auth0: 5. Enter Credentials<br/>(Username/Password or Social Login)
        
        alt Multi-Factor Authentication Enabled
            Auth0->>User: 6a. Request MFA Code<br/>(SMS/TOTP/Email)
            User->>Auth0: 6b. Submit MFA Code
            Auth0->>Auth0: 6c. Verify MFA Code
        end
        
        Auth0->>Auth0: 7. Validate Credentials
        Auth0->>Client: 8. Return Authorization Code
        Client->>Auth0: 9. Exchange Code for Tokens<br/>(Access Token + Refresh Token + ID Token)
        Auth0->>Client: 10. Return JWT Tokens
        Client->>SecureStorage: 11. Store Tokens Securely<br/>(Encrypted Storage)
        Client->>User: 12. Grant Application Access
    else Valid Token Exists
        Client->>User: 13. Grant Immediate Access
    end
```

**Key Process Characteristics**:
- **Authorization Code Flow with PKCE**: Provides enhanced security for public clients (mobile/desktop apps) by preventing authorization code interception attacks
- **Token Storage**: JWT tokens stored in secure, encrypted storage mechanisms appropriate to each platform (HTTP-only cookies for web, Keychain for iOS, KeyStore for Android, encrypted filesystem for desktop)
- **Token Lifetime**: Access tokens have short expiration (typically 1 hour), while refresh tokens enable longer session persistence
- **Social Authentication**: Auth0 supports integration with social identity providers (Google, GitHub, etc.) as authentication alternatives

#### 4.2.1.2 JWT Token Validation and Management

Once authenticated, every API request must include a valid JWT access token for authorization. The following workflow describes token validation:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([API Request Received]) --> HasToken{Request Contains<br/>JWT Token?}
    
    HasToken -->|No| Reject1[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Missing Authentication Token]
    Reject1 --> End1([Request Rejected])
    
    HasToken -->|Yes| ExtractToken[Extract Token from<br/>Authorization Header]
    ExtractToken --> ValidateFormat{Token Format<br/>Valid?}
    
    ValidateFormat -->|No| Reject2[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Malformed Token]
    Reject2 --> End1
    
    ValidateFormat -->|Yes| VerifySignature[Verify JWT Signature<br/>with Auth0 Public Key]
    VerifySignature --> SignatureValid{Signature<br/>Valid?}
    
    SignatureValid -->|No| Reject3[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid Token Signature]
    Reject3 --> End1
    
    SignatureValid -->|Yes| CheckExpiration{Token<br/>Expired?}
    
    CheckExpiration -->|Yes| Reject4[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Token Expired]
    Reject4 --> End1
    
    CheckExpiration -->|No| CheckIssuer{Issuer and<br/>Audience Valid?}
    
    CheckIssuer -->|No| Reject5[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid Token Claims]
    Reject5 --> End1
    
    CheckIssuer -->|Yes| ExtractClaims[Extract User Claims<br/>user_id, roles, permissions]
    ExtractClaims --> AttachContext[Attach User Context<br/>to Request Object]
    AttachContext --> ProcessRequest[Forward to<br/>Business Logic Layer]
    ProcessRequest --> End2([Request Authorized])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style Reject1 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject2 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject3 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject4 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject5 fill:#FF6B6B
```

#### 4.2.1.3 Token Refresh and Session Management

To maintain continuous user sessions without requiring re-authentication, the system implements automatic token refresh using refresh tokens:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant API as Flask API
    participant Auth0
    participant SecureStorage
    
    Note over Client,SecureStorage: Token Expiration and Refresh Flow
    
    Client->>API: 1. API Request with Access Token
    API->>API: 2. Validate Token
    API->>Client: 3. Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>(Token Expired)
    
    Client->>SecureStorage: 4. Retrieve Refresh Token
    SecureStorage->>Client: 5. Return Refresh Token
    
    alt Refresh Token Valid
        Client->>Auth0: 6. Request New Access Token<br/>(POST /oauth/token with Refresh Token)
        Auth0->>Auth0: 7. Validate Refresh Token
        Auth0->>Client: 8. Return New Access Token<br/>(and optionally new Refresh Token)
        Client->>SecureStorage: 9. Update Stored Tokens
        Client->>API: 10. Retry Original Request<br/>(with New Access Token)
        API->>Client: 11. Return Successful Response
    else Refresh Token Expired/Invalid
        Client->>Client: 12. Clear All Stored Tokens
        Client->>User: 13. Redirect to Login<br/>(Re-authentication Required)
    end
```

**Session Management Policies**:
- **Access Token Expiration**: 60 minutes (configurable)
- **Refresh Token Expiration**: 7 days (configurable)
- **Automatic Token Refresh**: Client-side logic attempts silent token refresh before expiration
- **Session Termination**: User logout invalidates all tokens and clears secure storage
- **Concurrent Sessions**: Multiple device sessions supported with independent token management

### 4.2.2 API Request and Response Flow

#### 4.2.2.1 Complete Request Processing Pipeline

The following comprehensive workflow illustrates the end-to-end journey of an authenticated API request through all system layers:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App<br/>(React/React Native)
    participant ALB as AWS Application<br/>Load Balancer
    participant Flask as Flask API<br/>(Gunicorn)
    participant AuthMW as Auth Middleware<br/>(JWT Validation)
    participant Auth0
    participant BizLogic as Business Logic<br/>Service
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant CloudWatch as AWS CloudWatch<br/>(Logging)
    
    Note over User,CloudWatch: Authenticated API Request Flow
    
    User->>Client: 1. Perform Action<br/>(e.g., Fetch User Profile)
    Client->>Client: 2. Retrieve JWT Token<br/>from Secure Storage
    Client->>ALB: 3. HTTPS Request<br/>Authorization: Bearer {JWT}
    
    ALB->>CloudWatch: 4. Log Request Metadata<br/>(IP, timestamp, path)
    ALB->>Flask: 5. Forward Request<br/>(with headers preserved)
    
    Flask->>AuthMW: 6. Pass to Auth Middleware
    AuthMW->>Auth0: 7. Verify JWT Signature<br/>(using Auth0 JWKS endpoint)
    
    alt Token Valid
        Auth0->>AuthMW: 8a. Token Verified
        AuthMW->>AuthMW: 8b. Extract User Context<br/>(user_id, roles, permissions)
        AuthMW->>BizLogic: 9. Forward Authenticated Request<br/>(with user context attached)
        
        Note over BizLogic,DB: Business Logic Processing
        BizLogic->>Cache: 10. Check Cache for Data<br/>(GET user:{user_id})
        
        alt Cache Hit
            Cache->>BizLogic: 11a. Return Cached Data
        else Cache Miss
            BizLogic->>DB: 11b. Query Database<br/>(db.users.findOne({_id: user_id}))
            DB->>BizLogic: 11c. Return User Document
            BizLogic->>Cache: 11d. Update Cache<br/>(SET user:{user_id}, TTL: 3600s)
        end
        
        BizLogic->>BizLogic: 12. Apply Business Logic<br/>(transform, validate, enrich data)
        BizLogic->>Flask: 13. Return Response Data
        Flask->>CloudWatch: 14. Log Successful Response<br/>(status: 200, latency: Xms)
        Flask->>ALB: 15. HTTP 200 OK<br/>(JSON response body)
        ALB->>Client: 16. Return Response
        Client->>User: 17. Display Result
        
    else Token Invalid
        Auth0->>AuthMW: 8c. Token Verification Failed
        AuthMW->>Flask: 8d. Raise Authentication Error
        Flask->>CloudWatch: 8e. Log Authentication Failure<br/>(user_id: unknown, reason: invalid_token)
        Flask->>ALB: 8f. HTTP 401 Unauthorized<br/>(error: "Invalid or expired token")
        ALB->>Client: 8g. Return Error Response
        Client->>Client: 8h. Attempt Token Refresh<br/>(see Section 4.2.1.3)
    end
```

#### 4.2.2.2 Rate Limiting and Request Throttling

To prevent abuse and ensure fair resource allocation, the system implements multi-tier rate limiting:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([API Request]) --> CheckIP{IP-Based<br/>Rate Limit?}
    
    CheckIP -->|Exceeded| RejectIP[Return 429 Too Many Requests<br/>Retry-After: X seconds<br/>Limit: 1000 req/hour per IP]
    RejectIP --> LogIP[Log Rate Limit Violation<br/>IP: source_ip, endpoint: path]
    LogIP --> End1([Request Rejected])
    
    CheckIP -->|Within Limit| CheckUser{User-Based<br/>Rate Limit?}
    
    CheckUser -->|Exceeded| RejectUser[Return 429 Too Many Requests<br/>Retry-After: X seconds<br/>Limit: 5000 req/hour per user]
    RejectUser --> LogUser[Log Rate Limit Violation<br/>User: user_id, endpoint: path]
    LogUser --> End1
    
    CheckUser -->|Within Limit| CheckEndpoint{Endpoint-Specific<br/>Rate Limit?}
    
    CheckEndpoint -->|Exceeded| RejectEndpoint[Return 429 Too Many Requests<br/>Endpoint: /api/expensive-operation<br/>Limit: 10 req/minute]
    RejectEndpoint --> LogEndpoint[Log Rate Limit Violation<br/>User: user_id, endpoint: specific_path]
    LogEndpoint --> End1
    
    CheckEndpoint -->|Within Limit| IncrementCounters[Increment Rate Limit Counters<br/>Redis INCR with TTL]
    IncrementCounters --> ProcessRequest[Forward to Authentication<br/>Middleware]
    ProcessRequest --> End2([Request Processed])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style RejectIP fill:#FF6B6B
    style RejectUser fill:#FF6B6B
    style RejectEndpoint fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Rate Limit Configuration**:
- **Global IP Limit**: 1,000 requests per hour per IP address
- **Authenticated User Limit**: 5,000 requests per hour per user
- **Endpoint-Specific Limits**: Configurable per-endpoint limits for resource-intensive operations
- **Rate Limit Storage**: Redis-based counters with automatic TTL expiration
- **Exemptions**: Administrative users and service accounts may have elevated limits

#### 4.2.2.3 Request Timeout and Circuit Breaker

The system implements timeout controls and circuit breaker patterns to prevent cascading failures:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed: Circuit Healthy
    
    Closed --> Open: Failure Threshold Exceeded<br/>(e.g., 5 failures in 60 seconds)
    Closed --> Closed: Request Success
    Closed --> Closed: Request Failure<br/>(below threshold)
    
    Open --> HalfOpen: Timeout Period Elapsed<br/>(e.g., 30 seconds)
    Open --> Open: Reject All Requests<br/>(Return 503 Service Unavailable)
    
    HalfOpen --> Closed: Test Request Succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open: Test Request Fails
    
    note right of Open
        During Open State:
        - All requests immediately fail
        - No downstream service calls
        - Return cached data if available
        - Log circuit breaker activation
    end note
    
    note right of HalfOpen
        During Half-Open State:
        - Allow single test request
        - Monitor test request outcome
        - Transition to Closed or Open
          based on test result
    end note
```

**Timeout Configuration**:
- **API Gateway Timeout**: 30 seconds (ALB idle timeout)
- **Database Query Timeout**: 10 seconds
- **External API Timeout**: 15 seconds (OpenAI, Anthropic, Auth0)
- **Cache Operation Timeout**: 1 second

### 4.2.3 Data Access and Caching Pattern

#### 4.2.3.1 Cache-First Retrieval Strategy

The system implements a cache-first data access pattern to optimize performance and reduce database load:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Data Request]) --> CheckCache[Query Redis Cache<br/>GET cache_key]
    
    CheckCache --> CacheExists{Cache<br/>Entry Exists?}
    
    CacheExists -->|Yes - Cache Hit| ValidateTTL{TTL<br/>Valid?}
    
    ValidateTTL -->|Yes| DeserializeCache[Deserialize Cached Data<br/>JSON → Object]
    DeserializeCache --> LogCacheHit[Log Cache Hit<br/>key: cache_key, latency: Xms]
    LogCacheHit --> ReturnCached[Return Cached Data]
    ReturnCached --> End1([Response Complete])
    
    ValidateTTL -->|No - Expired| InvalidateCache[Delete Expired Entry<br/>DEL cache_key]
    InvalidateCache --> QueryDB
    
    CacheExists -->|No - Cache Miss| QueryDB[Query MongoDB<br/>db.collection.find query]
    
    QueryDB --> DBSuccess{Query<br/>Successful?}
    
    DBSuccess -->|Yes| ProcessData[Process Database Result<br/>transform, validate]
    ProcessData --> UpdateCache[Update Redis Cache<br/>SET cache_key, TTL: X seconds]
    UpdateCache --> LogCacheMiss[Log Cache Miss<br/>key: cache_key, source: database]
    LogCacheMiss --> ReturnDB[Return Database Data]
    ReturnDB --> End1
    
    DBSuccess -->|No - Error| LogDBError[Log Database Error<br/>error: message, query: details]
    LogDBError --> CheckStaleCache{Stale Cache<br/>Available?}
    
    CheckStaleCache -->|Yes| ReturnStale[Return Stale Cached Data<br/>with warning flag]
    ReturnStale --> End2([Response with Degraded Data])
    
    CheckStaleCache -->|No| ReturnError[Return 503 Service Unavailable<br/>error: database_unavailable]
    ReturnError --> End3([Error Response])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#90EE90
    style End2 fill:#FFA500
    style End3 fill:#FFB6C1
    style ReturnError fill:#FF6B6B
```

#### 4.2.3.2 Cache Invalidation and Update Strategies

The system supports multiple cache invalidation patterns based on data consistency requirements:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Write-Through Pattern"
        WT1[Write Request] --> WT2[Update Database]
        WT2 --> WT3{DB Update<br/>Successful?}
        WT3 -->|Yes| WT4[Update Cache]
        WT4 --> WT5[Return Success]
        WT3 -->|No| WT6[Return Error<br/>No Cache Update]
    end
    
    subgraph "Write-Behind Pattern"
        WB1[Write Request] --> WB2[Update Cache<br/>Immediately]
        WB2 --> WB3[Return Success<br/>to Client]
        WB3 --> WB4[Async DB Update<br/>Background Task]
    end
    
    subgraph "Cache-Aside Pattern"
        CA1[Write Request] --> CA2[Update Database]
        CA2 --> CA3[Invalidate Cache<br/>DEL cache_key]
        CA3 --> CA4[Return Success<br/>Cache repopulated on next read]
    end
    
    subgraph "Event-Based Invalidation"
        EV1[Data Change Event] --> EV2[Publish to Event Bus]
        EV2 --> EV3[Cache Invalidation Subscriber]
        EV3 --> EV4[Delete Related Cache Keys<br/>Pattern matching]
    end
    
    style WT1 fill:#E8F4F8
    style WB1 fill:#E8F4F8
    style CA1 fill:#E8F4F8
    style EV1 fill:#E8F4F8
```

**Cache Invalidation Rules**:
- **User Profile Data**: Write-through pattern with 1-hour TTL
- **Session Data**: Write-through pattern with 15-minute TTL
- **AI Conversation History**: Write-behind pattern (eventual consistency acceptable)
- **File Metadata**: Cache-aside pattern with 24-hour TTL
- **Configuration Data**: Event-based invalidation with 1-hour default TTL

#### 4.2.3.3 Cache Warming and Pre-Population

For frequently accessed data, the system implements proactive cache warming strategies:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Scheduler as Cron Job / Scheduler
    participant WarmService as Cache Warming Service
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant Monitor as CloudWatch
    
    Note over Scheduler,Monitor: Scheduled Cache Warming (e.g., Daily at 2 AM)
    
    Scheduler->>WarmService: Trigger Cache Warming Job
    WarmService->>DB: Query High-Priority Data<br/>(popular content, active users)
    DB->>WarmService: Return Data Sets
    
    loop For Each Data Item
        WarmService->>Cache: SET cache_key with data<br/>(TTL: configured value)
        Cache->>WarmService: Confirmation
    end
    
    WarmService->>Monitor: Log Cache Warming Complete<br/>(items_cached: N, duration: Xms)
    WarmService->>Scheduler: Job Complete
    
    Note over Scheduler,Monitor: On-Demand Cache Warming (Triggered by Events)
    
    WarmService->>WarmService: Detect Warm Trigger<br/>(e.g., new product launch)
    WarmService->>DB: Query Related Data
    DB->>WarmService: Return Data
    WarmService->>Cache: Populate Cache Entries
    WarmService->>Monitor: Log Event-Based Warming
```

### 4.2.4 AI/ML Processing Workflow

#### 4.2.4.1 Large Language Model (LLM) Request Processing

The system integrates with multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) to deliver AI-powered capabilities. The following workflow illustrates the complete AI request processing pipeline:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant API as Flask API
    participant Auth as Auth Middleware
    participant AI as Langchain Service
    participant Vector as Vector Database<br/>(ChromaDB/Pinecone)
    participant LLM as LLM Provider<br/>(OpenAI/Anthropic)
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    
    Note over User,Cache: AI/ML Chat Interaction Flow
    
    User->>Client: 1. Enter Question/Prompt<br/>"Explain the authentication flow"
    Client->>API: 2. POST /api/chat<br/>Authorization: Bearer {JWT}<br/>Body: {prompt, conversation_id}
    
    API->>Auth: 3. Validate JWT Token
    Auth->>API: 4. Token Valid (user_id extracted)
    
    API->>AI: 5. Process LLM Request<br/>(prompt, user_id, conversation_id)
    
    Note over AI,Cache: Context Retrieval and Enhancement
    
    AI->>Cache: 6. Check Cache for Similar Query<br/>GET llm_cache:{hash(prompt)}
    
    alt Cache Hit - Similar Query Found
        Cache->>AI: 7a. Return Cached Response
        AI->>DB: 7b. Store Conversation Entry<br/>(reference to cached response)
        AI->>API: 7c. Return Cached Response<br/>(with cache_hit: true flag)
    else Cache Miss - New Query
        AI->>Vector: 8. Search for Relevant Context<br/>(vector similarity search on prompt embedding)
        Vector->>AI: 9. Return Top K Similar Documents<br/>(K=5, similarity threshold > 0.7)
        
        AI->>AI: 10. Construct Enhanced Prompt<br/>(system prompt + context + user prompt)
        
        AI->>LLM: 11. Generate Completion<br/>POST /v1/chat/completions<br/>model: gpt-4 / claude-3<br/>temperature: 0.7, max_tokens: 2000
        
        alt LLM Request Successful
            LLM->>AI: 12a. Stream Response Chunks<br/>(Server-Sent Events)
            
            loop For Each Response Chunk
                AI->>API: 12b. Forward Chunk to Client
                API->>Client: 12c. Stream Chunk
                Client->>User: 12d. Display Incremental Response
            end
            
            AI->>DB: 13. Store Complete Conversation<br/>{user_id, conversation_id, prompt,<br/>response, context_sources, timestamp}
            
            AI->>Cache: 14. Cache Response<br/>SET llm_cache:{hash(prompt)}<br/>TTL: 3600 seconds
            
            AI->>Vector: 15. Store New Embeddings<br/>(if response should be indexed)
            
            AI->>API: 16. Return Completion Metadata<br/>(tokens_used, latency, model)
            
        else LLM Request Failed
            LLM->>AI: 12e. Error Response<br/>(rate_limit / timeout / error)
            AI->>AI: 12f. Apply Fallback Strategy<br/>(retry with backoff / alternate model)
            
            alt Fallback Successful
                AI->>API: 12g. Return Fallback Response
            else Fallback Failed
                AI->>API: 12h. Return Error<br/>503 Service Unavailable<br/>error: "AI service temporarily unavailable"
            end
        end
    end
    
    API->>Client: 17. Return Final Response<br/>(with metadata)
    Client->>User: 18. Display Complete Answer
```

**LLM Processing Characteristics**:
- **Response Streaming**: Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time response delivery
- **Context Window Management**: Automatic prompt truncation if context exceeds model limits
- **Token Usage Tracking**: Monitor token consumption for cost optimization and rate limiting
- **Model Selection**: Dynamic model routing based on query complexity and user tier
- **Conversation Memory**: Maintain conversation history for context-aware multi-turn interactions

#### 4.2.4.2 Vector Database Context Retrieval

The vector database serves as a semantic search engine for retrieving relevant context to enhance LLM responses:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([LLM Request]) --> EmbedQuery[Generate Query Embedding<br/>Model: text-embedding-ada-002<br/>Dimensions: 1536]
    
    EmbedQuery --> SearchVector[Vector Similarity Search<br/>Distance Metric: Cosine Similarity]
    
    SearchVector --> CheckResults{Results<br/>Found?}
    
    CheckResults -->|No Results| UsePromptOnly[Proceed with Original Prompt<br/>No Context Augmentation]
    UsePromptOnly --> End1([Context Retrieval Complete])
    
    CheckResults -->|Results Found| FilterSimilarity{Similarity Score<br/>> Threshold?<br/>Threshold: 0.7}
    
    FilterSimilarity -->|No - Low Relevance| UsePromptOnly
    
    FilterSimilarity -->|Yes - High Relevance| RankResults[Rank Results by<br/>Relevance Score]
    RankResults --> SelectTopK[Select Top K Documents<br/>K = 5 default, configurable]
    
    SelectTopK --> ExtractContent[Extract Document Content<br/>and Metadata]
    ExtractContent --> FormatContext[Format Context for LLM<br/>Source: doc_title<br/>Content: doc_excerpt]
    
    FormatContext --> CheckTokenLimit{Total Context<br/>Within Token Limit?}
    
    CheckTokenLimit -->|No - Too Large| TruncateContext[Truncate Lower-Ranked Docs<br/>Ensure within model context window]
    TruncateContext --> AugmentPrompt
    
    CheckTokenLimit -->|Yes| AugmentPrompt[Augment Prompt with Context<br/>System: Use provided context<br/>Context: formatted_docs<br/>User: original_query]
    
    AugmentPrompt --> LogRetrieval[Log Context Retrieval<br/>sources: doc_ids<br/>similarity_scores: scores]
    LogRetrieval --> End2([Context Retrieval Complete])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFA500
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
```

**Vector Database Operations**:
- **Embedding Model**: OpenAI `text-embedding-ada-002` or `text-embedding-3-small`
- **Index Type**: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) for fast approximate nearest neighbor search
- **Metadata Filtering**: Support for filtering by document type, date range, user permissions
- **Incremental Updates**: New embeddings indexed asynchronously without service interruption

#### 4.2.4.3 AI Conversation State Persistence

All AI interactions are persisted for conversation continuity, analytics, and compliance:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConversationCreated: User Initiates Chat
    
    ConversationCreated --> AwaitingInput: Initial State
    
    AwaitingInput --> ProcessingPrompt: User Sends Message
    ProcessingPrompt --> GeneratingResponse: Context Retrieved
    GeneratingResponse --> StreamingResponse: LLM Generating
    StreamingResponse --> AwaitingInput: Response Complete<br/>(Store in MongoDB)
    
    AwaitingInput --> ConversationPaused: User Inactive > 15 min
    ConversationPaused --> AwaitingInput: User Returns
    ConversationPaused --> ConversationArchived: Inactive > 7 days
    
    AwaitingInput --> ConversationClosed: User Ends Session
    ConversationClosed --> ConversationArchived: Archive After 30 days
    
    ConversationArchived --> [*]
    
    note right of ProcessingPrompt
        State Actions:
        - Log prompt timestamp
        - Increment message count
        - Update last_active timestamp
    end note
    
    note right of StreamingResponse
        State Actions:
        - Store each message turn
        - Track token usage
        - Update conversation metadata
        - Index for future retrieval
    end note
    
    note right of ConversationArchived
        Archive Actions:
        - Move to cold storage (S3)
        - Remove from active DB
        - Retain metadata for analytics
        - Purge PII if required
    end note
```

**Conversation Data Model**:
```json
{
  "conversation_id": "conv_abc123",
  "user_id": "user_xyz789",
  "created_at": "2024-11-06T10:30:00Z",
  "last_active": "2024-11-06T11:45:00Z",
  "status": "active|paused|closed|archived",
  "messages": [
    {
      "message_id": "msg_001",
      "role": "user|assistant|system",
      "content": "message text",
      "timestamp": "2024-11-06T10:30:15Z",
      "metadata": {
        "model": "gpt-4",
        "tokens": 150,
        "latency_ms": 2340,
        "context_sources": ["doc_1", "doc_2"]
      }
    }
  ],
  "total_tokens": 4500,
  "message_count": 12
}
```

### 4.2.5 File Upload and Storage Flow

#### 4.2.5.1 Pre-Signed URL Generation for Direct S3 Upload

To minimize server load and optimize upload performance, the system implements direct client-to-S3 uploads using pre-signed URLs:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant API as Flask API
    participant Auth as Auth Middleware
    participant S3 as AWS S3
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant CloudWatch
    
    Note over User,CloudWatch: Secure File Upload Flow with Pre-Signed URLs
    
    User->>Client: 1. Select File to Upload<br/>(file.pdf, 2.5 MB)
    Client->>Client: 2. Validate File Client-Side<br/>(type, size, name)
    
    alt Validation Failed
        Client->>User: 2a. Display Validation Error<br/>"File size exceeds 10 MB limit"
    else Validation Passed
        Client->>API: 3. Request Pre-Signed Upload URL<br/>POST /api/files/upload-url<br/>Authorization: Bearer {JWT}<br/>Body: {filename, content_type, file_size}
        
        API->>Auth: 4. Validate JWT Token
        Auth->>API: 5. Token Valid (user_id)
        
        API->>API: 6. Validate Upload Request<br/>(file type allowed, size within limits)
        
        alt Upload Request Invalid
            API->>Client: 6a. Return 400 Bad Request<br/>error: "File type not allowed"
        else Upload Request Valid
            API->>S3: 7. Generate Pre-Signed Upload URL<br/>s3_client.generate_presigned_post(<br/>  Bucket: uploads-bucket,<br/>  Key: user_id/uuid/filename,<br/>  ExpiresIn: 300 seconds,<br/>  Conditions: [size, content-type]<br/>)
            
            S3->>API: 8. Return Pre-Signed URL and Fields<br/>(url, fields: {key, policy, signature})
            
            API->>DB: 9. Create Pending Upload Record<br/>{upload_id, user_id, filename, status: pending}
            
            API->>Client: 10. Return Pre-Signed URL<br/>(url, fields, upload_id, expires_in: 300)
            
            Client->>S3: 11. Direct HTTPS Upload to S3<br/>PUT to pre-signed URL<br/>(file binary data)
            
            Note over Client,S3: Upload Progress Tracking
            
            loop Upload Chunks
                Client->>User: Show Upload Progress<br/>(X% complete)
            end
            
            alt Upload Successful
                S3->>Client: 12a. 200 OK (Upload Complete)<br/>ETag: file_etag
                
                Client->>API: 13. Confirm Upload Success<br/>POST /api/files/confirm<br/>Body: {upload_id, etag, s3_key}
                
                API->>S3: 14. Verify File Exists<br/>HEAD s3://bucket/key
                S3->>API: 15. File Confirmed (metadata)
                
                API->>DB: 16. Update Upload Record<br/>{status: completed, s3_key, etag,<br/>upload_completed_at, file_metadata}
                
                API->>CloudWatch: 17. Log Upload Success<br/>(user_id, file_size, duration)
                
                API->>Client: 18. Return File Metadata<br/>{file_id, s3_key, download_url}
                
                Client->>User: 19. Display Upload Success<br/>"File uploaded successfully"
                
            else Upload Failed
                S3->>Client: 12b. 4xx/5xx Error<br/>Upload Failed
                
                Client->>API: 13b. Report Upload Failure<br/>POST /api/files/fail<br/>Body: {upload_id, error_code}
                
                API->>DB: 14b. Update Upload Record<br/>{status: failed, error_message}
                
                API->>CloudWatch: 15b. Log Upload Failure<br/>(user_id, error_code)
                
                API->>Client: 16b. Return Error Response
                Client->>User: 17b. Display Upload Error<br/>"Upload failed. Please retry."
            end
        end
    end
```

**Pre-Signed URL Security Controls**:
- **Time-Limited**: URLs expire after 5 minutes (300 seconds)
- **Condition-Based**: Enforced file size and content-type restrictions
- **User-Specific Paths**: Files stored in user-scoped S3 key prefixes (`user_id/uuid/filename`)
- **Signature Validation**: S3 validates signature before accepting upload
- **No Server Passthrough**: File data never touches application servers, reducing bandwidth and latency

#### 4.2.5.2 File Download and Access Control

File downloads implement authorization checks and support for both direct S3 access and CDN delivery:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Download Request]) --> ValidateAuth[Validate JWT Token<br/>Extract user_id]
    
    ValidateAuth --> AuthValid{Token<br/>Valid?}
    
    AuthValid -->|No| Reject1[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>error: invalid_token]
    Reject1 --> End1([Request Rejected])
    
    AuthValid -->|Yes| QueryMetadata[Query MongoDB for File Metadata<br/>db.files.findOne file_id]
    
    QueryMetadata --> FileExists{File<br/>Exists?}
    
    FileExists -->|No| Reject2[Return 404 Not Found<br/>error: file_not_found]
    Reject2 --> End1
    
    FileExists -->|Yes| CheckPermission{User Has<br/>Access Permission?}
    
    CheckPermission -->|No - Unauthorized| Reject3[Return 403 Forbidden<br/>error: access_denied]
    Reject3 --> End1
    
    CheckPermission -->|Yes - Authorized| CheckCache{File in<br/>CDN Cache?}
    
    CheckCache -->|Yes| ReturnCDN[Return CDN URL<br/>CloudFront signed URL]
    ReturnCDN --> LogAccess1[Log File Access<br/>user_id, file_id, source: CDN]
    LogAccess1 --> End2([Redirect to CDN])
    
    CheckCache -->|No| GenerateS3URL[Generate Pre-Signed Download URL<br/>s3_client.generate_presigned_url<br/>GET object, ExpiresIn: 3600s]
    
    GenerateS3URL --> ReturnS3[Return Pre-Signed S3 URL<br/>expires_in: 3600]
    ReturnS3 --> LogAccess2[Log File Access<br/>user_id, file_id, source: S3]
    LogAccess2 --> End3([Redirect to S3])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style End3 fill:#90EE90
    style Reject1 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject2 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Reject3 fill:#FF6B6B
```

**File Access Control Rules**:
- **Owner Access**: File uploader always has full access (read, delete)
- **Shared Access**: Files can be shared with specific users or made public
- **Role-Based Access**: Administrative users have access to all files within their scope
- **Audit Logging**: All file access events logged for compliance

#### 4.2.5.3 File Processing and Virus Scanning

Files undergo security scanning and optional processing after upload:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S3
    participant Lambda as AWS Lambda<br/>(S3 Trigger)
    participant Scanner as ClamAV Scanner<br/>(or AWS GuardDuty)
    participant Processor as File Processor<br/>(Thumbnail, OCR, etc.)
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant SNS as AWS SNS<br/>(Notifications)
    participant Client
    
    Note over S3,Client: Asynchronous Post-Upload Processing
    
    S3->>Lambda: 1. S3 Event Trigger<br/>ObjectCreated:Put
    
    Lambda->>Lambda: 2. Extract Event Metadata<br/>(bucket, key, size)
    
    Lambda->>Scanner: 3. Initiate Virus Scan<br/>scan_file(s3_uri)
    
    Scanner->>S3: 4. Download File Stream
    S3->>Scanner: 5. File Data
    Scanner->>Scanner: 6. Scan for Malware
    
    alt File Clean
        Scanner->>Lambda: 7a. Scan Result: CLEAN
        
        Lambda->>DB: 8. Update File Record<br/>{scan_status: clean, scan_timestamp}
        
        alt File Type Requires Processing
            Lambda->>Processor: 9a. Invoke Processing<br/>(e.g., generate thumbnail for image)
            Processor->>S3: 9b. Upload Processed Assets<br/>(thumbnail, preview)
            Processor->>Lambda: 9c. Processing Complete
            Lambda->>DB: 9d. Store Processed Asset URLs
        end
        
        Lambda->>SNS: 10. Publish Success Notification<br/>Topic: file-processing-complete
        SNS->>Client: 11. Push Notification<br/>"File ready for use"
        
    else File Infected
        Scanner->>Lambda: 7b. Scan Result: INFECTED<br/>virus: malware_type
        
        Lambda->>S3: 8b. Delete Infected File<br/>DELETE s3://bucket/key
        
        Lambda->>DB: 9b. Update File Record<br/>{scan_status: infected, deleted: true}
        
        Lambda->>SNS: 10b. Publish Alert Notification<br/>Topic: file-security-alert
        SNS->>Client: 11b. Alert Notification<br/>"File removed: security threat detected"
        
        Lambda->>Lambda: 12. Log Security Incident<br/>(user_id, file_id, threat_type)
    end
```

## 4.3 DEVELOPMENT AND DEPLOYMENT PROCESSES

### 4.3.1 Continuous Integration Pipeline

#### 4.3.1.1 Code Quality Validation Workflow

The CI pipeline enforces code quality standards through automated linting, type checking, and style validation:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Git Push / Pull Request]) --> Trigger[GitHub Actions Workflow Triggered<br/>on: push, pull_request]
    
    Trigger --> Checkout[Checkout Code<br/>actions/checkout@v3]
    
    Checkout --> SetupEnv{Programming<br/>Language?}
    
    SetupEnv -->|Python Backend| SetupPython[Setup Python 3.11<br/>actions/setup-python@v4]
    SetupEnv -->|TypeScript Frontend| SetupNode[Setup Node.js 18<br/>actions/setup-node@v3]
    
    SetupPython --> InstallPyDeps[Install Python Dependencies<br/>pip install -r requirements.txt<br/>pip install -r requirements-dev.txt]
    SetupNode --> InstallNodeDeps[Install Node Dependencies<br/>npm ci --prefer-offline]
    
    InstallPyDeps --> PyLint[Run Python Linting<br/>flake8 src/ --max-line-length=100]
    InstallNodeDeps --> NodeLint[Run ESLint<br/>npm run lint]
    
    PyLint --> PyLintPass{Linting<br/>Passed?}
    NodeLint --> NodeLintPass{Linting<br/>Passed?}
    
    PyLintPass -->|No| FailPyLint[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Linting Errors Found<br/>Annotate PR with errors]
    NodeLintPass -->|No| FailNodeLint[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Linting Errors Found<br/>Annotate PR with errors]
    
    FailPyLint --> End1([Build Failed])
    FailNodeLint --> End1
    
    PyLintPass -->|Yes| PyTypeCheck[Run Type Checking<br/>mypy src/ --strict]
    NodeLintPass -->|Yes| NodeTypeCheck[Run Type Checking<br/>npx tsc --noEmit]
    
    PyTypeCheck --> PyTypePass{Type Check<br/>Passed?}
    NodeTypeCheck --> NodeTypePass{Type Check<br/>Passed?}
    
    PyTypePass -->|No| FailPyType[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Type Errors Found]
    NodeTypePass -->|No| FailNodeType[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Type Errors Found]
    
    FailPyType --> End1
    FailNodeType --> End1
    
    PyTypePass -->|Yes| PyFormat[Check Code Formatting<br/>black --check src/]
    NodeTypePass -->|Yes| NodeFormat[Check Code Formatting<br/>prettier --check src/]
    
    PyFormat --> PyFormatPass{Formatting<br/>Correct?}
    NodeFormat --> NodeFormatPass{Formatting<br/>Correct?}
    
    PyFormatPass -->|No| FailPyFormat[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Code Not Formatted<br/>Run: black src/]
    NodeFormatPass -->|No| FailNodeFormat[❌ Pipeline Failed<br/>Code Not Formatted<br/>Run: prettier --write src/]
    
    FailPyFormat --> End1
    FailNodeFormat --> End1
    
    PyFormatPass -->|Yes| ProceedPyTest[✅ Code Quality Passed<br/>Proceed to Testing]
    NodeFormatPass -->|Yes| ProceedNodeTest[✅ Code Quality Passed<br/>Proceed to Testing]
    
    ProceedPyTest --> End2([Quality Gate Passed])
    ProceedNodeTest --> End2
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style FailPyLint fill:#FF6B6B
    style FailNodeLint fill:#FF6B6B
    style FailPyType fill:#FF6B6B
    style FailNodeType fill:#FF6B6B
    style FailPyFormat fill:#FF6B6B
    style FailNodeFormat fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Code Quality Standards**:
- **Python Linting**: Flake8 with max line length 100, PEP 8 compliance required
- **Python Type Checking**: mypy in strict mode, all functions must have type annotations
- **Python Formatting**: Black formatter with default settings
- **TypeScript Linting**: ESLint with Airbnb style guide, React best practices
- **TypeScript Type Checking**: Strict TypeScript configuration with `noImplicitAny`
- **JavaScript Formatting**: Prettier with default settings

#### 4.3.1.2 Automated Testing Workflow

Comprehensive automated testing ensures code correctness and prevents regressions:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant GH as GitHub Actions
    participant Runner as CI Runner
    participant TestEnv as Test Environment<br/>(Docker Compose)
    participant Backend as Backend Tests<br/>(pytest)
    participant Frontend as Frontend Tests<br/>(Jest)
    participant Coverage as Coverage Report<br/>(Codecov)
    
    Note over GH,Coverage: Automated Test Execution Pipeline
    
    GH->>Runner: 1. Trigger Test Workflow<br/>(after code quality passes)
    
    Runner->>TestEnv: 2. Start Test Dependencies<br/>docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up
    
    TestEnv->>TestEnv: 3. Initialize Services<br/>- MongoDB (testdb)<br/>- Redis (test instance)<br/>- Mock Auth0 server
    
    TestEnv->>Runner: 4. Services Ready
    
    par Backend Testing
        Runner->>Backend: 5a. Execute Backend Tests<br/>pytest tests/ -v --cov=src --cov-report=xml
        
        Backend->>Backend: Unit Tests<br/>(test individual functions/classes)
        Backend->>Backend: Integration Tests<br/>(test component interactions)
        Backend->>Backend: API Tests<br/>(test endpoint behaviors)
        
        Backend->>Runner: 6a. Test Results<br/>(passed: X, failed: Y, coverage: Z%)
        
    and Frontend Testing
        Runner->>Frontend: 5b. Execute Frontend Tests<br/>npm test -- --coverage --watchAll=false
        
        Frontend->>Frontend: Unit Tests<br/>(test components, utilities)
        Frontend->>Frontend: Integration Tests<br/>(test component interactions)
        Frontend->>Frontend: Snapshot Tests<br/>(test UI rendering)
        
        Frontend->>Runner: 6b. Test Results<br/>(passed: X, failed: Y, coverage: Z%)
    end
    
    alt All Tests Passed
        Runner->>Coverage: 7a. Upload Coverage Reports<br/>codecov/codecov-action@v3
        Coverage->>Coverage: 8. Analyze Coverage<br/>- Generate trend reports<br/>- Check coverage thresholds
        Coverage->>GH: 9. Post Coverage Comment on PR<br/>"Coverage: 85% (+2%)"
        Runner->>GH: 10. ✅ Test Pipeline Passed
        
    else Any Tests Failed
        Runner->>GH: 7b. ❌ Test Pipeline Failed<br/>Annotate failing tests
        GH->>GH: 8b. Block PR Merge<br/>(branch protection rules)
    end
    
    Runner->>TestEnv: 11. Teardown Test Environment<br/>docker-compose down -v
```

**Testing Strategy**:
- **Unit Tests**: 80% minimum coverage for critical business logic
- **Integration Tests**: Test component interactions and data flow
- **API Tests**: Validate all endpoint behaviors, error handling, authentication
- **Test Isolation**: Each test runs in isolated environment with fresh database
- **Test Data**: Factories and fixtures for consistent test data generation
- **Mocking**: External services (Auth0, LLM providers) mocked in tests

#### 4.3.1.3 Coverage Reporting and Quality Gates

Test coverage is tracked and enforced to maintain code quality:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Test Execution Complete]) --> UploadCoverage[Upload Coverage Reports<br/>Backend: coverage.xml<br/>Frontend: coverage/lcov.info]
    
    UploadCoverage --> Codecov[Process in Codecov<br/>Analyze line/branch coverage]
    
    Codecov --> CheckTotal{Total Project<br/>Coverage >= 80%?}
    
    CheckTotal -->|No| CheckDiff{Diff Coverage<br/>>= 90%?}
    
    CheckDiff -->|No| FailCoverage[❌ Coverage Check Failed<br/>Status: failure<br/>Comment: Coverage below threshold]
    FailCoverage --> BlockMerge[Block PR Merge<br/>Require coverage improvement]
    BlockMerge --> End1([Pipeline Failed])
    
    CheckDiff -->|Yes| WarnCoverage[⚠️ Coverage Warning<br/>Status: success<br/>Comment: Total coverage low, but diff covered]
    WarnCoverage --> AllowMerge[Allow PR Merge<br/>With warning annotation]
    AllowMerge --> End2([Pipeline Passed with Warning])
    
    CheckTotal -->|Yes| PassCoverage[✅ Coverage Check Passed<br/>Status: success<br/>Post coverage report]
    PassCoverage --> End3([Pipeline Passed])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#FFA500
    style End3 fill:#90EE90
    style FailCoverage fill:#FF6B6B
    style WarnCoverage fill:#FFA500
```

**Coverage Thresholds**:
- **Total Project Coverage**: 80% minimum (line coverage)
- **Diff Coverage**: 90% minimum (new/changed code must be well-tested)
- **Critical Paths**: 100% coverage required for authentication, authorization, payment processing
- **Exclusions**: Configuration files, migrations, generated code excluded from coverage

### 4.3.2 Container Build and Registry Management

#### 4.3.2.1 Docker Image Build and Optimization

Container images are built using multi-stage builds for optimization and security:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Merge to Main Branch]) --> TriggerBuild["GitHub Actions: Build Workflow<br/>on: push to main"]
    
    TriggerBuild --> Checkout["Checkout Repository<br/>Full Git history for versioning"]
    
    Checkout --> AWSAuth["Configure AWS Credentials<br/>OIDC or AWS Access Key"]
    
    AWSAuth --> ECRLogin["Login to Amazon ECR<br/>aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v1"]
    
    ECRLogin --> BuildContext["Prepare Build Context<br/>Copy source code, dependencies"]
    
    BuildContext --> MultiStage["Multi-Stage Docker Build"]
    
    subgraph "Multi-Stage Build Process"
        Stage1["Stage 1: Base Dependencies<br/>FROM python:3.11-slim<br/>Install system packages"]
        Stage2["Stage 2: Build Stage<br/>Copy requirements.txt<br/>pip install dependencies"]
        Stage3["Stage 3: Runtime Stage<br/>Copy only runtime artifacts<br/>Create non-root user"]
        
        Stage1 --> Stage2
        Stage2 --> Stage3
    end
    
    MultiStage --> OptimizeImage["Image Optimization<br/>- Layer caching<br/>- Remove build artifacts<br/>- Minimize layer count"]
    
    OptimizeImage --> TagImage["Tag Image<br/>- SHA: git commit hash<br/>- latest: most recent build<br/>- vVERSION: semantic version"]
    
    TagImage --> ScanImage["Scan Image for Vulnerabilities<br/>Trivy / Snyk / ECR scanning"]
    
    ScanImage --> VulnCheck{"Critical<br/>Vulnerabilities?"}
    
    VulnCheck -->|Yes| FailBuild["❌ Build Failed<br/>Security vulnerabilities detected<br/>Notify developers"]
    FailBuild --> End1([Build Failed])
    
    VulnCheck -->|No| PushECR["Push Images to ECR<br/>docker push all tags"]
    
    PushECR --> UpdateManifest["Update Deployment Manifests<br/>- ECS task definition<br/>- Kubernetes deployment YAML"]
    
    UpdateManifest --> NotifySuccess["✅ Build Complete<br/>Post to Slack/Teams<br/>Image: ECR_URI:TAG"]
    
    NotifySuccess --> End2([Build Successful])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style FailBuild fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Docker Build Best Practices**:
- **Multi-Stage Builds**: Separate build and runtime stages, final image contains only runtime dependencies
- **Layer Caching**: Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changed
- **Minimal Base Images**: Use `slim` or `alpine` variants to reduce image size and attack surface
- **Security Scanning**: Automated vulnerability scanning before pushing to registry
- **Image Signing**: Optionally sign images with Docker Content Trust or Sigstore

#### 4.3.2.2 ECR Push and Tag Strategy

Container images follow a comprehensive tagging strategy for traceability and rollback:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Image Tagging Strategy"
        Image[Built Docker Image]
        
        Image --> Tag1[Tag 1: SHA<br/>backend-service:a1b2c3d]
        Image --> Tag2[Tag 2: latest<br/>backend-service:latest]
        Image --> Tag3[Tag 3: Semantic Version<br/>backend-service:v1.2.3]
        Image --> Tag4[Tag 4: Environment<br/>backend-service:staging]
    end
    
    subgraph "Push to ECR"
        Tag1 --> ECR1[ECR Repository<br/>123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com]
        Tag2 --> ECR1
        Tag3 --> ECR1
        Tag4 --> ECR1
    end
    
    subgraph "Image Lifecycle Management"
        ECR1 --> Lifecycle[ECR Lifecycle Policy]
        Lifecycle --> Keep1[Keep: latest<br/>Retain: always]
        Lifecycle --> Keep2[Keep: tagged versions<br/>Retain: 90 days]
        Lifecycle --> Keep3[Keep: SHA tags<br/>Retain: 30 days]
        Lifecycle --> Delete[Delete: untagged images<br/>After: 7 days]
    end
    
    style Image fill:#E8F4F8
    style ECR1 fill:#FF9900
```

**Tagging Strategy**:
- **Immutable Tags**: SHA-based tags are immutable and reference-specific builds
- **Mutable Tags**: `latest` and environment tags are mutable and point to current versions
- **Semantic Versioning**: Version tags follow SemVer (v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH})
- **Retention Policy**: Automatic cleanup of old images to manage storage costs

#### 4.3.2.3 Image Vulnerability Scanning

All container images undergo automated security scanning:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Build as Build Pipeline
    participant ECR as Amazon ECR
    participant Scanner as Trivy / ECR Scanner
    participant SecurityDB as Vulnerability Database
    participant Notify as Notification System
    participant Jira as Jira / Issue Tracker
    
    Build->>ECR: 1. Push Docker Image<br/>image:tag
    
    ECR->>Scanner: 2. Trigger Scan on Push<br/>(automatic ECR scanning enabled)
    
    Scanner->>ECR: 3. Download Image Layers
    ECR->>Scanner: 4. Return Image Layers
    
    Scanner->>SecurityDB: 5. Query Known Vulnerabilities<br/>(CVE database, vendor advisories)
    SecurityDB->>Scanner: 6. Return Vulnerability Data
    
    Scanner->>Scanner: 7. Analyze Image<br/>- OS packages<br/>- Language dependencies<br/>- Application binaries
    
    Scanner->>Scanner: 8. Classify Vulnerabilities<br/>- Critical<br/>- High<br/>- Medium<br/>- Low
    
    alt Critical or High Vulnerabilities Found
        Scanner->>Notify: 9a. Send Alert<br/>Severity: critical<br/>Vulnerabilities: CVE-XXXX-XXXX
        
        Notify->>Jira: 10a. Create Security Ticket<br/>Priority: P1 (Critical) or P2 (High)<br/>Assignee: Security team
        
        Notify->>Build: 11a. Fail Build Pipeline<br/>❌ Security scan failed
        
        Scanner->>ECR: 12a. Tag Image as Vulnerable<br/>scan_status: failed
        
    else Only Medium/Low Vulnerabilities
        Scanner->>Notify: 9b. Send Info Notification<br/>Vulnerabilities: non-critical
        
        Notify->>Jira: 10b. Create Backlog Ticket<br/>Priority: P3 (Medium) or P4 (Low)
        
        Scanner->>ECR: 11b. Tag Image as Pass with Warnings<br/>scan_status: passed_with_warnings
        
        Scanner->>Build: 12b. Continue Pipeline<br/>✅ Security scan passed
        
    else No Vulnerabilities
        Scanner->>ECR: 9c. Tag Image as Clean<br/>scan_status: passed
        
        Scanner->>Build: 10c. Continue Pipeline<br/>✅ Security scan passed (clean)
    end
```

### 4.3.3 Deployment Orchestration

#### 4.3.3.1 Environment Promotion Workflow

The system implements a multi-environment deployment strategy with promotion gates:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Build Complete]) --> DevDeploy[Auto-Deploy to Development<br/>Branch: develop<br/>Environment: dev.6nove4.com]

    WaitMerge --> MergeMain
    
    MergeMain -->|Yes| StagingDeploy[Auto-Deploy to Staging<br/>Branch: main<br/>Environment: staging.6nove4.com]
    
    StagingDeploy --> StagingTest[Automated Testing in Staging<br/>- Full regression suite<br/>- Performance tests<br/>- Security scans]
    
    StagingTest --> StagingPass{Staging Tests<br/>Passed?}
    
    StagingPass -->|No| NotifyStgFail[Notify Team<br/>❌ Staging deployment failed<br/>Rollback to previous version]

    UATApproval -->|No| UATFeedback[Collect UAT Feedback<br/>Create issues in backlog]
    UATFeedback --> End1
    
    UATApproval -->|Yes| ProdApproval{Manual Production<br/>Approval?}
    
    ProdApproval -->|No| WaitApproval[Wait for Approval<br/>Product Owner / Release Manager]

    ProdApproval -->|Yes| ProdDeploy[Deploy to Production<br/>Environment: 6nove4.com<br/>Strategy: Blue-Green or Rolling]

    ProdRollback --> Incident[Create Incident<br/>Post-mortem analysis]

    ProdHealth -->|Yes| ProdSuccess[✅ Production Deployment Successful<br/>Update status page<br/>Notify stakeholders]
```
