| **Development** | dev.6nove4.com | Push to `develop` | No | Feature development and testing |
| **Staging** | staging.6nove4.com | Merge to `main` | No | Pre-production validation and UAT |
| **Production** | 6nove4.com | Manual approval | Yes | Live production system |

#### 4.3.3.2 Rolling Update Deployment Strategy

The recommended deployment strategy uses ECS/EKS rolling updates for zero-downtime deployments:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CD as CD Pipeline
    participant ECS as AWS ECS Cluster
    participant ALB as Load Balancer
    participant OldTask as Old Task Containers<br/>(Version 1.0)
    participant NewTask as New Task Containers<br/>(Version 1.1)
    participant Monitor as CloudWatch<br/>Health Checks
    
    Note over CD,Monitor: Rolling Update Deployment Process
    
    CD->>ECS: 1. Update Task Definition<br/>New image: backend:v1.1
    
    ECS->>ECS: 2. Register New Task Definition<br/>Revision: 5
    
    ECS->>NewTask: 3. Launch New Task Instance<br/>Desired count: 1 of 4
    
    NewTask->>NewTask: 4. Container Starting<br/>Initialize application
    
    NewTask->>Monitor: 5. Health Check Request<br/>GET /health
    
    alt Health Check Passed
        Monitor->>ECS: 6a. Container Healthy<br/>Status: running
        
        ECS->>ALB: 7. Register New Task with ALB<br/>Target Group: backend-tg
        
        ALB->>NewTask: 8. Send Test Traffic<br/>Verify responsiveness
        
        NewTask->>ALB: 9. Successful Responses
        
        ECS->>ECS: 10. Increment Desired Count<br/>Launch next new task (2 of 4)
        
        Note over ECS,NewTask: Repeat for each task instance
        
        loop Until All Tasks Updated
            ECS->>NewTask: Launch Additional New Task
            NewTask->>Monitor: Health Check
            Monitor->>ECS: Healthy
            ECS->>ALB: Register with ALB
        end
        
        ECS->>ALB: 11. Deregister Old Tasks<br/>Stop sending new connections
        
        ALB->>OldTask: 12. Drain Existing Connections<br/>Wait for active requests to complete<br/>Timeout: 300 seconds
        
        OldTask->>ALB: 13. All Connections Closed
        
        ECS->>OldTask: 14. Stop Old Task Containers<br/>Graceful shutdown
        
        ECS->>CD: 15. ✅ Rolling Update Complete<br/>All tasks running version 1.1
        
    else Health Check Failed
        Monitor->>ECS: 6b. Container Unhealthy<br/>Status: unhealthy
        
        ECS->>NewTask: 7b. Stop Failed Container<br/>Terminate unhealthy task
        
        ECS->>CD: 8b. ❌ Deployment Failed<br/>Rollback: revert to task definition revision 4
        
        CD->>ECS: 9b. Restore Previous Task Definition
        
        ECS->>CD: 10b. Rollback Complete<br/>All tasks running version 1.0
    end
```

**Rolling Update Configuration**:
- **Minimum Healthy Percentage**: 50% (at least half of tasks must remain healthy during update)
- **Maximum Percentage**: 200% (can run up to double capacity during update for faster rollout)
- **Health Check Grace Period**: 60 seconds (allow container startup time before health checks)
- **Deregistration Delay**: 300 seconds (wait for existing connections to complete before stopping)

#### 4.3.3.3 Blue-Green Deployment Strategy (Alternative)

For critical deployments requiring instant rollback capability, blue-green deployment is available:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Initiate Blue-Green Deploy]) --> PrepGreen[Prepare Green Environment<br/>Full duplicate of production Blue]
    
    PrepGreen --> DeployGreen[Deploy New Version to Green<br/>All infrastructure and services]
    
    DeployGreen --> TestGreen[Test Green Environment<br/>- Smoke tests<br/>- Health checks<br/>- Performance validation]
    
    TestGreen --> GreenHealthy{Green Environment<br/>Healthy?}
    
    GreenHealthy -->|No| DestroyGreen[Destroy Green Environment<br/>Rollback to Blue<br/>Investigate failures]
    DestroyGreen --> End1([Deployment Failed])
    
    GreenHealthy -->|Yes| SwitchTraffic[Switch Traffic to Green<br/>Update DNS/Load Balancer<br/>Route: Blue → Green]
    
    SwitchTraffic --> MonitorSwitch[Monitor Post-Switch<br/>- Error rates<br/>- Latency<br/>- User reports<br/>Duration: 30-60 minutes]
    
    MonitorSwitch --> SwitchSuccess{Green Environment<br/>Stable?}
    
    SwitchSuccess -->|No| InstantRollback[Instant Rollback<br/>Switch traffic back to Blue<br/>Incident investigation]
    InstantRollback --> End1
    
    SwitchSuccess -->|Yes| DestroyBlue[Destroy Blue Environment<br/>Or retain as backup]
    
    DestroyBlue --> PromoteGreen[Promote Green to Blue<br/>Green becomes new production baseline]
    
    PromoteGreen --> End2([Deployment Successful])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style DestroyGreen fill:#FF6B6B
    style InstantRollback fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Blue-Green Deployment Advantages**:
- **Instant Rollback**: Switch traffic back to blue environment in seconds if issues detected
- **Full Testing**: Test complete production environment before switching traffic
- **Zero Downtime**: No service interruption during deployment
- **Database Challenges**: Requires careful schema migration planning for database compatibility

### 4.3.4 Infrastructure Provisioning

#### 4.3.4.1 Terraform Infrastructure as Code Workflow

All infrastructure is managed through Terraform for consistency, version control, and repeatability:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Infrastructure Change Required]) --> CreateBranch[Create Feature Branch<br/>feature/add-redis-cluster]
    
    CreateBranch --> ModifyTF[Modify Terraform Files<br/>- Add/modify .tf files<br/>- Update variables<br/>- Adjust outputs]
    
    ModifyTF --> TFValidate[Validate Terraform Syntax<br/>terraform validate]
    
    TFValidate --> ValidPass{Validation<br/>Passed?}
    
    ValidPass -->|No| FixErrors[Fix Syntax Errors<br/>Review error messages]
    FixErrors --> TFValidate
    
    ValidPass -->|Yes| TFFormat[Format Terraform Code<br/>terraform fmt -recursive]
    
    TFFormat --> TFLint[Run Terraform Linting<br/>tflint --config .tflint.hcl]
    
    TFLint --> LintPass{Linting<br/>Passed?}
    
    LintPass -->|No| FixLint[Fix Linting Issues<br/>Best practices violations]
    FixLint --> TFLint
    
    LintPass -->|Yes| TFPlan[Generate Terraform Plan<br/>terraform plan -out=tfplan]
    
    TFPlan --> ReviewPlan[Review Plan Output<br/>- Resources to add<br/>- Resources to modify<br/>- Resources to destroy]
    
    ReviewPlan --> PlanApproved{Plan<br/>Reviewed and Approved?}
    
    PlanApproved -->|No| ModifyTF
    
    PlanApproved -->|Yes| CommitPush[Commit and Push<br/>git commit & git push origin]
    
    CommitPush --> OpenPR[Open Pull Request<br/>Include terraform plan output<br/>Request infrastructure review]
    
    OpenPR --> PRReview{PR Approved<br/>by Infrastructure Team?}
    
    PRReview -->|No| AddressComments[Address Review Comments<br/>Modify Terraform files]
    AddressComments --> ModifyTF
    
    PRReview -->|Yes| MergePR[Merge PR to Main<br/>Trigger Terraform Apply workflow]
    
    MergePR --> TFApply[Terraform Apply<br/>terraform apply tfplan<br/>-auto-approve flag in CI]
    
    TFApply --> ApplySuccess{Apply<br/>Successful?}
    
    ApplySuccess -->|No| TFError[Terraform Apply Failed<br/>- Review error logs<br/>- Identify failed resources<br/>- Manual intervention required]
    TFError --> CreateIncident[Create Infrastructure Incident<br/>Assign to infrastructure team]
    CreateIncident --> End1([Infrastructure Change Failed])
    
    ApplySuccess -->|Yes| UpdateState[Update Terraform State<br/>terraform state push<br/>Store in S3 backend]
    
    UpdateState --> VerifyInfra[Verify Infrastructure<br/>- Check AWS console<br/>- Run health checks<br/>- Validate connectivity]
    
    VerifyInfra --> InfraHealthy{Infrastructure<br/>Healthy?}
    
    InfraHealthy -->|No| RollbackInfra[Rollback Infrastructure<br/>terraform apply with previous state<br/>or manual intervention]
    RollbackInfra --> End1
    
    InfraHealthy -->|Yes| UpdateDocs[Update Infrastructure Docs<br/>- Architecture diagrams<br/>- Resource inventory<br/>- Cost tracking]
    
    UpdateDocs --> End2([Infrastructure Change Complete])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style TFError fill:#FF6B6B
    style RollbackInfra fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Terraform Best Practices**:
- **Remote State**: Terraform state stored in S3 with DynamoDB locking
- **State Encryption**: State file encrypted at rest with AWS KMS
- **Modular Structure**: Reusable modules for common infrastructure patterns
- **Environment Separation**: Separate state files for dev, staging, production
- **Workspace Usage**: Terraform workspaces for environment isolation

#### 4.3.4.2 Terraform State Management

State management is critical for infrastructure consistency and team collaboration:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant TF as Terraform CLI
    participant S3 as S3 State Backend<br/>(terraform-state-bucket)
    participant DDB as DynamoDB Lock Table<br/>(terraform-locks)
    participant AWS as AWS Resources
    
    Note over Dev,AWS: Terraform State Locking and Management
    
    Dev->>TF: 1. terraform plan<br/>or terraform apply
    
    TF->>S3: 2. Initialize Backend<br/>Download current state
    S3->>TF: 3. Return State File<br/>(current infrastructure state)
    
    TF->>DDB: 4. Acquire State Lock<br/>PutItem: {LockID: state_path, Operation: terraform plan}
    
    alt Lock Acquired
        DDB->>TF: 5a. Lock Acquired<br/>Proceed with operation
        
        TF->>TF: 6. Generate Execution Plan<br/>Compare desired vs current state
        
        TF->>Dev: 7. Display Plan Output<br/>Resources to change
        
        alt Apply Approved
            Dev->>TF: 8a. terraform apply -auto-approve
            
            TF->>AWS: 9. Create/Modify/Destroy Resources<br/>Execute planned changes
            
            AWS->>TF: 10. Resource Operations Complete<br/>Return resource attributes
            
            TF->>TF: 11. Update Local State<br/>Reflect infrastructure changes
            
            TF->>S3: 12. Push Updated State<br/>PutObject: terraform.tfstate
            
            S3->>TF: 13. State Upload Confirmed
            
            TF->>DDB: 14. Release State Lock<br/>DeleteItem: {LockID: state_path}
            
            DDB->>TF: 15. Lock Released
            
            TF->>Dev: 16. ✅ Apply Complete<br/>Resources created/updated
            
        else Apply Cancelled
            Dev->>TF: 8b. Cancel Operation
            TF->>DDB: 9b. Release State Lock
        end
        
    else Lock Unavailable
        DDB->>TF: 5b. Lock Held by Another Process<br/>Locked by: user@timestamp
        
        TF->>Dev: 6b. ❌ Operation Blocked<br/>State locked by another operation<br/>Wait or force-unlock (caution!)
        
        alt Force Unlock (Emergency Only)
            Dev->>TF: 7b. terraform force-unlock {LOCK_ID}
            TF->>DDB: 8b. Delete Lock Entry
            TF->>Dev: 9b. ⚠️ Lock Forcibly Removed<br/>Verify no concurrent operations
        end
    end
```

**State Management Policies**:
- **Backend Configuration**: S3 bucket with versioning enabled for state history
- **State Locking**: DynamoDB table prevents concurrent state modifications
- **Access Control**: IAM policies restrict state access to authorized personnel and CI/CD systems
- **State Inspection**: `terraform state list` and `terraform state show` for resource inspection
- **State Recovery**: S3 versioning enables recovery from accidental state corruption

#### 4.3.4.3 Infrastructure Change Approval Process

Critical infrastructure changes require multi-level approval:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ChangeProposed: Engineer Submits Terraform PR
    
    ChangeProposed --> PeerReview: Automated Checks Pass
    
    PeerReview --> TechLeadReview: Peer Approval Received
    PeerLeadReview --> SecurityReview: Tech Lead Approval
    
    SecurityReview --> RiskAssessment: Security Team Reviews
    
    RiskAssessment --> LowRisk: Low Risk Changes<br/>(e.g., variable updates)
    RiskAssessment --> MediumRisk: Medium Risk Changes<br/>(e.g., new resources)
    RiskAssessment --> HighRisk: High Risk Changes<br/>(e.g., database modifications)
    
    LowRisk --> AutoApproved: Auto-Approve for Low Risk
    AutoApproved --> Scheduled: Schedule Deployment
    
    MediumRisk --> InfraApproval: Infrastructure Team Review
    InfraApproval --> Scheduled
    
    HighRisk --> CABReview: Change Advisory Board<br/>(CAB) Meeting Required
    CABReview --> CABDecision: CAB Reviews<br/>Impact, Rollback Plan
    
    CABDecision --> Approved: CAB Approves
    CABDecision --> Rejected: CAB Rejects
    
    Rejected --> ChangeProposed: Revise and Resubmit
    
    Approved --> Scheduled
    
    Scheduled --> MaintenanceWindow: Wait for Maintenance Window<br/>(if applicable)
    
    MaintenanceWindow --> Executing: Execute Terraform Apply
    
    Executing --> Success: Infrastructure Deployed
    Executing --> Failed: Deployment Failed
    
    Failed --> Rollback: Initiate Rollback
    Rollback --> PostMortem: Analyze Failure
    PostMortem --> [*]
    
    Success --> Verification: Verify Infrastructure Health
    Verification --> Documented: Update Documentation
    Documented --> [*]
    
    note right of CABReview
        CAB Reviews:
        - Business impact
        - Risk assessment
        - Rollback plan
        - Testing strategy
        - Stakeholder notification
    end note
    
    note right of HighRisk
        High Risk Includes:
        - Production database changes
        - Network topology modifications
        - Security policy updates
        - Major version upgrades
    end note
```

## 4.4 REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT PROCESSES

### 4.4.1 Requirements Elicitation Workflow

#### 4.4.1.1 Stakeholder Engagement and Discovery

The requirements gathering process begins with comprehensive stakeholder identification and engagement:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Project Initiation]) --> IdentifyStakeholders[Phase 1: Identify Stakeholders<br/>- Business sponsors<br/>- End users<br/>- Technical teams<br/>- Compliance officers]
    
    IdentifyStakeholders --> ConductInterviews[Conduct Stakeholder Interviews<br/>- Individual sessions<br/>- Group workshops<br/>- Surveys and questionnaires]
    
    ConductInterviews --> DocumentExpectations[Document Stakeholder Expectations<br/>- Business objectives<br/>- Success criteria<br/>- Constraints<br/>- Assumptions]
    
    DocumentExpectations --> DiscoverRequirements[Phase 2: Requirements Discovery<br/>- Analyze business objectives<br/>- Review existing systems<br/>- Conduct user research<br/>- Benchmark competitors]
    
    DiscoverRequirements --> CollectRequirements[Collect Raw Requirements<br/>- Functional needs<br/>- Non-functional requirements<br/>- Technical constraints<br/>- Integration points]
    
    CollectRequirements --> AnalyzeRequirements[Phase 3: Requirements Analysis<br/>- Decompose high-level needs<br/>- Identify dependencies<br/>- Assign priorities<br/>- Resolve conflicts]
    
    AnalyzeRequirements --> ValidateRequirements{Requirements<br/>Validated?}
    
    ValidateRequirements -->|No - Issues Found| ReworkRequirements[Clarify Ambiguities<br/>Resolve conflicts<br/>Re-validate with stakeholders]
    ReworkRequirements --> CollectRequirements
    
    ValidateRequirements -->|Yes| DocumentRequirements[Phase 4: Requirements Documentation<br/>- Populate feature catalog Section 2.3<br/>- Create functional requirements Section 2.4<br/>- Establish traceability Section 2.5<br/>- Map dependencies Section 2.6]
    
    DocumentRequirements --> QualityCheck{Requirements Meet<br/>Quality Criteria?}
    
    QualityCheck -->|No| ImproveQuality[Improve Requirements Quality<br/>Ensure: Complete, Consistent,<br/>Unambiguous, Testable, Traceable]
    ImproveQuality --> DocumentRequirements
    
    QualityCheck -->|Yes| FormalReview[Phase 5: Requirements Approval<br/>- Conduct formal review sessions<br/>- Present to stakeholders<br/>- Address final questions]
    
    FormalReview --> StakeholderApproval{Stakeholder<br/>Sign-Off?}
    
    StakeholderApproval -->|No| CollectFeedback[Collect Stakeholder Feedback<br/>Document objections<br/>Identify revisions needed]
    CollectFeedback --> AnalyzeRequirements
    
    StakeholderApproval -->|Yes| BaselineRequirements[Establish Requirements Baseline<br/>- Version and freeze requirements<br/>- Establish change control<br/>- Transition to development]
    
    BaselineRequirements --> End([Requirements Elicitation Complete])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End fill:#90EE90
```

**Requirements Gathering Techniques**:
- **Interviews**: One-on-one sessions with key stakeholders to understand detailed needs
- **Workshops**: Facilitated group sessions for collaborative requirements definition
- **Surveys**: Structured questionnaires for broad user base input
- **Observation**: Shadowing users to understand actual workflows and pain points
- **Prototyping**: Creating mockups and prototypes to elicit feedback
- **Document Analysis**: Reviewing existing documentation, processes, and system specifications

#### 4.4.1.2 Requirements Quality Assurance

All documented requirements undergo quality validation to ensure they meet established criteria:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Quality Criteria Validation"
        Requirement[Documented Requirement]
        
        Requirement --> Check1{Complete?<br/>All necessary<br/>information included}
        Check1 -->|No| Fail1[❌ Incomplete]
        Check1 -->|Yes| Check2{Consistent?<br/>No conflicts with<br/>other requirements}
        
        Check2 -->|No| Fail2[❌ Inconsistent]
        Check2 -->|Yes| Check3{Unambiguous?<br/>Single clear<br/>interpretation}
        
        Check3 -->|No| Fail3[❌ Ambiguous]
        Check3 -->|Yes| Check4{Testable?<br/>Objectively<br/>verifiable}
        
        Check4 -->|No| Fail4[❌ Not Testable]
        Check4 -->|Yes| Check5{Traceable?<br/>Linked to business<br/>need and implementation}
        
        Check5 -->|No| Fail5[❌ Not Traceable]
        Check5 -->|Yes| Check6{Feasible?<br/>Implementable with<br/>available resources}
        
        Check6 -->|No| Fail6[❌ Not Feasible]
        Check6 -->|Yes| Check7{Necessary?<br/>Adds value and<br/>aligns with objectives}
        
        Check7 -->|No| Fail7[❌ Not Necessary]
        Check7 -->|Yes| Pass[✅ Quality<br/>Validated]
    end
    
    subgraph "Failed Requirements"
        Fail1 --> Rework[Return for Rework<br/>Provide feedback to author]
        Fail2 --> Rework
        Fail3 --> Rework
        Fail4 --> Rework
        Fail5 --> Rework
        Fail6 --> Rework
        Fail7 --> Rework
        
        Rework --> Requirement
    end
    
    Pass --> Approved[Approved for Baseline]
    
    style Requirement fill:#E8F4F8
    style Pass fill:#90EE90
    style Approved fill:#90EE90
    style Fail1 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail2 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail3 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail4 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail5 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail6 fill:#FFB6C1
    style Fail7 fill:#FFB6C1
```

### 4.4.2 Requirements Change Management

#### 4.4.2.1 Change Request Submission and Triage

Once requirements are baselined, all changes follow a formal change management process:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ChangeRequest: Stakeholder Submits Change
    
    ChangeRequest --> Triage: Product Owner Reviews
    
    Triage --> ValidChange: Change Valid and Complete
    Triage --> InvalidChange: Change Invalid or Incomplete
    
    InvalidChange --> Rejected: Reject with Feedback
    Rejected --> [*]
    
    ValidChange --> ImpactAnalysis: Technical Team Assesses
    
    ImpactAnalysis --> StakeholderReview: Analysis Complete
    
    StakeholderReview --> CABReview: Change Advisory Board Reviews
    
    CABReview --> Approved: Change Approved
    CABReview --> Deferred: Change Deferred to Future Release
    CABReview --> Rejected: Change Denied
    
    Deferred --> Backlog: Add to Future Backlog
    Backlog --> [*]
    
    Rejected --> [*]
    
    Approved --> RequirementsUpdate: Update Requirements Documentation
    
    RequirementsUpdate --> Notification: Notify Affected Teams
    
    Notification --> Implementation: Implement Change
    
    Implementation --> Verification: Verify Implementation
    
    Verification --> Complete: Change Complete
    Complete --> [*]
    
    note right of ImpactAnalysis
        Impact Assessment Includes:
        - Scope of affected components
        - Effort estimation
        - Schedule impact
        - Cost implications
        - Risk assessment
        - Dependency analysis
    end note
    
    note right of StakeholderReview
        CAB Reviews:
        - Business value vs cost
        - Priority relative to roadmap
        - Resource availability
        - Risk tolerance
        - Customer impact
    end note
```

#### 4.4.2.2 Requirements Change Impact Analysis

The technical team conducts comprehensive impact analysis for each change request:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Requester
    participant PO as Product Owner
    participant Tech as Technical Team
    participant Trace as Traceability Matrix
    participant Arch as Architecture Team
    participant QA as QA Team
    participant Report as Impact Report
    
    Requester->>PO: 1. Submit Change Request<br/>Description, Justification, Priority
    
    PO->>PO: 2. Validate Change Request<br/>Complete? Aligned with objectives?
    
    alt Request Valid
        PO->>Tech: 3. Assign for Impact Analysis<br/>Change Request #CR-123
        
        Tech->>Trace: 4. Query Traceability Matrix<br/>Find related requirements, features, components
        
        Trace->>Tech: 5. Return Dependency Map<br/>Affected: Req-45, Req-78, Feature-12
        
        Tech->>Tech: 6. Analyze Code Impact<br/>Identify files, modules, APIs to change
        
        Tech->>Arch: 7. Consult Architecture Team<br/>Architectural implications?
        
        Arch->>Tech: 8. Architectural Guidance<br/>Design patterns, infrastructure changes
        
        Tech->>QA: 9. Consult QA Team<br/>Testing scope, regression risks
        
        QA->>Tech: 10. Testing Impact<br/>Test cases to update, new tests needed
        
        Tech->>Tech: 11. Estimate Effort<br/>Development hours, story points
        
        Tech->>Report: 12. Compile Impact Report<br/>- Affected components<br/>- Effort: 40 hours<br/>- Risk: Medium<br/>- Schedule impact: +2 sprints
        
        Report->>PO: 13. Return Impact Analysis
        
        PO->>Requester: 14. Present Findings<br/>Cost-benefit analysis for review
        
    else Request Invalid
        PO->>Requester: 3b. Return for Clarification<br/>Missing information, unclear rationale
    end
```

**Impact Analysis Outputs**:
- **Scope Assessment**: Detailed list of affected requirements, features, and components
- **Effort Estimation**: Development effort in hours or story points
- **Schedule Impact**: Effect on current sprint/release timeline
- **Cost Analysis**: Financial implications including development and testing
- **Risk Assessment**: Technical risks, dependencies, potential for regression
- **Recommendation**: Approve, defer, or reject with rationale

#### 4.4.2.3 Requirements Update and Communication

Approved changes are systematically implemented and communicated:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Change Approved]) --> UpdateSpec[Update Technical Specification<br/>- Modify affected sections<br/>- Version control changes<br/>- Document rationale]
    
    UpdateSpec --> UpdateTrace[Update Traceability Matrix<br/>- Link new requirements<br/>- Update dependencies<br/>- Maintain audit trail]
    
    UpdateTrace --> UpdateBacklog[Update Product Backlog<br/>- Create/modify user stories<br/>- Update acceptance criteria<br/>- Assign to sprint]
    
    UpdateBacklog --> NotifyTeams[Notify Affected Teams<br/>Development, QA, Design, DevOps]
    
    NotifyTeams --> ConductKickoff[Conduct Change Kickoff<br/>- Review requirements<br/>- Clarify questions<br/>- Align on approach]
    
    ConductKickoff --> ImplementChange[Development Team Implements<br/>Following standard SDLC]
    
    ImplementChange --> UpdateTests[QA Updates Test Cases<br/>- Modify existing tests<br/>- Create new test scenarios<br/>- Update automation]
    
    UpdateTests --> Verification[Verify Implementation<br/>- Requirements met?<br/>- Acceptance criteria satisfied?<br/>- No regression?]
    
    Verification --> VerifyPass{Verification<br/>Passed?}
    
    VerifyPass -->|No| Rework[Rework Implementation<br/>Address verification failures]
    Rework --> ImplementChange
    
    VerifyPass -->|Yes| UpdateDocs[Update All Documentation<br/>- API docs<br/>- User guides<br/>- Release notes]
    
    UpdateDocs --> CloseChange[Close Change Request<br/>- Mark as complete<br/>- Document lessons learned<br/>- Archive artifacts]
    
    CloseChange --> NotifyStakeholders[Notify Stakeholders<br/>Change deployed and available]
    
    NotifyStakeholders --> End([Change Process Complete])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End fill:#90EE90
```

## 4.5 STATE MANAGEMENT AND DATA FLOW

### 4.5.1 Application State Transitions

#### 4.5.1.1 User Session State Lifecycle

User sessions transition through multiple states throughout their lifecycle:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unauthenticated: Application Opened
    
    Unauthenticated --> Authenticating: Login Initiated
    
    Authenticating --> Authenticated: Auth Success (JWT received)
    Authenticating --> Unauthenticated: Auth Failed (invalid credentials)
    
    Authenticated --> Active: User Activity Detected
    
    Active --> Active: Ongoing Interactions<br/>(API requests, UI interactions)
    Active --> Idle: Inactivity > 5 minutes
    
    Idle --> Active: User Activity Resumes
    Idle --> SessionExpiring: Inactivity > 25 minutes
    
    SessionExpiring --> Active: User Activity (Token Refreshed)
    SessionExpiring --> Expired: Inactivity > 30 minutes
    
    Authenticated --> RefreshingToken: Access Token Expired
    RefreshingToken --> Authenticated: Refresh Success (new tokens)
    RefreshingToken --> Unauthenticated: Refresh Failed (re-auth required)
    
    Active --> LoggingOut: User Initiates Logout
    Idle --> LoggingOut: User Initiates Logout
    
    LoggingOut --> Unauthenticated: Tokens Cleared
    
    Expired --> Unauthenticated: Session Terminated
    
    Authenticated --> [*]: Application Closed (background)
    
    note right of SessionExpiring
        Display Warning:
        "Your session will expire in 5 minutes.
        Click to stay logged in."
    end note
    
    note right of RefreshingToken
        Automatic Process:
        - Attempt silent token refresh
        - No user intervention required
        - Retry with backoff on failure
    end note
```

**Session State Persistence**:
- **Active Session Data**: Stored in Redis with 30-minute TTL, extended on activity
- **User Preferences**: Persisted in MongoDB, cached in Redis
- **UI State**: Maintained in client-side state management (Redux/Context API)
- **Form Data**: Auto-saved to local storage every 30 seconds to prevent data loss

#### 4.5.1.2 Data Entity State Transitions

Core data entities (e.g., documents, tasks, workflows) follow state machine patterns:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft: Entity Created
    
    Draft --> Draft: Edit Operations
    Draft --> Submitted: User Submits
    Draft --> Deleted: User Deletes
    
    Submitted --> InReview: Auto-Assigned to Reviewer
    
    InReview --> Approved: Reviewer Approves
    InReview --> Rejected: Reviewer Rejects
    InReview --> Draft: Returned for Revision
    
    Approved --> Published: Publish Action
    
    Published --> Published: Read Operations
    Published --> Archived: Archive Action
    Published --> Draft: Edit Requested (creates new version)
    
    Rejected --> Draft: Revise and Resubmit
    Rejected --> Deleted: Abandon Entity
    
    Archived --> Published: Restore from Archive
    Archived --> Deleted: Permanent Deletion
    
    Deleted --> [*]
    
    note right of InReview
        Review State Actions:
        - Notify reviewer
        - Start SLA timer
        - Log review assignment
    end note
    
    note right of Published
        Published State:
        - Visible to all authorized users
        - Read-only unless edit initiated
        - Indexed for search
    end note
```

**State Transition Rules**:
- **Authorization**: State transitions enforce role-based access control (only reviewers can approve)
- **Validation**: Data validation enforced before state transitions (e.g., required fields must be complete before submit)
- **Audit Trail**: All state transitions logged with timestamp, user, and reason
- **Event Notifications**: State changes trigger events for dependent systems and notification services

#### 4.5.1.3 Background Job State Management

Asynchronous background jobs (file processing, batch operations) have distinct lifecycle states:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Job Submitted]) --> Queued[State: QUEUED<br/>Job added to task queue<br/>Position: #45 in queue]
    
    Queued --> Pending[State: PENDING<br/>Worker assigned<br/>Awaiting execution]
    
    Pending --> Running[State: RUNNING<br/>Job execution started<br/>Progress: 0%]
    
    Running --> UpdateProgress{Progress<br/>Updates?}
    
    UpdateProgress -->|Yes| Running
    
    Running --> CheckCompletion{Job<br/>Completed?}
    
    CheckCompletion -->|In Progress| Running
    
    CheckCompletion -->|Completed| Success[State: SUCCESS<br/>Job completed successfully<br/>Result: output_data]
    
    Success --> Cleanup[Cleanup Resources<br/>Remove temporary files<br/>Release locks]
    
    Cleanup --> End1([Job Complete])
    
    Running --> Error{Error<br/>Occurred?}
    
    Error -->|Transient Error| Retry{Retry<br/>Attempts < Max?}
    
    Retry -->|Yes| Backoff[State: RETRYING<br/>Wait with exponential backoff<br/>Attempt: 2 of 5]
    Backoff --> Queued
    
    Retry -->|No| Failed[State: FAILED<br/>Max retries exceeded<br/>Error: error_message]
    
    Error -->|Fatal Error| Failed
    
    Failed --> AlertOps[Alert Operations Team<br/>Log error details<br/>Create incident ticket]
    
    AlertOps --> End2([Job Failed])
    
    Running --> Cancelled{Job<br/>Cancelled?}
    
    Cancelled -->|Yes| CancelledState[State: CANCELLED<br/>User or system cancelled job]
    CancelledState --> End3([Job Cancelled])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#90EE90
    style End2 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End3 fill:#FFA500
    style Success fill:#90EE90
    style Failed fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Job State Persistence**:
- **Job Metadata**: Stored in MongoDB with job_id, status, created_at, started_at, completed_at
- **Job Progress**: Updated in Redis for real-time progress tracking
- **Job Results**: Large results stored in S3, reference stored in MongoDB
- **Job Logs**: Streamed to CloudWatch Logs for debugging and audit

### 4.5.2 Transaction and Data Consistency

#### 4.5.2.1 Database Transaction Boundaries

Multi-step operations requiring atomicity use explicit transaction boundaries:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant API
    participant Service as Business Service
    participant MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant EventBus
    
    Note over Client,EventBus: Multi-Step Transaction Pattern
    
    Client->>API: 1. Complex Operation Request<br/>(e.g., Transfer funds, Update order)
    
    API->>Service: 2. Invoke Business Logic
    
    Service->>MongoDB: 3. Start Transaction<br/>session.start_transaction()
    
    MongoDB->>Service: 4. Transaction Started<br/>transaction_id
    
    Service->>MongoDB: 5. Operation 1: Update Doc A<br/>within transaction
    
    alt Operation 1 Success
        MongoDB->>Service: 6a. Update Successful
        
        Service->>MongoDB: 7. Operation 2: Update Doc B<br/>within transaction
        
        alt Operation 2 Success
            MongoDB->>Service: 8a. Update Successful
            
            Service->>MongoDB: 9. Commit Transaction<br/>session.commit_transaction()
            
            MongoDB->>Service: 10. Transaction Committed<br/>All changes persisted
            
            Service->>Cache: 11. Invalidate Related Cache<br/>DEL cache_keys
            
            Service->>EventBus: 12. Publish Success Event<br/>"transaction_completed"
            
            Service->>API: 13. Return Success
            API->>Client: 14. 200 OK
            
        else Operation 2 Failed
            MongoDB->>Service: 8b. Update Failed<br/>Constraint violation
            
            Service->>MongoDB: 9b. Abort Transaction<br/>session.abort_transaction()
            
            MongoDB->>Service: 10b. Transaction Rolled Back<br/>All changes reverted
            
            Service->>API: 11b. Return Error<br/>Operation 2 failed
            API->>Client: 12b. 400 Bad Request
        end
        
    else Operation 1 Failed
        MongoDB->>Service: 6b. Update Failed
        
        Service->>MongoDB: 7b. Abort Transaction
        MongoDB->>Service: 8b. Transaction Rolled Back
        
        Service->>API: 9b. Return Error
        API->>Client: 10b. 400 Bad Request
    end
```

**Transaction Isolation Levels**:
- **MongoDB Transactions**: Snapshot isolation for multi-document ACID transactions
- **Read Concern**: "majority" to ensure data is acknowledged by majority of replica set
- **Write Concern**: "majority" to ensure durability of committed transactions
- **Causal Consistency**: Client sessions maintain causal consistency across operations

#### 4.5.2.2 Distributed Transaction Patterns (Saga Pattern)

For operations spanning multiple services or external systems, the Saga pattern provides eventual consistency:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Orchestrator as Saga Orchestrator
    participant ServiceA as Service A<br/>(e.g., Inventory)
    participant ServiceB as Service B<br/>(e.g., Payment)
    participant ServiceC as Service C<br/>(e.g., Shipping)
    participant EventBus
    
    Note over Client,EventBus: Saga Pattern: Order Processing Example
    
    Client->>Orchestrator: 1. Initiate Order<br/>{items, payment_info, address}
    
    Orchestrator->>EventBus: 2. Publish: OrderStarted<br/>saga_id, order_details
    
    Note over Orchestrator,ServiceC: Step 1: Reserve Inventory
    
    Orchestrator->>ServiceA: 3. Reserve Inventory<br/>(items, quantities)
    
    alt Inventory Available
        ServiceA->>Orchestrator: 4a. Inventory Reserved<br/>reservation_id
        
        Note over Orchestrator,ServiceC: Step 2: Process Payment
        
        Orchestrator->>ServiceB: 5. Process Payment<br/>(amount, payment_info)
        
        alt Payment Successful
            ServiceB->>Orchestrator: 6a. Payment Confirmed<br/>transaction_id
            
            Note over Orchestrator,ServiceC: Step 3: Arrange Shipping
            
            Orchestrator->>ServiceC: 7. Create Shipment<br/>(items, address)
            
            alt Shipping Created
                ServiceC->>Orchestrator: 8a. Shipment Scheduled<br/>tracking_id
                
                Orchestrator->>EventBus: 9. Publish: OrderCompleted<br/>saga_id, success
                
                Orchestrator->>Client: 10. Return Success<br/>{order_id, tracking_id}
                
            else Shipping Failed
                ServiceC->>Orchestrator: 8b. Shipment Failed<br/>carrier_unavailable
                
                Note over Orchestrator,ServiceC: Compensating Transactions
                
                Orchestrator->>ServiceB: 9b. Refund Payment<br/>transaction_id
                ServiceB->>Orchestrator: 10b. Refund Processed
                
                Orchestrator->>ServiceA: 11b. Release Inventory<br/>reservation_id
                ServiceA->>Orchestrator: 12b. Inventory Released
                
                Orchestrator->>EventBus: 13b. Publish: OrderFailed<br/>saga_id, reason: shipping_failed
                
                Orchestrator->>Client: 14b. Return Error<br/>503 Service Unavailable
            end
            
        else Payment Failed
            ServiceB->>Orchestrator: 6b. Payment Declined<br/>insufficient_funds
            
            Note over Orchestrator,ServiceB: Compensate: Release Inventory
            
            Orchestrator->>ServiceA: 7b. Release Inventory<br/>reservation_id
            ServiceA->>Orchestrator: 8b. Inventory Released
            
            Orchestrator->>EventBus: 9b. Publish: OrderFailed<br/>saga_id, reason: payment_failed
            
            Orchestrator->>Client: 10b. Return Error<br/>402 Payment Required
        end
        
    else Inventory Unavailable
        ServiceA->>Orchestrator: 4b. Insufficient Inventory<br/>out_of_stock
        
        Orchestrator->>EventBus: 5b. Publish: OrderFailed<br/>saga_id, reason: out_of_stock
        
        Orchestrator->>Client: 6b. Return Error<br/>409 Conflict (Out of Stock)
    end
```

**Saga Pattern Characteristics**:
- **Choreography vs Orchestration**: This example uses orchestration (central coordinator), alternative is choreography (event-driven)
- **Compensating Transactions**: Each step has a corresponding compensation action for rollback
- **Idempotency**: All saga steps must be idempotent to handle retries safely
- **Saga State Persistence**: Saga state and progress persisted in MongoDB for recovery after failures

### 4.5.3 Caching Strategy and Invalidation

#### 4.5.3.1 Multi-Layer Caching Architecture

The system implements multiple caching layers for optimal performance:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Client Layer"
        Browser[Browser Cache<br/>Static Assets: 7 days<br/>API Responses: 5 minutes]
        LocalStorage[Local Storage<br/>User Preferences<br/>UI State]
    end
    
    subgraph "CDN Layer"
        CloudFront[AWS CloudFront<br/>Static Content<br/>Public Assets<br/>TTL: 24 hours]
    end
    
    subgraph "Application Layer"
        APIGateway[API Gateway<br/>Response Cache<br/>TTL: 60 seconds]
        
        ApplicationCache[Application Memory Cache<br/>Python: functools.lru_cache<br/>Node: node-cache]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distributed Cache Layer"
        Redis[Redis Cache<br/>Session Data: 30 min<br/>Query Results: 1 hour<br/>LLM Responses: 1 hour]
    end
    
    subgraph "Database Layer"
        MongoDB[(MongoDB<br/>Source of Truth<br/>Persistent Storage)]
    end
    
    Browser -->|Cache Miss| CloudFront
    CloudFront -->|Cache Miss| APIGateway
    APIGateway -->|Cache Miss| ApplicationCache
    ApplicationCache -->|Cache Miss| Redis
    Redis -->|Cache Miss| MongoDB
    
    MongoDB -->|Populate| Redis
    Redis -->|Populate| ApplicationCache
    ApplicationCache -->|Populate| APIGateway
    APIGateway -->|Populate| CloudFront
    CloudFront -->|Populate| Browser
    
    style Browser fill:#E8F4F8
    style CloudFront fill:#FF9900
    style Redis fill:#DC382D
    style MongoDB fill:#4DB33D
```

**Cache TTL Configuration**:
- **Static Assets**: 7 days (HTML, CSS, JS bundles with versioned filenames)
- **User Session Data**: 30 minutes (extended on activity)
- **API Query Results**: 1 hour (configurable per endpoint)
- **LLM Responses**: 1 hour (for repeated similar queries)
- **User Profile Data**: 1 hour (updated on profile changes)

#### 4.5.3.2 Cache Invalidation Patterns

The system supports multiple cache invalidation strategies based on data criticality:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Data Update Event]) --> IdentifyPattern{Invalidation<br/>Pattern?}
    
    IdentifyPattern -->|Time-Based| TTLExpiry[TTL Expiration<br/>Cache entry expires automatically<br/>No manual invalidation]
    TTLExpiry --> End1([Cache Refreshed on Next Access])
    
    IdentifyPattern -->|Event-Based| EventTrigger[Event-Driven Invalidation<br/>Listen for data change events]
    EventTrigger --> PublishEvent[Publish InvalidateCache Event<br/>Event Bus: cache_invalidation]
    PublishEvent --> Subscribers[Cache Invalidation Subscribers<br/>Delete affected cache keys]
    Subscribers --> End2([Cache Invalidated])
    
    IdentifyPattern -->|Tag-Based| TagInvalidation[Tag-Based Invalidation<br/>Delete all keys with specific tag]
    TagInvalidation --> FindTags[Find All Keys with Tag<br/>e.g., user:123:*]
    FindTags --> DeleteKeys[Delete Matching Keys<br/>Redis DEL commands]
    DeleteKeys --> End2
    
    IdentifyPattern -->|Manual| ManualInvalidation[Manual Invalidation<br/>Admin action or API call]
    ManualInvalidation --> ValidateAuth[Validate Admin Authorization]
    ValidateAuth --> FlushCache[Flush Specified Cache Entries<br/>Single key or pattern-based]
    FlushCache --> LogAction[Log Invalidation Action<br/>admin_id, timestamp, keys]
    LogAction --> End2
    
    IdentifyPattern -->|Write-Through| WriteThrough[Write-Through Pattern<br/>Update DB and cache atomically]
    WriteThrough --> UpdateDB[1. Update Database]
    UpdateDB --> DBSuccess{DB Update<br/>Successful?}
    DBSuccess -->|No| RollbackFailed[Abort Operation<br/>No cache update]
    RollbackFailed --> End3([Update Failed])
    DBSuccess -->|Yes| UpdateCache[2. Update Cache with New Data]
    UpdateCache --> End4([Data and Cache Synchronized])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#E8F4F8
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style End3 fill:#FFB6C1
    style End4 fill:#90EE90
```

## 4.6 ERROR HANDLING AND RECOVERY

### 4.6.1 Error Detection and Classification

#### 4.6.1.1 Error Taxonomy and Severity Levels

The system categorizes errors into a hierarchical taxonomy for appropriate handling:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Error Detected]) --> ClassifyType{Error<br/>Type?}
    
    ClassifyType -->|Client Error| ClientError[Client Error 4xx<br/>User or client-side issue]
    ClassifyType -->|Server Error| ServerError[Server Error 5xx<br/>Backend or infrastructure issue]
    ClassifyType -->|Application Error| AppError[Application Logic Error<br/>Business rule violation]
    ClassifyType -->|Integration Error| IntError[Integration Error<br/>External service failure]
    
    ClientError --> ClientSeverity{Severity?}
    ServerError --> ServerSeverity{Severity?}
    AppError --> AppSeverity{Severity?}
    IntError --> IntSeverity{Severity?}
    
    ClientSeverity -->|Low| Log1[Log: INFO<br/>400 Bad Request<br/>User correctable]
    ClientSeverity -->|Medium| Log2[Log: WARN<br/>401/403 Auth issues<br/>Security relevant]
    
    ServerSeverity -->|High| Log3[Log: ERROR<br/>500 Internal Error<br/>Alert on-call team]
    ServerSeverity -->|Critical| Log4[Log: CRITICAL<br/>503 Service Unavailable<br/>Page on-call<br/>Initiate incident]
    
    AppSeverity -->|Medium| Log5[Log: ERROR<br/>Business rule violated<br/>Review logic]
    
    IntSeverity -->|High| Log6[Log: ERROR<br/>External service down<br/>Activate circuit breaker<br/>Use fallback]
    
    Log1 --> Handle1[Return user-friendly message<br/>Include corrective action]
    Log2 --> Handle2[Return auth error<br/>Prompt re-authentication]
    Log3 --> Handle3[Return generic error message<br/>Log stack trace<br/>Create support ticket]
    Log4 --> Handle4[Return service unavailable<br/>Activate degraded mode<br/>Incident response]
    Log5 --> Handle5[Return business error<br/>Guide user to valid action]
    Log6 --> Handle6[Return integration error<br/>Attempt retry or fallback]
    
    Handle1 --> End1([Error Handled])
    Handle2 --> End1
    Handle3 --> End1
    Handle4 --> End1
    Handle5 --> End1
    Handle6 --> End1
    
    style Start fill:#FFA500
    style End1 fill:#90EE90
    style Log3 fill:#FF6B6B
    style Log4 fill:#8B0000,color:#FFF
    style Log6 fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Error Severity Levels**:

| Severity | HTTP Code | Description | Response Action | Notification |
|----------|-----------|-------------|----------------|--------------|
| **INFO** | 400, 404 | User input errors, not found | Return corrective message | None |
| **WARN** | 401, 403, 429 | Authentication, authorization, rate limits | Prompt user action | Log only |
| **ERROR** | 500, 502, 504 | Server errors, integration failures | Log, retry, fallback | Email team |
| **CRITICAL** | 503 | Service outage, data corruption | Page on-call, incident | SMS + Email |

#### 4.6.1.2 Error Logging and Monitoring

All errors are systematically logged with context for troubleshooting and trend analysis:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Logger as Logging Service
    participant CloudWatch as AWS CloudWatch
    participant Metrics as CloudWatch Metrics
    participant Alarms as CloudWatch Alarms
    participant SNS as AWS SNS
    participant OnCall as On-Call Engineer
    
    Note over App,OnCall: Error Logging and Alerting Flow
    
    App->>App: 1. Exception Caught<br/>try-except block
    
    App->>Logger: 2. Log Error with Context<br/>level: ERROR<br/>message: error_description<br/>context: {user_id, request_id, stack_trace}
    
    Logger->>CloudWatch: 3. Stream Log to CloudWatch Logs<br/>Log Group: /aws/ecs/backend-service
    
    CloudWatch->>CloudWatch: 4. Index and Store Log Entry<br/>Timestamp, searchable fields
    
    Logger->>Metrics: 5. Increment Error Metric<br/>Metric: ErrorCount<br/>Dimensions: {ErrorType, Endpoint}
    
    Metrics->>Metrics: 6. Aggregate Metrics<br/>5-minute intervals
    
    Metrics->>Alarms: 7. Evaluate Alarm Thresholds<br/>ErrorCount > 10 in 5 minutes?
    
    alt Threshold Exceeded
        Alarms->>SNS: 8a. Trigger Alarm<br/>AlarmName: HighErrorRate<br/>State: ALARM
        
        SNS->>OnCall: 9a. Send Alert<br/>SMS + Email: "High error rate detected"
        
        OnCall->>CloudWatch: 10a. Query Logs<br/>Filter: ERROR level, last 10 minutes
        
        CloudWatch->>OnCall: 11a. Return Log Entries<br/>Stack traces, context
        
        OnCall->>App: 12a. Investigate and Remediate<br/>Deploy hotfix or rollback
        
    else Threshold Not Exceeded
        Alarms->>Alarms: 8b. Alarm State: OK<br/>Continue monitoring
    end
```

**Structured Logging Format**:
```json
{
  "timestamp": "2024-11-06T12:34:56.789Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "backend-api",
  "environment": "production",
  "request_id": "req_abc123",
  "user_id": "user_xyz789",
  "endpoint": "/api/v1/users/profile",
  "method": "GET",
  "status_code": 500,
  "error_type": "DatabaseConnectionError",
  "error_message": "Unable to connect to MongoDB",
  "stack_trace": "...",
  "context": {
    "query": "findOne({_id: ObjectId(...)})",
    "connection_pool_status": "exhausted",
    "retry_attempt": 3
  }
}
```

### 4.6.2 Recovery and Retry Mechanisms

#### 4.6.2.1 Automatic Retry with Exponential Backoff

Transient failures are automatically retried with exponential backoff to prevent overwhelming failing services:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([API Call to External Service]) --> Attempt[Attempt Request<br/>Attempt: 1 of 5]
    
    Attempt --> Success{Request<br/>Successful?}
    
    Success -->|Yes - 2xx Response| LogSuccess[Log Success<br/>Duration: Xms<br/>Attempt: current]
    LogSuccess --> End1([Return Response])
    
    Success -->|No - Error| ClassifyError{Error<br/>Retriable?}
    
    ClassifyError -->|Non-Retriable Error| LogFatal[Log Fatal Error<br/>4xx client errors<br/>Invalid auth, bad request]
    LogFatal --> End2([Return Error to Caller])
    
    ClassifyError -->|Retriable Error| CheckAttempts{Attempts<br/>< Max Retries?}
    
    CheckAttempts -->|No - Max Reached| LogMaxRetries[Log Max Retries Exceeded<br/>All attempts failed<br/>Total duration: Xs]
    LogMaxRetries --> ActivateCircuit[Activate Circuit Breaker<br/>Stop further requests<br/>Use fallback if available]
    ActivateCircuit --> End2
    
    CheckAttempts -->|Yes - Retry| CalculateBackoff[Calculate Backoff Delay<br/>delay = base_delay * 2^attempt<br/>+ random_jitter]
    
    CalculateBackoff --> Wait[Wait for Backoff Period<br/>Attempt 1: 1s<br/>Attempt 2: 2s + jitter<br/>Attempt 3: 4s + jitter<br/>Attempt 4: 8s + jitter]
    
    Wait --> IncrementAttempt[Increment Attempt Counter<br/>attempt = attempt + 1]
    
    IncrementAttempt --> LogRetry[Log Retry Attempt<br/>Attempt: current<br/>Reason: previous_error<br/>Backoff: Xs]
    
    LogRetry --> Attempt
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#90EE90
    style End2 fill:#FFB6C1
    style LogFatal fill:#FF6B6B
    style LogMaxRetries fill:#FF6B6B
```

**Retry Configuration**:
- **Max Retries**: 5 attempts for most operations
- **Base Delay**: 1 second
- **Backoff Multiplier**: 2 (exponential)
- **Jitter**: ±20% random jitter to prevent thundering herd
- **Max Backoff**: 30 seconds (cap on delay)
- **Retriable Status Codes**: 429 (rate limit), 500, 502, 503, 504 (server errors)
- **Non-Retriable**: 400, 401, 403, 404 (client errors requiring correction)

#### 4.6.2.2 Circuit Breaker Implementation

Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by stopping requests to failing services:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed: Initial State (Healthy)
    
    Closed --> Closed: Requests Success<br/>(Reset failure count)
    
    Closed --> Open: Failure Threshold Exceeded<br/>(e.g., 5 failures in 60s)
    
    Open --> Open: Reject All Requests<br/>(Return cached data or error)
    
    Open --> HalfOpen: Timeout Elapsed<br/>(e.g., 30 seconds)
    
    HalfOpen --> Closed: Test Request Succeeds<br/>(Service recovered)
    
    HalfOpen --> Open: Test Request Fails<br/>(Service still unhealthy)
    
    note right of Closed
        Closed State (Normal Operation):
        - All requests allowed
        - Track failure rate
        - Threshold: 5 failures in 60s
    end note
    
    note right of Open
        Open State (Service Unavailable):
        - All requests immediately fail
        - Return fallback response or error
        - Duration: 30 seconds
        - Log circuit open event
    end note
    
    note right of HalfOpen
        Half-Open State (Testing):
        - Allow 1 test request
        - Monitor result closely
        - Quick transition to Closed or Open
    end note
```

**Circuit Breaker Configuration**:

| Service | Failure Threshold | Timeout Duration | Fallback Strategy |
|---------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Auth0** | 3 failures in 30s | 60 seconds | Cache last known valid token state |
| **OpenAI API** | 5 failures in 60s | 30 seconds | Use cached similar responses or Anthropic fallback |
| **MongoDB** | 3 failures in 30s | 60 seconds | Return stale cached data with warning |
| **Redis** | 5 failures in 60s | 30 seconds | Continue without cache (direct DB access) |

When primary services fail, the system activates fallback mechanisms to maintain partial functionality:

# 5. System Architecture

## 5.1 HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE

### 5.1.1 System Overview

The 6nove_4 system is architected as a modern, cloud-native application following an API-first design philosophy. The architecture is designed to support a greenfield implementation that prioritizes scalability, security, and maintainability from inception. This section documents the planned architectural approach that will guide the system's development and deployment.

#### Architecture Style and Rationale

The system employs a **multi-tier, containerized architecture** with clear separation of concerns across presentation, application, and data layers. This architectural style provides several strategic advantages:

The **API-first approach** positions RESTful JSON APIs as the primary interface, enabling multiple client types—web applications, mobile applications (iOS and Android), and desktop applications (Windows, macOS, Linux)—to consume the same backend services. This design eliminates the need for separate backend implementations per platform and ensures consistency in business logic execution across all user touchpoints.

The **containerized deployment model** using Docker provides infrastructure portability and enables horizontal scaling patterns. Services are deployed as independent containers orchestrated through AWS ECS or EKS, allowing individual components to scale based on demand without affecting other system parts. This approach also facilitates blue-green deployments, canary releases, and rapid rollback capabilities.

The architecture is **microservices-ready**, though initially implemented as a modular monolith. This design allows the system to start with lower operational complexity while maintaining clear service boundaries that enable future decomposition into independent microservices as scale requirements increase.

#### Key Architectural Principles

The system architecture is guided by several foundational principles:

**Cloud-Native Design**: The system is built specifically for AWS cloud infrastructure, leveraging managed services (MongoDB Atlas, ElastiCache, S3) to reduce operational overhead. All components assume ephemeral compute resources, stateless application servers, and externalized configuration through AWS Secrets Manager.

**Defense in Depth Security**: Security is implemented at every architectural layer rather than relying on perimeter defenses alone. This includes network isolation through VPC and security groups, TLS 1.3 for all data in transit, encryption at rest for all data stores, OAuth 2.0 + PKCE for authentication, JWT-based authorization, input validation, and output encoding.

**Horizontal Scalability**: The architecture eliminates single points of failure and enables scaling through replication rather than vertical scaling. Stateless application servers allow unlimited horizontal scaling, while data layers use replication (MongoDB replica sets) and sharding capabilities for distributed data.

**Observable by Design**: Comprehensive observability is architected from the beginning through structured JSON logging, distributed tracing with request correlation IDs, custom application metrics, and integration with AWS CloudWatch. This enables proactive issue detection and rapid troubleshooting.

**Infrastructure as Code**: All infrastructure components are defined in Terraform configurations, ensuring reproducibility across environments, version control for infrastructure changes, and the ability to provision entire environments through automated pipelines.

#### System Boundaries and Major Interfaces

The system architecture defines clear boundaries between internal and external components:

**Internal System Components** include the client applications (web, mobile, desktop), Flask-based API gateway, business logic services, AI/ML integration services, and data persistence layers. These components operate within the system's trust boundary and share common authentication and authorization frameworks.

**External System Boundaries** are established at integration points with third-party services: Auth0 for identity management, MongoDB Atlas for database hosting, AWS infrastructure services (S3, CloudFront, ElastiCache, CloudWatch), and LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic). Each external integration point implements specific security controls including API key management, network access restrictions, and rate limiting.

**Major Interface Patterns** include:
- HTTPS REST APIs with JWT bearer token authentication for all client-to-server communication
- OAuth 2.0 authorization flows for user authentication through Auth0
- MongoDB wire protocol over TLS for database connectivity with connection pooling
- AWS SDK interfaces for S3 object storage with IAM role-based authentication
- HTTPS APIs with API key authentication for LLM provider integration
- CloudWatch APIs for log streaming and metrics publishing

### 5.1.3 Data Flow Architecture

The system's data flow architecture defines how information moves through various components and the patterns that govern these interactions.

#### Primary Data Flow Patterns

**Authentication Flow**: User authentication begins when a user initiates login through any client application. The client redirects to the Auth0 hosted login interface, where the user provides credentials and completes any multi-factor authentication requirements. Upon successful authentication, Auth0 returns an authorization code to the client application. The client exchanges this code for access and refresh tokens using the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). The client stores these tokens securely—in HTTP-only cookies or secure storage depending on the platform—and includes the JWT access token in the Authorization header of all subsequent API requests.

**Standard API Request Flow**: Client requests follow a consistent path through the architecture. The client sends an HTTPS request including the JWT token in the Authorization header. The AWS Application Load Balancer terminates SSL and routes the request to an available Flask API container based on health check status and current load. The API's authentication middleware validates the JWT token by verifying its signature against Auth0's JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) endpoint and checking token expiration. Once authenticated, the business logic layer processes the request, implementing a cache-first strategy where the Redis cache is queried before accessing MongoDB. The response travels back through these layers to the client, maintaining request correlation through a unique request ID for tracing and debugging purposes.

**AI/ML Processing Flow**: AI-powered features follow a specialized data flow optimized for large language model integration. When a user submits a query requiring AI processing, the system first searches the vector database for semantically similar content that can provide relevant context. The query embedding is generated using OpenAI's text embedding model, and a cosine similarity search retrieves the top K most relevant documents (typically K=5 with a similarity threshold above 0.7). This retrieved context is combined with the user's query and conversation history to construct a comprehensive prompt. The prompt is sent to the configured LLM provider (OpenAI GPT-4 as primary, Anthropic Claude as fallback), with the response streamed back to the client using Server-Sent Events for real-time token-by-token delivery. The complete conversation, including user query and AI response, is stored in MongoDB for history and future context. Similar queries are cached in Redis with a one-hour TTL to reduce API costs and improve response times for repeated questions.

**File Upload Flow**: File uploads are optimized to reduce server load by enabling direct client-to-S3 uploads. The flow begins when a client requests permission to upload a file by sending file metadata (name, size, type) to the API. The API validates the request, checks user quotas and permissions, then generates a pre-signed S3 POST URL with a five-minute expiration. This pre-signed URL is returned to the client, which uploads the file directly to S3 without routing through application servers. S3 confirms successful upload and optionally triggers Lambda functions for virus scanning and post-processing. The client notifies the API of upload completion, and the API stores file metadata in MongoDB, linking the file to the user's account. This pattern significantly reduces bandwidth costs and server load while maintaining security through time-limited, purpose-specific pre-signed URLs.

#### Integration Patterns and Protocols

The system employs multiple integration patterns optimized for different use cases:

**Synchronous Request-Response**: The primary integration pattern for client-server communication uses REST APIs over HTTPS. Each request receives an immediate response containing either the requested data or an error message. This pattern is appropriate for operations requiring immediate feedback, such as user authentication, data retrieval, and form submissions. Request timeouts are enforced at multiple levels: 30 seconds at the Application Load Balancer to prevent resource exhaustion, and 10 seconds for database queries to detect slow operations early.

**Asynchronous Background Processing**: Long-running operations that exceed practical request timeout limits are processed asynchronously through task queues. File processing pipelines, batch operations, and data exports are submitted as background jobs that return an immediate acknowledgment with a job ID. Clients poll a status endpoint or receive webhook notifications when job processing completes. This pattern prevents request timeouts and improves perceived performance by allowing users to continue working while operations complete in the background.

**Event-Driven Processing**: S3 upload events automatically trigger Lambda functions for post-processing workflows such as virus scanning, thumbnail generation, and metadata extraction. This event-driven pattern decouples the upload process from processing logic, enabling independent scaling and fault isolation. If processing fails, the event can be retried without requiring client involvement.

**Streaming Responses**: AI-generated content uses Server-Sent Events (SSE) to stream response tokens as they are generated by the LLM provider. This streaming pattern dramatically improves perceived performance, allowing users to begin reading responses before generation completes. The pattern requires maintaining an open HTTP connection with chunked transfer encoding, with the server pushing data as it becomes available.

#### Data Transformation Points

Data undergoes transformation at specific architectural boundaries to ensure consistency, validation, and appropriate formatting:

At the **API Gateway**, incoming HTTP requests are validated against expected schemas, rate limits are enforced, JWT tokens are extracted from Authorization headers, and CORS policies are applied. Request bodies are parsed from JSON to Python dictionaries, and query parameters are extracted and type-validated.

Within the **Business Logic Layer**, Pydantic models validate and transform request data, enforcing type constraints, value ranges, and business rules. Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) map between API representations and internal domain models, abstracting persistence details from API contracts. Business rules are applied to transform raw input into validated domain objects ready for persistence.

The **AI Service Layer** transforms user queries into structured prompts by combining the user's input with system instructions, retrieved context from the vector database, and conversation history. Token counting ensures prompts fit within model context windows, with intelligent truncation of conversation history if needed. Response streaming transforms the raw token stream from the LLM into formatted markdown or structured data as specified by the application requirements.

At the **Database Layer**, Python dictionaries are serialized to BSON format for MongoDB storage, with datetime objects converted to UTC timestamps and complex objects mapped to embedded documents or references. On retrieval, BSON documents are deserialized back to Python objects with MongoDB ObjectIDs converted to strings for JSON serialization.

#### Key Data Stores and Caching Strategy

The architecture employs multiple data stores, each optimized for specific access patterns:

**MongoDB Primary Database** serves as the system of record for all application data including user profiles, conversation history, application state, and configuration data. The document-oriented model provides schema flexibility crucial for a greenfield project where data structures may evolve rapidly. MongoDB's aggregation framework enables complex data transformations and analytics queries without requiring separate data warehouse infrastructure.

**Redis Cache Layer** implements a multi-tier caching strategy to optimize performance. Session data is cached with a 30-minute TTL, automatically extended on user activity to maintain active sessions while allowing inactive sessions to expire naturally. API response data is cached for one hour, with cache keys constructed from the request path, query parameters, and user identity. LLM responses are aggressively cached for one hour to reduce API costs, with cache keys based on query similarity hashes. Rate limit counters use Redis's atomic increment operations with sliding window TTLs to enforce API usage limits across distributed application instances.

**S3 Object Storage** provides virtually unlimited, cost-effective storage for user-uploaded files, application assets, database backups, and ML model artifacts. Files are organized using user-specific prefixes (`user_id/uuid/filename`) to enable efficient access control and quota management. CloudFront CDN provides global edge caching with 24-hour TTLs for static assets, dramatically reducing latency for international users.

**Vector Database** (ChromaDB or Pinecone) stores document embeddings for semantic search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Each document is represented as a 1536-dimensional vector generated by OpenAI's text-embedding model, enabling similarity searches that find conceptually related content even when exact keyword matches don't exist. Metadata filtering allows restricting searches to specific document types, user access permissions, or content categories.

Each external integration implements specific security controls and error handling patterns. Auth0 integration uses JWKS endpoint caching to reduce latency and API calls, with automatic key rotation support through the `kid` (key ID) field in JWT headers. LLM provider integrations implement circuit breaker patterns to fail fast when providers are unavailable, automatically falling back to Anthropic when OpenAI fails, or returning cached similar responses when both providers are down. MongoDB Atlas connections use TLS encryption and IP whitelisting to restrict access to application servers only. AWS service integrations leverage IAM roles for EC2 instances or ECS tasks, eliminating the need to manage long-lived credentials. All external API calls include exponential backoff retry logic with jitter to handle transient failures gracefully.

## 5.2 COMPONENT DETAILS

### 5.2.1 Client Applications Layer

#### Purpose and Responsibilities

The Client Applications Layer provides user-facing interfaces across web, mobile, and desktop platforms, delivering a consistent user experience while respecting platform-specific conventions and capabilities. This layer is responsible for rendering user interfaces, capturing user input, managing local application state, handling authentication flows, communicating with backend APIs, and providing responsive, accessible experiences across diverse devices and screen sizes.

#### Technologies and Frameworks

**Web Application Stack**: The web application leverages React 18+ as the UI framework, taking advantage of concurrent rendering features for improved performance and user experience. TypeScript 5.0+ provides static type checking to catch errors during development rather than runtime, improving code quality and maintainability. TailwindCSS 3.4+ enables rapid UI development through utility-first CSS classes while maintaining design consistency. Vite 5.0+ serves as the build tool, providing fast Hot Module Replacement (HMR) during development and optimized production builds with automatic code splitting. React Query 5+ manages server state, providing automatic caching, background refetching, and optimistic updates that significantly improve perceived performance.

**Mobile Application Stack**: The mobile applications use React Native 0.72+, enabling significant code sharing with the web application while compiling to native iOS and Android applications. TypeScript ensures type safety across the codebase. React Navigation 6+ provides the navigation framework with platform-appropriate transitions and gestures. React Native Paper delivers Material Design components that feel native on both iOS and Android. Platform-specific modules bridge to native APIs when needed for capabilities like camera access, biometric authentication, and push notifications.

**Desktop Application Stack**: The desktop applications use Electron 28+, which embeds the web application within a native application shell. This approach maximizes code reuse from the web application while providing desktop-specific capabilities like system tray integration, global keyboard shortcuts, and direct filesystem access. Electron Builder handles packaging for Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms, creating platform-specific installers and auto-update mechanisms.

#### Key Interfaces and APIs

**REST API Consumption**: All client applications communicate with the backend through a consistent REST API interface. Axios serves as the HTTP client library, configured with interceptors that automatically attach JWT tokens to requests, handle token refresh when access tokens expire, and implement retry logic for transient failures. API responses follow a standard structure with `data`, `error`, and `metadata` fields, enabling consistent error handling across all client applications.

**Authentication Integration**: The Auth0 SDK integrates authentication flows into each client platform. Web and desktop applications use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE, redirecting to Auth0's hosted login page for authentication and receiving tokens through a callback URL. Mobile applications use the same flow but with platform-specific browser tabs (SFSafariViewController on iOS, Chrome Custom Tabs on Android) to maintain security while providing a seamless user experience. The SDK handles token storage, automatic refresh, and logout flows.

**State Management Architecture**: Application state is managed through Zustand or Redux Toolkit, providing a centralized store for application-wide state like user profile, application settings, and UI state. Server state is managed separately through React Query, which maintains its own cache of API responses with automatic invalidation and refetching logic. Form state uses React Hook Form with Zod schemas for validation, providing performant, type-safe form handling with minimal re-renders.

#### Data Persistence Requirements

**Web Application**: Browser-based storage leverages LocalStorage for user preferences and application settings that should persist across sessions. SessionStorage holds temporary state that should clear when the browser tab closes, such as navigation state or form drafts. The Cache API stores static assets for offline availability when configured as a Progressive Web Application (PWA). IndexedDB may be used for larger datasets or more complex offline data requirements.

**Mobile Application**: AsyncStorage provides simple key-value storage for application data, with encrypted storage using the Keychain (iOS) or KeyStore (Android) for sensitive data like authentication tokens. SQLite databases can be used for more complex local data requirements, with encryption at rest through SQLCipher. Local files can store downloaded content, with appropriate encryption for sensitive files.

**Desktop Application**: Electron applications store data in platform-appropriate locations using the electron-store library, which provides atomic write operations and encryption capabilities. The filesystem provides direct storage for larger files, with user data stored in standard application data directories for each operating system.

#### Scaling Considerations

**Web Application Scaling**: The web application scales through CDN distribution via CloudFront, which serves the static application bundle from edge locations globally, dramatically reducing initial load times for international users. Code splitting ensures users download only the JavaScript required for the current route, with additional chunks loaded on demand. Lazy loading of images and components defers loading until content enters the viewport. Service workers enable aggressive caching strategies for returning users, allowing near-instant application startup.

**Mobile Application Scaling**: Over-the-air updates through CodePush enable rapid bug fixes and minor feature deployments without requiring app store review and user updates. This capability is crucial for maintaining application quality and responding quickly to issues. Native optimizations like list virtualization ensure smooth scrolling even with large datasets. Background synchronization allows deferred uploads and syncs when network quality is poor.

**Desktop Application Scaling**: Auto-update mechanisms via electron-updater ensure users run current application versions without manual intervention. The delta updates capability minimizes download sizes by downloading only changed files rather than full application packages. Multiple windows or worker threads can leverage multi-core processors for computational tasks without blocking the UI thread.
