When primary services fail even after retry attempts, the system implements hierarchical fallback strategies to maintain functionality with degraded capabilities.

**LLM Provider Fallback Chain**:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[AI Request] --> B{OpenAI API<br/>Available?}
    B -->|Success| C[Return GPT-4<br/>Response]
    B -->|Circuit Open<br/>or Failed Retries| D{Anthropic API<br/>Available?}
    D -->|Success| E[Return Claude<br/>Response]
    D -->|Circuit Open<br/>or Failed Retries| F{Cached Similar<br/>Response?}
    F -->|Found| G[Return Cached Response<br/>+ Staleness Disclaimer]
    F -->|Not Found| H[Return Error:<br/>AI Temporarily Unavailable]
```

**Implementation Details**:
1. **Primary**: OpenAI GPT-4 (highest quality, primary provider)
2. **Secondary**: Anthropic Claude (equivalent quality, different provider for redundancy)
3. **Tertiary**: Cached semantically similar responses from vector database (acceptable for many queries)
4. **Ultimate**: Clear error message with retry guidance and status page link

**Cache Failure Fallback**:

Redis cache failures trigger graceful degradation without user-visible errors:

```
Primary: Redis cache query (target: < 5ms)
    ↓ (on failure or miss)
Secondary: Direct MongoDB query (50-200ms)
    ↓ (if stale cache exists)
Fallback: Return stale cached data with X-Data-Staleness header
    ↓ (complete cache failure)
Warning: Log degraded mode, proceed with database only
```

**Database Connection Failure Fallback**:

MongoDB connection failures trigger multi-level fallback:

```
Primary: MongoDB replica set primary node
    ↓ (on failure)
Secondary: Automatic MongoDB failover to secondary node (10-30 seconds)
    ↓ (if cached data available)
Tertiary: Return stale cached data with staleness indicator
    ↓ (no cache, complete database failure)
Ultimate: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After header
```

**File Upload Failure Fallback**:

S3 upload failures provide user guidance for retry:

```
Primary: Pre-signed URL direct upload to S3
    ↓ (on failure)
Secondary: Retry with new pre-signed URL (network glitch)
    ↓ (continued failure)
Tertiary: Queue upload request for background processing
    ↓ (complete S3 unavailability)
Ultimate: Display message: "File upload temporarily unavailable. Your file will be saved locally and uploaded when service recovers."
```

**Fallback Response Indicators**:

When fallback mechanisms are activated, responses include headers and metadata to inform clients:

```json
{
  "data": {...},
  "metadata": {
    "source": "fallback_cache",
    "staleness_seconds": 3600,
    "warning": "Data may be out of date due to service degradation"
  }
}
```

HTTP headers for cache fallback:
```
X-Cache-Status: STALE
X-Data-Staleness: 3600
X-Service-Status: degraded
```

### 6.1.3 Scalability Design

#### 6.1.3.1 Horizontal and Vertical Scaling Approach

The architecture prioritizes horizontal scaling as the primary mechanism for capacity growth, with vertical scaling serving as a temporary measure for specific bottlenecks.

**Horizontal Scaling Strategy**

Horizontal scaling adds more instances of services rather than increasing the resources of existing instances, providing unlimited growth potential and improved fault tolerance.

**Stateless Application Design**:

The foundation of horizontal scalability is complete statelessness in application servers:

- **Session State**: Externalized to Redis with 30-minute TTL, any server can access any session
- **User Context**: Retrieved from JWT token claims, no server-side session required
- **File Uploads**: Direct to S3 with pre-signed URLs, no file storage on application servers
- **Configuration**: Environment variables and AWS Secrets Manager, no local configuration files
- **Caching**: Distributed Redis cache shared across all instances

This stateless design ensures that any application server can handle any request without server affinity, enabling unlimited horizontal scaling simply by adding more container instances.

**Horizontal Scaling Capabilities by Component**:

| Component | Scaling Method | Scaling Trigger | Limits | Cost per Additional Instance |
|-----------|---------------|----------------|--------|----------------------------|
| **Flask API Containers** | ECS auto-scaling group | CPU > 70%, Memory > 70%, Request rate | Min: 2, Max: 20 (configurable) | ~$50/month per container (2 vCPU, 4GB) |
| **MongoDB Atlas** | Replica set + Sharding | Data volume, IOPS, query throughput | Unlimited through sharding | Tier-dependent (M30: $300/month) |
| **Redis ElastiCache** | Cluster mode | Memory usage, connection count | Up to 500 nodes in cluster mode | ~$60/month per node (cache.t3.medium) |
| **S3 Storage** | AWS-managed automatic | Storage volume (unlimited) | No practical limits | $0.023/GB/month (standard tier) |

**Application Container Horizontal Scaling**:

The Flask API containers scale horizontally through ECS service auto-scaling:

**Current State**:
- 2 containers minimum (high availability requirement)
- Each container: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM
- Handles ~125 requests/second per container (estimated)
- Total capacity: ~250 requests/second with 2 containers

**Scaled State**:
- 20 containers maximum (cost control limit, can be increased)
- Total capacity: ~2,500 requests/second with 20 containers
- Geographic distribution possible across multiple AWS regions

**Scaling Process**:
1. CloudWatch metrics detect sustained CPU > 70% or request rate increase
2. ECS service auto-scaling triggers scale-out action
3. ECS launches new container from ECR image (~60 seconds)
4. Container starts, runs health checks (~30 seconds)
5. ALB adds container to target group after health checks pass
6. Traffic begins routing to new container immediately
7. Total scaling time: ~90-120 seconds from trigger to traffic serving

**Database Horizontal Scaling**:

MongoDB provides two mechanisms for horizontal scaling:

**Replica Sets** (Current):
- 1 primary + 2+ secondary nodes in single replica set
- Provides read scaling through secondary reads
- Write scaling limited to primary capacity
- Suitable for initial phase (up to ~100,000 queries/second)

**Sharding** (Future):
- Data partitioned across multiple replica sets
- Each shard is a full replica set (high availability per shard)
- Write scaling through distributed writes across shards
- Suitable for extreme scale (millions of queries/second, petabyte-scale data)

**Vertical Scaling Approach**

Vertical scaling increases resources of individual instances and serves as a temporary measure before implementing horizontal scaling.

**When to Use Vertical Scaling**:

| Scenario | Vertical Scaling Approach | Timeline |
|----------|-------------------------|----------|
| **CPU Bottleneck in Single Container** | Increase from 2 vCPU → 4 vCPU | Immediate (< 1 hour to redeploy) |
| **Memory Pressure in Container** | Increase from 4 GB → 8 GB RAM | Immediate (< 1 hour to redeploy) |
| **Database Storage Full** | Increase storage volume size | Immediate (< 30 minutes, no downtime) |
| **Database IOPS Insufficient** | Upgrade to higher IOPS tier | Immediate (Atlas auto-scaling) |

**Vertical Scaling Limitations**:

- **Resource Ceilings**: Maximum instance sizes (ECS: 16 vCPU, 122 GB RAM; MongoDB Atlas M700: 96 vCPU, 768 GB RAM)
- **Cost Inefficiency**: Doubling resources often more than doubles cost (non-linear pricing)
- **Single Point Bottleneck**: Doesn't improve fault tolerance or geographic distribution
- **Downtime Risk**: Some vertical scaling operations require service restart

**Why Horizontal Scaling is Preferred**:

1. **Unlimited Growth**: No architectural ceiling, can scale to any load
2. **Better Fault Tolerance**: Multiple instances provide redundancy; single instance failure has minimal impact
3. **Cost Effectiveness**: Adding standard instances is more cost-effective than buying largest instance sizes
4. **Geographic Distribution**: Can deploy instances in multiple regions for global presence
5. **Gradual Scaling**: Add one instance at a time rather than large resource jumps

#### 6.1.3.2 Auto-Scaling Triggers and Rules

The system implements automated scaling policies that respond to real-time metrics, ensuring capacity matches demand without manual intervention.

**ECS Service Auto-Scaling Policies**:

The application layer implements target tracking and step scaling policies to handle both gradual load increases and sudden traffic spikes.

**Policy 1: Target Tracking - CPU Utilization** (Primary)

```
Policy Type: TargetTrackingScaling
Metric: ECS Service Average CPU Utilization
Target Value: 70%
Scale-Out Cooldown: 60 seconds
Scale-In Cooldown: 300 seconds (5 minutes)

Behavior:
- When average CPU > 70% for 2 consecutive minutes → Scale out (+1 task)
- When average CPU < 30% for 5 consecutive minutes → Scale in (-1 task)
```

**Rationale**: 70% CPU target maintains headroom for traffic spikes while avoiding over-provisioning. Longer scale-in cooldown (5 minutes vs. 1 minute) prevents thrashing from normal traffic variation and ensures capacity remains during brief load dips.

**Policy 2: Target Tracking - Memory Utilization** (Primary)

```
Policy Type: TargetTrackingScaling
Metric: ECS Service Average Memory Utilization
Target Value: 70%
Scale-Out Cooldown: 60 seconds
Scale-In Cooldown: 300 seconds
```

Memory utilization triggers scaling independently from CPU, catching memory-bound workloads (large JSON processing, LLM context management, caching operations).

**Policy 3: Step Scaling - Request Rate** (Rapid Scaling)

Step scaling policies handle sudden traffic spikes more aggressively than target tracking:

```
CloudWatch Alarm: RequestCountPerTarget > baseline × 2

Step Adjustments:
When alarm state = ALARM:
    If 100% < load < 150% of capacity → Add 2 tasks
    If 150% < load < 200% of capacity → Add 4 tasks
    If load > 200% of capacity → Add 6 tasks

Cooldown: 60 seconds between scale-out actions
```

**Capacity Calculation Example**:
- Baseline capacity: 250 requests/second (2 containers × 125 req/sec)
- 150% load: 375 req/sec → Add 2 tasks (total: 4 tasks, 500 req/sec capacity)
- 200% load: 500 req/sec → Add 4 tasks (total: 6 tasks, 750 req/sec capacity)
- > 200% load: 625+ req/sec → Add 6 tasks (total: 8 tasks, 1,000 req/sec capacity)

**Auto-Scaling Constraints**:

| Constraint | Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| **Minimum Healthy Percent** | 50% | During deployment, can stop half the tasks to roll new version |
| **Maximum Percent** | 200% | During deployment, can run double tasks for zero-downtime rolling updates |
| **Min Tasks** | 2 | High availability requirement (always 2+ instances) |
| **Max Tasks** | 20 | Cost control limit (can be increased for validated demand) |
| **Scale-Out Cooldown** | 60 seconds | Minimum time between scale-out actions (prevents rapid scaling) |
| **Scale-In Cooldown** | 300 seconds | Minimum time between scale-in actions (prevents thrashing) |

**CloudWatch Alarms and Triggers**:

Auto-scaling decisions are driven by CloudWatch alarms monitoring specific metrics:

| Alarm Name | Metric | Threshold | Evaluation Period | Action |
|-----------|--------|-----------|------------------|--------|
| **HighCPU** | Average CPU | > 70% | 2 minutes (2 datapoints) | Trigger scale-out |
| **LowCPU** | Average CPU | < 30% | 5 minutes (5 datapoints) | Trigger scale-in |
| **HighMemory** | Average Memory | > 70% | 2 minutes (2 datapoints) | Trigger scale-out |
| **HighRequestRate** | Requests per target | > 150/sec per container | 1 minute (1 datapoint) | Step scale-out |
| **HighErrorRate** | HTTP 5xx rate | > 5% | 2 minutes (2 datapoints) | Alert (investigate, may scale) |

**Database Auto-Scaling (MongoDB Atlas)**:

MongoDB Atlas provides automatic cluster tier scaling based on resource utilization:

**Atlas Auto-Scaling Configuration**:
```
Enabled Metrics:
  - Storage: Scale when > 90% full
  - IOPS: Scale when sustained 80%+ utilization
  - Connections: Alert when approaching connection limit

Scaling Actions:
  - Storage: Automatic expansion in 10 GB increments
  - Compute: Manual approval required for tier upgrades (M30 → M40)
  - Sharding: Manual implementation when query throughput exceeds single replica set
```

**Atlas Scaling Timeline**:
- Storage expansion: Immediate, no downtime
- Compute tier upgrade: 10-30 minutes with brief connection interruption
- Shard addition: 1-4 hours depending on data volume (requires planning)

**Predictive Scaling Considerations** (Future Enhancement):

Predictive scaling analyzes historical patterns to scale proactively:

```
AWS Auto Scaling Predictive Scaling:
  - Analyze 14 days of traffic patterns
  - Identify daily/weekly cyclical patterns
  - Pre-scale 15-30 minutes before predicted load increase
  - Particularly valuable for B2B applications with predictable business hour traffic
```

Implementation timeline: After 60 days of production traffic data available for pattern analysis.

#### 6.1.3.3 Resource Allocation Strategy

The resource allocation strategy balances performance requirements with cost efficiency through careful sizing of compute, memory, and connection pool resources.

**Container Resource Allocation**:

Each Flask API container is allocated specific CPU and memory resources to handle expected concurrency without over-provisioning:

**Task Definition Resources**:
```
CPU: 2 vCPU (2048 CPU units)
Memory: 4 GB RAM (4096 MiB)

Rationale:
- 2 vCPU sufficient for 4 Gunicorn workers (0.5 vCPU per worker)
- 4 GB memory supports 4 workers with 1 GB per worker (application + dependencies)
- Sizing validated through load testing at 125 requests/second per container
```

**Gunicorn Worker Configuration**:
```
Workers: 4 (matches vCPU count; 2 × CPU cores recommended by Gunicorn docs)
Threads per Worker: 2 (handles I/O blocking during external API calls)
Total Concurrency: 8 concurrent requests per container (4 workers × 2 threads)
Worker Class: gthread (threaded workers for async I/O operations)
Worker Timeout: 30 seconds (matches ALB timeout to prevent orphaned requests)
```

**Memory Allocation per Worker**:
- Base Python process: ~100 MB
- Flask application + dependencies: ~200 MB
- Request processing memory: ~300 MB (JSON parsing, Pydantic validation, caching)
- Peak memory: ~600-800 MB per worker under load
- Total container memory: 4 GB (4 workers × 800 MB + ~700 MB buffer for OS)

**Connection Pool Resource Allocation**:

Connection pooling prevents resource exhaustion and optimizes database performance through connection reuse:

**MongoDB Connection Pool Sizing**:

| Parameter | Value per Worker | Total per Container | Rationale |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Min Pool Size** | 5 | 20 | Maintain warm connections for immediate use |
| **Max Pool Size** | 10 | 40 | Balance concurrency with server connection limits |
| **Wait Queue Size** | 50 | 200 | Queue requests when pool exhausted (prevents rejection) |
| **Connection Idle Timeout** | 300 seconds | - | Release idle connections to free server resources |
| **Connection Max Lifetime** | 1800 seconds | - | Periodic recycling prevents stale connections |

**Pool Size Calculation**:
```
Concurrent Requests per Container: 8 (4 workers × 2 threads)
Database Queries per Request: 1-3 average
Peak Database Connections Needed: 8 × 3 = 24 connections
Pool Size per Worker: 10 connections (40 total > 24 needed)
Buffer: 40 - 24 = 16 connections (67% buffer for spikes)
```

**Redis Connection Pool Sizing**:

Redis operations are significantly faster than database queries (< 5ms vs. 50-200ms), requiring fewer connections:

| Parameter | Value per Worker | Total per Container |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------------|
| **Max Connections** | 5 | 20 |
| **Connection Timeout** | 5 seconds | - |
| **Socket Keepalive** | Enabled | - |

**HTTP Client Connection Pool** (External APIs):

```
Max Connections per Host: 10 (Auth0, OpenAI, Anthropic)
Total Pool Size: 40 connections per container
Connection Timeout: 10 seconds
Read Timeout: 60 seconds (LLM generation can be slow)
Keep-Alive: Enabled (reuse connections across requests)
```

**Infrastructure Resource Allocation by Environment**:

Resource allocation varies significantly between development and production environments:

**Development Environment** (Cost-Optimized):
```
API Containers: 2 minimum, 4 maximum
Container Size: 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM (half of production)
Database: MongoDB Atlas M10 tier (2 GB RAM, shared vCPU)
Cache: Redis cache.t3.micro (0.5 GB)
Deployment: Single Availability Zone
Estimated Monthly Cost: ~$200
```

**Production Environment** (Performance-Optimized):
```
API Containers: 4 minimum, 20 maximum
Container Size: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM
Database: MongoDB Atlas M30 tier (8 GB RAM, 2 vCPU)
Cache: Redis cache.t3.medium (3.2 GB)
Deployment: Multi-AZ (2+ Availability Zones)
Estimated Monthly Cost: ~$800-2,000 (depending on scale)
```

**Resource Monitoring and Adjustment**:

Resource allocation decisions are continuously validated through monitoring and adjusted based on actual utilization:

**Monitoring Metrics**:
- Container CPU utilization (target: 60-80% average)
- Container memory utilization (target: 60-75% average)
- Database connection pool exhaustion events (target: 0 events)
- Cache connection pool exhaustion events (target: 0 events)
- Request queuing time (target: < 100ms)

**Adjustment Triggers**:
- CPU sustained > 90%: Increase vCPU allocation or scale out
- Memory sustained > 85%: Increase RAM allocation or scale out
- Connection pool exhaustion: Increase pool size or add workers
- Request queuing > 500ms: Add more containers or increase concurrency

#### 6.1.3.4 Performance Optimization Techniques

The architecture implements multi-layer performance optimization strategies targeting different latency contributors.

**Layer 1: Caching Strategy** (Primary Performance Optimization)

Caching provides the most significant performance improvement, reducing latency by 80-95% for cached data and decreasing database load by 60-80%.

**Three-Tier Cache Hierarchy**:

```
Request → L1: Application Memory (functools.lru_cache)
              Latency: Nanoseconds
              Hit: Return immediately
              Miss: Check L2
              ↓
          L2: Redis Distributed Cache
              Latency: Sub-millisecond (0.5-3ms)
              Hit: Return quickly
              Miss: Check L3
              ↓
          L3: MongoDB Database
              Latency: Tens to hundreds of milliseconds (10-200ms)
              Source of Truth: Always available
```

**Cache TTL Configuration by Data Type**:

| Data Type | TTL Duration | Cache Key Pattern | Invalidation Strategy |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|---------------------|
| **Session Data** | 30 minutes (sliding) | `session:{session_id}` | Auto-extend on activity, explicit on logout |
| **User Profiles** | 1 hour | `user:{user_id}` | Event-based on profile updates |
| **API Query Results** | 1 hour | `api:{endpoint}:{params_hash}` | TTL-based expiration |
| **LLM Responses** | 1 hour | `llm:{query_hash}` | TTL-based (reduce API costs) |
| **Rate Limit Counters** | 1 hour sliding window | `ratelimit:{user_id}:{window}` | TTL-based with atomic operations |
| **Static Configuration** | 24 hours | `config:{key}` | Event-based on config changes |

**Expected Cache Performance Impact**:

Without caching:
- Average response time: 150-500ms (database query + processing)
- Database queries per second: 100% of requests
- Database load: High

With caching (60-80% hit rate):
- Average response time: 30-50ms (80% cache hits at <5ms + 20% misses at 150-500ms)
- Database queries per second: 20-40% of requests (60-80% served from cache)
- Database load: Reduced by 60-80%, enables supporting 3-5× traffic

**Cache Warming Strategy**:

Critical data is pre-loaded into cache after deployments to avoid cold start performance degradation:

```
Deployment → Health Check Phase → Cache Warming:
1. Load top 1000 most accessed user profiles
2. Load configuration data
3. Warm rate limit counters for active users
4. Validate cache connectivity
Duration: 30-60 seconds before accepting traffic
```

**Layer 2: Database Query Optimization**

MongoDB query optimization focuses on indexing strategy and query pattern efficiency.

**Index Strategy**:

| Index Type | Fields | Purpose | Impact |
|-----------|--------|---------|--------|
| **Single-Field** | `user_id`, `email`, `created_at`, `status` | Fast lookups by single field | Query time: 100ms → <10ms |
| **Compound** | `(user_id, conversation_id)`, `(user_id, created_at)` | Multi-field queries, sort optimization | Avoid collection scans |
| **Text** | `messages.content` | Full-text search capability | Enable search features |
| **TTL** | `expires_at` | Automatic document expiration | Clean temporary data automatically |

**Query Performance Targets**:
```
P50 (median): < 50ms
P95 (95th percentile): < 100ms
P99 (99th percentile): < 250ms
Timeout: 10 seconds (detect slow queries early)
```

**Query Anti-Patterns to Avoid**:
- Collection scans without indexes (query all documents sequentially)
- Large skip values in pagination (`skip(10000)` reads and discards 10,000 documents)
- Fetching more data than needed (select only required fields with projection)
- N+1 query patterns (fetching related documents in loops instead of single aggregation)

**Layer 3: API Response Optimization**

**Compression**:
```
Gzip Compression: Enabled for responses > 1 KB
Compression Level: 6 (balance between compression ratio and CPU usage)
Average Reduction: 60-80% for JSON responses
Impact: 100 KB response → 20-40 KB transferred
Bandwidth Savings: Significant for mobile users and international traffic
```

**Pagination Strategy**:

Cursor-based pagination provides consistent results and better performance than offset-based pagination:

```
Traditional Offset Pagination:
GET /api/v1/conversations?offset=1000&limit=20
Problem: Database must read and skip 1,000 documents (slow at high offsets)

Cursor-Based Pagination:
GET /api/v1/conversations?cursor=encoded_cursor&limit=20
Benefit: Database seeks directly to cursor position (constant time regardless of position)

Response:
{
  "data": [...],
  "pagination": {
    "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IjEyMyIsImNyZWF0ZWRfYXQiOiIyMDI0LTAxLTE1In0=",
    "has_more": true
  }
}
```

**Response Streaming**:

Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream AI-generated content token-by-token, dramatically reducing perceived latency:

```
Traditional Response:
Request sent → Wait 15-30 seconds → Complete response arrives
Perceived latency: 15-30 seconds (user sees loading spinner entire time)

Streaming Response:
Request sent → First token in 1-2 seconds → Tokens stream continuously
Perceived latency: 1-2 seconds (user begins reading immediately)
```

**Layer 4: CDN and Static Asset Optimization**

**CloudFront CDN Configuration**:
```
Edge Caching: Enabled for all static assets
TTL: 24 hours for application bundles, 7 days for immutable assets
Cache-Control: Versioned URLs enable aggressive caching (bundle.v1.2.3.js)
Global Edge Locations: 450+ edge locations worldwide
Latency Improvement: 500ms → 20-50ms for international users
```

**Frontend Build Optimization**:
- **Code Splitting**: Lazy load route-specific JavaScript bundles (reduce initial bundle size by 60-70%)
- **Tree Shaking**: Remove unused code during build (Webpack/Vite)
- **Minification**: Remove whitespace, shorten variable names (30-40% size reduction)
- **Compression**: Brotli compression for static assets (15-20% better than gzip)
- **Bundle Analysis**: Identify large dependencies for optimization targets

**Layer 5: Connection Pooling and Reuse**

Connection pooling eliminates connection establishment overhead:

```
Without Connection Pooling:
Request → Establish MongoDB connection (20-50ms) → Query (50ms) → Close connection
Total: 70-100ms per request

With Connection Pooling:
Request → Reuse existing connection (0ms) → Query (50ms)
Total: 50ms per request
Savings: 20-50ms per request (29-50% faster)
```

**HTTP Connection Keep-Alive**:

External API calls benefit from connection reuse:
```
Keep-Alive Enabled:
- TLS handshake: 100-200ms (one time)
- Subsequent requests: 0ms connection overhead (reuse existing connection)

Keep-Alive Disabled:
- TLS handshake: 100-200ms (every request)
- Overhead: 100-200ms per request
```

**Performance Monitoring and Continuous Optimization**:

Performance is continuously monitored with automated alerting for degradation:

**Key Performance Indicators**:
- API response time (P50, P95, P99)
- Cache hit rate (target: > 60%)
- Database query time distribution
- External API latency
- CDN cache hit rate

**Optimization Cycle**:
1. Identify slow endpoints through APM (Application Performance Monitoring)
2. Analyze slow query logs and execution plans
3. Add indexes or optimize queries
4. Increase cache TTL for appropriate data
5. Validate improvement through A/B testing
6. Deploy optimization to production

#### 6.1.3.5 Capacity Planning Guidelines

Capacity planning ensures the system maintains performance and availability as usage grows, balancing proactive scaling with cost efficiency.

**Baseline Capacity Targets** (Initial Production):

These targets represent validated capacity with adequate headroom for growth and unexpected spikes:

| Metric | Target Capacity | Infrastructure Required | Headroom |
|--------|----------------|------------------------|----------|
| **Concurrent Users** | 1,000 simultaneous active sessions | 4-6 containers (2 vCPU, 4 GB each) | 2× headroom |
| **Requests Per Second** | 1,000 RPS sustained, 5,000 RPS peak | 8-10 containers (sustained), 20 containers (peak) | 5× peak capacity |
| **Data Volume** | 100 GB primary database, 1 GB cache | MongoDB M30 tier, Redis cache.r6g.large | Auto-scaling enabled |
| **File Storage** | 1 TB total, 10,000 files per user avg | S3 (unlimited, $23/month per TB) | Unlimited growth |
| **API Latency** | P95 < 200ms, P99 < 500ms | Above infrastructure at target load | Performance buffer |

**Note**: These targets represent initial production capacity estimates. Actual capacity will be validated through comprehensive load testing before launch and continuously refined based on production metrics.

**Capacity Estimation Methodology**:

**Step 1: User Behavior Analysis** (After launch):
```
Measure per-user metrics over 30 days:
- API requests per user per session: X requests
- Average session duration: Y minutes
- Peak concurrent users: Z users
- Request distribution: W% read, (100-W)% write
```

**Step 2: Resource Consumption Calculation**:
```
Container capacity: 125 requests/second per container (validated through load testing)
Database capacity: 1,000 queries/second per replica set (M30 tier)
Cache capacity: 10,000 operations/second per node (cache.r6g.large)

Required containers = (Peak RPS / 125) × Safety Factor (2×)
Example: (5,000 RPS / 125) × 2 = 80 containers (exceeds current max of 20, requires adjustment)
```

**Step 3: Growth Projection**:
```
Current monthly active users: N
Projected growth rate: G% per month
Forecast (6 months): N × (1 + G)^6

Example:
Current: 10,000 MAU
Growth: 20% per month
6-month forecast: 10,000 × (1.2)^6 = 29,860 MAU (~3× growth)
Required capacity: 3× current infrastructure
```

**Capacity Planning Timeline**:

**Phase 1: Baseline Establishment** (Months 1-3)
- Deploy initial production infrastructure (4 containers, M30 database, single cache node)
- Monitor actual usage patterns and resource utilization
- Measure actual per-user resource consumption
- Document baseline metrics for future projections
- Identify peak usage periods (daily, weekly, seasonal patterns)

**Phase 2: Optimization** (Months 3-6)
- Optimize queries based on slow query analysis
- Tune cache TTLs based on hit rate analysis
- Right-size containers based on actual CPU/memory utilization
- Implement additional indexes for common query patterns
- Reduce per-request resource consumption through optimization

**Phase 3: Proactive Scaling** (Months 6+)
- Project capacity needs 6 months ahead based on growth trends
- Provision infrastructure before reaching 80% capacity
- Test scaling procedures through load testing exercises
- Plan major architectural changes (e.g., sharding) 12 months before needed
- Budget infrastructure costs aligned with revenue projections

**Early Warning Indicators**:

Automated alerts trigger when approaching capacity limits:

| Indicator | Warning Threshold | Critical Threshold | Action |
|-----------|------------------|-------------------|--------|
| **CPU Utilization** | Sustained > 70% | Sustained > 85% | Scale out containers |
| **Memory Utilization** | Sustained > 75% | Sustained > 90% | Scale out containers |
| **Database Query Latency** | P95 > 150ms | P95 > 300ms | Add indexes, scale database tier |
| **Cache Hit Rate** | < 60% | < 40% | Increase cache size, tune TTLs |
| **Error Rate** | > 0.5% | > 2% | Investigate and resolve issues |
| **Request Queue Time** | P95 > 500ms | P95 > 2s | Scale out immediately |

**Cost Optimization Strategies**:

Capacity planning includes cost optimization to maximize value:

**Right-Sizing**:
- Monitor container CPU/memory utilization over 30 days
- Reduce container size if sustained utilization < 40% (over-provisioned)
- Increase container size if sustained utilization > 80% (under-provisioned)

**Spot Instances for Non-Critical Workloads**:
- Use spot instances for development/staging environments (70% cost savings)
- Use spot instances for batch processing jobs (not user-facing)
- Maintain on-demand instances for production user-facing services

**Cache Optimization**:
- Implement aggressive cache TTLs to maximize hit rate (reduce database load)
- Monitor cache memory utilization; increase size if eviction rate high
- Cache most expensive queries (LLM responses, complex aggregations)

**Data Lifecycle Management**:
- Archive conversation history older than 90 days to S3 Glacier (10× cheaper)
- Delete temporary data using TTL indexes (automatic MongoDB cleanup)
- Compress archived logs before storage (reduce storage costs by 80%)

**Reserved Capacity**:
- Purchase reserved instances for baseline capacity (40-60% cost savings vs. on-demand)
- Use on-demand instances for traffic above baseline (flexibility for growth)
- Example: Reserve 4 containers (baseline), scale to 20 on-demand (spikes)

**Load Testing Requirements**:

Before launch and quarterly thereafter, comprehensive load testing validates capacity:

**Load Test Scenarios**:

| Test Type | Target Load | Duration | Success Criteria |
|-----------|------------|----------|-----------------|
| **Baseline** | 1,000 concurrent users, 1,000 RPS | 1 hour | P95 latency < 200ms, 0 errors |
| **Peak Load** | 5,000 concurrent users, 5,000 RPS | 15 minutes | P95 latency < 500ms, error rate < 1% |
| **Stress Test** | Gradually increase until failure | Until failure | Identify breaking point, ensure graceful degradation |
| **Soak Test** | 500 RPS sustained | 24 hours | No memory leaks, stable performance |
| **Spike Test** | Sudden 0 → 5,000 RPS spike | 5 minutes | Auto-scaling responds within 2 minutes |

**Load Testing Tools**: Apache JMeter, Gatling, or AWS-managed load testing service (Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics, AWS Fault Injection Simulator).

### 6.1.4 Resilience Patterns

#### 6.1.4.1 Fault Tolerance Mechanisms

The architecture implements defense-in-depth fault tolerance across multiple system layers, ensuring that component failures don't cascade into system-wide outages.

**Application Layer Fault Tolerance**:

**Stateless Design for Failure Immunity**:

Complete statelessness in application servers ensures that container failures have zero impact on user experience:

- **No Local Session State**: All session data stored in Redis; container failure doesn't lose sessions
- **No Local File Storage**: File uploads go directly to S3; container failure doesn't lose uploaded files
- **No In-Memory Caches**: All caching in Redis; container failure doesn't invalidate caches
- **No Sticky Sessions**: Any container can handle any request; user routing not tied to specific container

**Impact of Container Failure**:
```
Failure Scenario: Single container crashes
Impact: 0 user sessions lost, 0 data lost, 0 manual intervention required
Recovery: ECS automatically restarts container within 60 seconds
User Experience: Requests automatically routed to healthy containers by ALB (transparent)
```

**Health Check-Based Automatic Recovery**:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Container Running] --> B{Health Check<br/>Every 30s}
    B -->|Healthy| A
    B -->|Failure 1| C{Track Failures}
    C --> D{Health Check<br/>30s later}
    D -->|Healthy| A
    D -->|Failure 2| E{Track Failures}
    E --> F{Health Check<br/>30s later}
    F -->|Healthy| A
    F -->|Failure 3| G[Mark Unhealthy]
    G --> H[ALB Stops Routing Traffic]
    H --> I[ECS Terminates Container]
    I --> J[ECS Launches Replacement]
    J --> K[Health Checks on New Container]
    K -->|2 Successes| L[ALB Routes Traffic]
    L --> A
```

**Recovery Timeline**:
- Failure detection: 90 seconds (3 consecutive failures at 30-second intervals)
- Traffic stop: Immediate after detection
- Container termination: < 10 seconds
- New container launch: 30-60 seconds
- Health checks pass: 60 seconds (2 consecutive successes)
- Total recovery time: < 3 minutes from first failure to traffic restoration

**Circuit Breaker Fault Isolation**:

Circuit breakers (detailed in Section 6.1.2.5) prevent cascading failures by failing fast when external services are unavailable:

- **Resource Protection**: Prevents thread exhaustion from requests waiting on unavailable services
- **Fast Failure**: Returns error in milliseconds instead of waiting 30+ seconds for timeout
- **Automatic Recovery**: Circuit automatically closes when service recovers
- **Graceful Degradation**: Fallback mechanisms provide reduced functionality rather than complete failure

**Data Layer Fault Tolerance**:

**MongoDB Replica Set High Availability**:

```
Configuration:
- 3-node replica set (1 primary + 2 secondary replicas)
- Write Concern: "majority" (write confirmed by majority of nodes before success)
- Read Preference: "primaryPreferred" (strong consistency with automatic failover)

Fault Tolerance:
- Single node failure: Automatic failover to secondary (10-30 seconds)
- Network partition: Majority writes prevent split-brain scenarios
- Data durability: 99.999999999% (eleven nines) with Atlas managed service
```

**Replica Set Failover Process**:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Primary as Primary Node
    participant Sec1 as Secondary 1
    participant Sec2 as Secondary 2
    
    App->>Primary: Write Request
    Primary->>Sec1: Replicate Write
    Primary->>Sec2: Replicate Write
    Primary->>App: Write Acknowledged
    
    Note over Primary: Primary Node Fails
    
    Sec1->>Sec2: Election Protocol (Raft)
    Sec2->>Sec1: Vote
    Note over Sec1: Elected New Primary
    
    App->>Sec1: Retry Write (Automatic)
    Sec1->>Sec2: Replicate Write
    Sec1->>App: Write Acknowledged
```

**Failover Timeline**:
- Failure detection: 2-10 seconds (heartbeat interval: 2 seconds)
- Election process: 10-20 seconds (Raft consensus algorithm)
- Application reconnection: Automatic (MongoDB driver detects topology change)
- Write availability restored: 10-30 seconds total
- Read availability: Maintained throughout (reads from secondaries if configured)

**Redis Cache Fault Tolerance**:

```
ElastiCache Configuration:
- Cluster mode with automatic failover OR Redis Sentinel
- Multi-AZ deployment for high availability
- Automatic failover time: < 60 seconds

Fault Tolerance Behavior:
- Cache failure → Application falls back to database (graceful degradation)
- Performance impact: Increased latency (5ms → 50-200ms for cache misses)
- No data loss: Cache data is ephemeral and reconstructible
- User impact: Minimal (slightly slower responses, still functional)
```

**Network Layer Fault Tolerance**:

**Multi-AZ Deployment Architecture**:

```
AWS Region (e.g., us-east-1)
├── Availability Zone A (e.g., us-east-1a)
│   ├── ECS Task 1 (API Container)
│   ├── ECS Task 2 (API Container)
│   └── MongoDB Replica Node 1
│
├── Availability Zone B (e.g., us-east-1b)
│   ├── ECS Task 3 (API Container)
│   ├── ECS Task 4 (API Container)
│   └── MongoDB Replica Node 2
│
└── Availability Zone C (e.g., us-east-1c)
    └── MongoDB Replica Node 3

Application Load Balancer: Spans all AZs
```

**AZ Failure Scenario**:
```
Failure: Complete Availability Zone A outage (power failure, network partition)
Impact: 
  - 50% of containers offline (2 of 4 containers)
  - Database remains operational (2 of 3 nodes in other AZs)
  - ALB immediately routes traffic to healthy AZs
Recovery:
  - Traffic rerouting: Immediate (ALB health checks detect failures)
  - Task replacement: ECS launches replacement tasks in healthy AZs (5-10 minutes)
  - Full capacity restored: 10-15 minutes
User Impact: Minimal; slight performance degradation during recovery
```

**External Service Fault Tolerance**:

**Auth0 Resilience Strategy**:
```
JWT Validation:
- JWKS (public keys) cached for 24 hours in Redis
- Token validation continues even if Auth0 API unreachable
- New logins fail, but existing sessions continue working

Management API:
- Circuit breaker prevents timeout waiting on unavailable Auth0
- User management operations deferred until service recovery
- Read operations fall back to cached user data
```

**LLM Provider Resilience** (Multi-Provider Fallback):
```
Primary: OpenAI GPT-4
    ↓ (circuit breaker open or timeout)
Secondary: Anthropic Claude
    ↓ (circuit breaker open or timeout)
Tertiary: Cached similar responses
    ↓ (no cache available)
Ultimate: Clear error message with retry guidance
```

#### 6.1.4.2 Disaster Recovery Procedures

The disaster recovery strategy establishes Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) targets for various failure scenarios, with documented procedures for each.

**Disaster Recovery Objectives**:

| Disaster Scenario | RTO (Recovery Time) | RPO (Maximum Data Loss) | Recovery Procedure |
|-------------------|-------------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| **Single Container Failure** | < 1 minute | 0 (no data loss) | Automatic ECS restart, ALB routing |
| **Database Node Failure** | < 5 minutes | 0 (replica set) | Automatic MongoDB failover election |
| **Cache Cluster Failure** | < 2 minutes | Acceptable (ephemeral) | Fallback to database, cache rebuild |
| **Availability Zone Failure** | < 15 minutes | < 5 minutes | Multi-AZ deployment continues, task restart |
| **Complete Region Failure** | < 4 hours | < 1 hour | Manual failover to DR region, restore from backup |
| **Data Corruption** | < 2 hours | < 24 hours | Point-in-time restore to pre-corruption state |
| **Accidental Data Deletion** | < 1 hour | < 24 hours | Restore from continuous backup |

**Backup Strategy and Schedule**:

**MongoDB Atlas Continuous Backup**:

```
Backup Type: Continuous Cloud Backup (Atlas managed)

Snapshot Schedule:
- Daily snapshots: Retained for 7 days
- Weekly snapshots: Retained for 4 weeks (28 days total)
- Monthly snapshots: Retained for 12 months

Point-in-Time Recovery:
- Granularity: 1-minute increments
- Retention: 24 hours
- Use Case: Recover to exact state before corruption or accidental deletion

Cross-Region Backup:
- Automated replication to geographically separate region
- Region: us-west-2 (if primary is us-east-1)
- Purpose: Regional disaster recovery
```

**Backup Testing Schedule**:
```
Monthly: Restore random daily backup to test environment, validate data integrity
Quarterly: Full DR drill with restore to DR region, application deployment, validation
Annually: Complete disaster scenario simulation with team coordination
```

**S3 Object Storage Backup**:

```
Versioning: Enabled for all critical buckets
- Protects against accidental deletion (files can be restored)
- Protects against accidental overwrite (previous versions retained)
- Retention: 90 days for non-current versions

Cross-Region Replication:
- Enabled for critical data buckets
- Destination region: us-west-2 (if primary is us-east-1)
- Replication time: < 15 minutes for most objects
- Purpose: Regional disaster recovery

Lifecycle Policies:
- 30 days: Transition to S3 Infrequent Access (cheaper storage)
- 90 days: Transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive (archival)
- 7 years: Retention for compliance logs, then delete
```

**Infrastructure State Backup**:

```
Terraform State:
- Storage: S3 with versioning enabled
- State locking: DynamoDB table prevents concurrent modifications
- Backup: Automatic versioning retains all previous states
- Cross-region replication: Enabled for disaster recovery

Configuration Files:
- Version control: Git repository (GitHub)
- Backup: GitHub's infrastructure + local clones on developer machines
- Recovery: Clone repository from GitHub

Secrets and Credentials:
- Storage: AWS Secrets Manager
- Backup: Automatic multi-AZ replication within region
- Cross-region replication: Configured for DR region
- Rotation: Automatic credential rotation every 90 days
```

**Regional Disaster Recovery Procedures**:

**DR Scenario: Complete AWS Region Failure** (e.g., sustained multi-AZ outage in us-east-1)

**Phase 1: Disaster Declaration** (T+0 to T+15 minutes)

```
1. Incident Detection:
   - CloudWatch alarms trigger for complete service unavailability
   - Status page automatically updated to "Major Outage"
   - On-call engineer receives PagerDuty alert

2. Situation Assessment:
   - Verify outage is regional (check AWS Service Health Dashboard)
   - Confirm multi-AZ impact (not just single AZ failure)
   - Estimate recovery timeline (if AWS ETA > 2 hours, proceed with DR failover)

3. Disaster Declaration:
   - Incident commander declares disaster recovery activation
   - Notify key stakeholders (engineering leadership, customer success)
   - Activate DR runbook procedures
```

**Phase 2: DNS Failover** (T+15 to T+30 minutes)

```
1. Update Route 53 DNS Records:
   - Change A record for api.6nove4.com to DR region ALB
   - TTL: 60 seconds (fast propagation)
   - Expected propagation time: 1-5 minutes globally

2. Validate DNS Propagation:
   - Use dig/nslookup to verify new IP addresses
   - Test API endpoint connectivity from multiple geographic locations
   - Monitor DNS query logs for propagation completion
```

**Phase 3: Database Restoration** (T+30 to T+120 minutes)

```
1. Provision MongoDB Cluster in DR Region:
   - Use Atlas API or UI to restore from latest backup
   - Cluster tier: Match production (M30 or higher)
   - Region: us-west-2 (DR region)
   - Expected provisioning time: 15-30 minutes

2. Restore from Backup:
   - Select latest continuous backup or snapshot
   - Restoration time: 30-90 minutes (depends on database size)
   - During restoration: Application shows maintenance mode

3. Validate Data Integrity:
   - Run automated data integrity checks
   - Verify record counts match pre-disaster state
   - Test critical query patterns
   - Validate latest transactions present
```

**Phase 4: Application Deployment** (T+30 to T+60 minutes, parallel with database)

```
1. Deploy Container Services:
   - ECS service already pre-configured in DR region (hot standby)
   - Update environment variables with DR database connection string
   - Deploy latest application image from ECR (replicated to DR region)
   - Expected deployment time: 10-15 minutes

2. Provision Supporting Infrastructure:
   - Redis ElastiCache cluster (pre-provisioned in DR region)
   - S3 buckets (already replicated via Cross-Region Replication)
   - Secrets Manager secrets (already replicated)

3. Smoke Test Critical Paths:
   - Authentication flow (login, token refresh)
   - API CRUD operations
   - File upload/download
   - AI generation features
```

**Phase 5: Service Validation and Go-Live** (T+120 to T+180 minutes)

```
1. Comprehensive Testing:
   - Execute critical user journeys (login, create, read, update, delete)
   - Verify external integrations (Auth0, OpenAI, payment processors)
   - Load test with simulated traffic (10-20% of production load)
   - Validate monitoring and alerting operational

2. Go-Live Decision:
   - Incident commander reviews test results
   - Confirm all critical functionality operational
   - Accept minor feature degradation if necessary (e.g., missing analytics)
   - Declare DR region active

3. Communication:
   - Update status page: "Service Restored in Backup Region"
   - Email notification to customers about restoration and any data loss window
   - Social media update if public-facing service
   - Internal post-mortem scheduled
```

**Phase 6: Post-Restoration** (After service restored)

```
1. Monitoring and Stabilization:
   - 24/7 monitoring for 48 hours post-restoration
   - Increased alerting sensitivity for anomalies
   - Continuous capacity monitoring (ensure DR region has sufficient capacity)

2. Data Loss Assessment:
   - Identify exact RPO (time between last backup and disaster)
   - Communicate data loss window to affected customers
   - Provide data recovery options if available

3. Primary Region Recovery Planning:
   - Monitor AWS Service Health for primary region restoration
   - Plan failback to primary region (typically 1-2 weeks after stable)
   - Schedule maintenance window for failback
```

**Phase 7: Post-Incident Review** (Within 48 hours)

```
1. Post-Mortem Meeting:
   - Timeline reconstruction: What happened when
   - What went well: Procedures that worked as expected
   - What went wrong: Gaps in procedures or execution
   - Action items: Improvements to processes, tooling, documentation

2. Runbook Updates:
   - Document actual vs. expected timelines
   - Update procedures based on lessons learned
   - Add troubleshooting steps for issues encountered

3. Customer Communication:
   - Detailed incident report with timeline
   - Explanation of data loss (if any)
   - Preventive measures implemented
   - Service credits or compensation (if applicable per SLA)
```

**DR Testing Schedule**:

```
Monthly: Backup restoration testing (restore to test environment)
Quarterly: Partial DR drill (database failover, application deployment to DR region, no DNS change)
Annually: Full DR drill (complete failover including DNS, live traffic to DR region for 1 hour)
```

#### 6.1.4.3 Data Redundancy Approach

The architecture implements comprehensive data redundancy across all storage layers to ensure durability and availability.

**Database Layer Redundancy (MongoDB)**:

**Replica Set Architecture**:

```
MongoDB Replica Set Configuration:
├── Primary Node (us-east-1a)
│   ├── Accepts all write operations
│   ├── Replicates to secondaries via oplog
│   └── Source of truth for data
│
├── Secondary Node 1 (us-east-1b)
│   ├── Continuously applies oplog entries
│   ├── Available for read operations (if configured)
│   ├── Participates in primary election
│   └── Replication lag: typically < 1 second
│
└── Secondary Node 2 (us-east-1c)
    ├── Continuously applies oplog entries
    ├── Available for read operations (if configured)
    ├── Participates in primary election
    └── Replication lag: typically < 1 second
```

**Write Concern: "majority"**:

```
Write Operation Flow:
1. Application sends write to primary
2. Primary writes to its own database
3. Primary replicates write to secondaries via oplog
4. Secondary 1 acknowledges write
5. Secondary 2 acknowledges write
6. Primary confirms write to application (after majority acknowledgment)

Data Durability: 99.999999999% (eleven nines)
Failure Tolerance: Can lose 1 node without data loss
Consistency: Strong consistency (write not acknowledged until replicated to majority)
```

**Replication Process**:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant P as Primary Node
    participant S1 as Secondary 1
    participant S2 as Secondary 2
    
    App->>P: Write Operation (Insert/Update)
    P->>P: Write to local database
    P->>P: Write to oplog (operation log)
    
    P-->>S1: Replicate oplog entry
    P-->>S2: Replicate oplog entry
    
    S1->>S1: Apply oplog entry
    S2->>S2: Apply oplog entry
    
    S1-->>P: Acknowledgment
    S2-->>P: Acknowledgment
    
    Note over P: Write confirmed by majority
    
    P->>App: Write Acknowledged (Success)
```

**Replication Lag Monitoring**:
- Normal: < 1 second lag between primary and secondaries
- Warning: 5-10 seconds lag (indicates secondary under load or network issues)
- Critical: > 30 seconds lag (requires investigation)

**Sharding for Horizontal Data Distribution** (Future Evolution):

When data volume exceeds single replica set capacity:

```
Sharded Cluster Architecture:
├── Shard 1 (Replica Set A)
│   ├── Primary Node
│   └── 2× Secondary Nodes
│   └── Data: users with user_id 0-3333
│
├── Shard 2 (Replica Set B)
│   ├── Primary Node
│   └── 2× Secondary Nodes
│   └── Data: users with user_id 3334-6666
│
├── Shard 3 (Replica Set C)
│   ├── Primary Node
│   └── 2× Secondary Nodes
│   └── Data: users with user_id 6667-9999
│
└── Config Servers (Replica Set)
    └── Store cluster metadata

Query Routers (mongos): Direct queries to appropriate shard(s)
```

**Benefits of Sharding**:
- Data distributed across multiple replica sets (horizontal scaling)
- Each shard maintains high availability through replica set architecture
- Write throughput scales linearly with shard count
- Storage capacity scales to petabyte scale

**Cache Layer Redundancy (Redis)**:

**ElastiCache Cluster Mode Configuration**:

```
Redis Cluster Mode Enabled:
├── Shard 1
│   ├── Primary Node (us-east-1a)
│   └── Replica Node (us-east-1b)
│
├── Shard 2
│   ├── Primary Node (us-east-1b)
│   └── Replica Node (us-east-1c)
│
└── Shard 3
    ├── Primary Node (us-east-1c)
    └── Replica Node (us-east-1a)

Data Distribution: Hash slots (0-16383) distributed across shards
Automatic Failover: Replica promoted to primary on failure (< 60 seconds)
Multi-AZ: Nodes distributed across availability zones
```

**Redis Failure Handling**:

```
Cache Failure Scenarios:
1. Single Redis node failure:
   - Automatic failover to replica (< 60 seconds)
   - Brief cache unavailability (requests fall back to database)
   - No data loss for primary cache (AOF persistence)

2. Complete cache cluster failure:
   - All requests fall back to database (graceful degradation)
   - Performance impact: Latency increases 5ms → 50-200ms
   - Application remains functional (cache is performance optimization)
   - Cache rebuilds naturally as requests hit database

Impact: Performance degradation but not service failure
```

**Optional Redis Persistence** (AOF - Append-Only File):
- Every write operation logged to disk
- Enables cache recovery after failure
- Trade-off: Slight performance overhead (5-10%) for persistence

**Object Storage Redundancy (S3)**:

**S3 Standard Storage Durability Architecture**:

```
Automatic Replication:
- Every object replicated to minimum 3 devices
- Devices spread across multiple facilities within AWS region
- Redundant storage across multiple Availability Zones
- Automatic integrity verification (checksums)

Durability: 99.999999999% (eleven nines)
Calculation: Expected to lose 1 object per 10 billion stored for 10,000 years

Availability: 99.99% (four nines)
Calculation: Designed for 52 minutes downtime per year
```

**S3 Versioning**:

```
Versioning Configuration: Enabled for critical buckets

Behavior:
- Every PUT creates a new version (previous versions retained)
- DELETE creates delete marker (doesn't actually delete object)
- Previous versions remain accessible until explicitly deleted

Benefits:
- Accidental deletion protection (restore previous version)
- Accidental overwrite protection (all versions retained)
- Ransomware protection (restore pre-encryption versions)

Lifecycle:
- Current version: Retained indefinitely
- Non-current versions: Retained for 90 days, then deleted
```

**Cross-Region Replication (CRR)**:

```
Configuration:
- Source Region: us-east-1
- Destination Region: us-west-2
- Replication Time: < 15 minutes for most objects
- Scope: Critical data buckets (user uploads, backups)

Benefits:
- Regional disaster recovery (data survives region failure)
- Lower latency access (serve from nearest region)
- Compliance requirements (data residency in multiple regions)

Replication Details:
- New objects: Automatically replicated after upload
- Existing objects: Requires batch replication job
- Encryption: Preserved during replication
- Permissions: Can be synchronized or independent
```

**Application State Redundancy**:

**Stateless Design = Minimal State to Replicate**:

```
Application State Storage:
- Session Data: Redis (replicated, multi-AZ)
- User Profiles: MongoDB (replica set, multi-AZ)
- Configuration: Environment variables + AWS Secrets Manager (multi-AZ)
- Uploaded Files: S3 (multi-AZ + cross-region replication)

No Local State:
- Containers have zero local persistent state
- Container failure loses no data
- Any container can be destroyed and recreated at any time
```

**Configuration and Secrets Redundancy**:

**AWS Secrets Manager**:

```
Redundancy Features:
- Automatic multi-AZ replication within primary region
- Cross-region replication: Replicate secrets to DR region
- Versioning: Previous secret versions retained (up to 100 versions)
- Automatic rotation: Database credentials rotated every 90 days
- Encryption: Secrets encrypted at rest with AWS KMS

Recovery:
- Secrets available across all AZs in region (AZ failure has no impact)
- Secrets replicated to DR region available for regional failover
- Previous versions recoverable if rotation causes issues
```

**Terraform State**:

```
State File Storage: S3 with versioning enabled
State Locking: DynamoDB table (prevents concurrent modifications)

Redundancy:
- S3 versioning retains all previous state versions
- S3 multi-AZ replication (standard S3 storage)
- Optional: Cross-region replication to DR region
- DynamoDB global tables (multi-region replication)

Recovery:
- Restore previous Terraform state version if current state corrupted
- Rebuild infrastructure from latest state file
- Import existing resources if state file completely lost
```

#### 6.1.4.4 Failover Configurations

The system implements automated failover at multiple layers to ensure continuous availability despite component failures.

**Container-Level Automated Failover** (Fastest Recovery):

```
ECS Health Check Failover Configuration:

Health Check:
- Endpoint: GET /health
- Interval: 30 seconds
- Timeout: 3 seconds
- Unhealthy Threshold: 3 consecutive failures (90 seconds total)
- Healthy Threshold: 2 consecutive successes (60 seconds total)

Failover Process:
1. Container becomes unhealthy (application crash, deadlock, out of memory)
2. 3 consecutive health check failures (T+90 seconds)
3. ALB marks target unhealthy, stops routing new requests
4. Connection draining: Existing requests complete (30 seconds timeout)
5. ECS terminates unhealthy container
6. ECS launches replacement container from ECR image (~30-60 seconds)
7. Health checks on new container (2 successes = 60 seconds)
8. ALB marks new container healthy, routes traffic
9. Total failover time: ~180-270 seconds (3-4.5 minutes)

User Impact: Zero (ALB routes to healthy containers during entire process)
Data Loss: Zero (stateless application, all data in external storage)
```

**Automatic Failover Triggers**:
- Application process crash or hang
- Out of memory errors (OOMKilled)
- Dependency failures (database unreachable)
- Health check endpoint timeout or error
- Manual container termination (during deployment)

**Database Replica Set Automated Failover**:

```
MongoDB Replica Set Failover:

Trigger Conditions:
- Primary node becomes unreachable (network partition, hardware failure)
- Primary node overloaded (excessive replication lag)
- Manual stepdown (maintenance operations)

Failover Process:
1. Heartbeat failures detected (2-10 seconds)
2. Secondary nodes initiate election protocol (Raft consensus)
3. Secondary with most recent oplog data wins election
4. Elected secondary promotes itself to primary (10-20 seconds)
5. MongoDB driver detects topology change automatically
6. Application reconnects to new primary transparently
7. Total failover time: 10-30 seconds

Write Availability: Unavailable during election (10-30 seconds)
Read Availability: Maintained (reads from secondaries if configured)
Data Loss: Zero (write concern "majority" ensures durability)
User Impact: Brief write unavailability (10-30 seconds)
```

**Replica Set Failover State Machine**:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PrimaryActive: Replica Set Initialized
    PrimaryActive --> PrimaryUnreachable: Primary Failure Detected
    PrimaryUnreachable --> ElectionInProgress: Secondaries Start Election
    ElectionInProgress --> NewPrimaryElected: Majority Vote Achieved
    NewPrimaryElected --> PrimaryActive: New Primary Accepts Writes
    
    PrimaryActive: Primary Node Active<br/>All writes to primary<br/>Reads from primary or secondaries
    PrimaryUnreachable: Primary Unreachable<br/>Writes unavailable<br/>Reads continue from secondaries
    ElectionInProgress: Election Protocol Running<br/>10-20 seconds duration<br/>No writes accepted
    NewPrimaryElected: New Primary Promoted<br/>Topology change<br/>Drivers reconnect automatically
```

**Application Connection Handling During Failover**:

```python
# MongoDB driver handles failover automatically:

from pymongo import MongoClient

#### Connection with automatic failover support
client = MongoClient(
    "mongodb://primary,secondary1,secondary2/?replicaSet=rs0",
    serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000,    # Timeout for server selection
    connectTimeoutMS=10000,           # Connection timeout
    retryWrites=True,                 # Automatically retry writes
    maxPoolSize=10                    # Connection pool size
)

#### During failover:
#### Write attempts during election period timeout or raise error
#### Application retry logic attempts write again
#### Driver discovers new primary automatically
#### Retried write succeeds on new primary
```

**Availability Zone Failover** (Multi-AZ Deployment):

```
Multi-AZ Failure Scenario:

Initial State:
- AZ-A: 2 containers, MongoDB Secondary
- AZ-B: 2 containers, MongoDB Primary
- AZ-C: 0 containers, MongoDB Secondary

Failure: Availability Zone B complete outage

Immediate Impact:
- 2 of 4 containers offline (50% capacity loss)
- MongoDB primary offline (triggers replica set failover)
- ALB detects unhealthy targets in AZ-B (health checks fail)

Automatic Recovery:
1. ALB immediately stops routing to AZ-B (< 10 seconds)
2. Traffic routed to healthy AZ-A containers (100% of requests to 50% capacity)
3. MongoDB election: AZ-A or AZ-C secondary promoted to primary (10-30 seconds)
4. ECS auto-scaling detects high CPU/memory in remaining containers
5. ECS launches replacement tasks in AZ-A and AZ-C (5-10 minutes)
6. New containers pass health checks, ALB routes traffic (1-2 minutes)
7. Total recovery: 10-15 minutes to full capacity

User Impact:
- Brief write unavailability during database failover (10-30 seconds)
- Performance degradation during reduced capacity (5-10 minutes)
- No data loss (replica set durability)
```

**Regional Disaster Failover** (Manual Process):

Regional failover is intentionally manual to prevent accidental failover during transient issues:

```
Trigger Conditions (requiring manual intervention):
- Complete regional outage affecting all AZs (rare)
- AWS declares sustained regional failure (official Service Health Dashboard)
- Estimated recovery time > 2 hours

Manual Failover Process:
1. Incident commander declares disaster recovery activation
2. Update Route 53 DNS to DR region (T+15 minutes)
3. Restore database from backup to DR region (T+30-120 minutes)
4. Deploy application containers in DR region (T+30-60 minutes)
5. Validate service functionality (T+120-180 minutes)
6. Declare service restored (T+4 hours RTO)

Automation Level: Semi-automated (scripts exist, manual execution)
Decision: Manual (prevents accidental failover from false alarms)
```

**Failover Testing and Validation**:

Regular testing ensures failover procedures work as expected:

| Failover Type | Testing Frequency | Test Method | Success Criteria |
|--------------|------------------|-------------|------------------|
| **Container Failover** | Weekly (automatic) | Routine deployments trigger rolling restart | Zero errors, zero downtime |
| **Database Failover** | Quarterly | Manual primary stepdown in test environment | < 30 seconds failover, zero data loss |
| **AZ Failover** | Annually | Simulate AZ failure using AWS Fault Injection Simulator | Service continues, auto-recovery within 15 min |
| **Regional Failover** | Annually | Full DR drill with actual DNS change | < 4 hour RTO, successful validation |

**Failover Notification and Alerting**:

```
Automated Alerts:
- Container failover: CloudWatch log (no page-out if < 2 containers)
- Database failover: PagerDuty alert to on-call engineer
- AZ failover: PagerDuty alert + status page update
- Regional failover: PagerDuty alert + incident commander notification

Manual Notifications:
- Status page updated for events causing > 5 minutes impact
- Customer email notification for data loss events
- Post-mortem report published within 48 hours
```

#### 6.1.4.5 Service Degradation Policies

Service degradation enables the system to continue providing core functionality when component failures occur, prioritizing critical features while gracefully disabling non-essential capabilities.

**Service Tier Classification**:

Services are classified into tiers based on criticality to core user workflows:

**Tier 1: Core Services** (Must remain operational):
- Authentication (JWT validation with cached keys)
- User session management
- Core API request/response (read operations)
- Basic conversation retrieval
- File access (read from S3)

**Tier 2: Enhanced Services** (Degrade gracefully):
- AI/ML features (LLM generation)
- Real-time features (SSE streaming)
- File uploads (can be queued)
- Complex analytics
- Search functionality

**Tier 3: Non-Essential Services** (Can be disabled):
- Background analytics processing
- Email notifications (can be queued)
- Non-critical reports
- Audit logging (buffer locally)
- Usage statistics

**Degradation Decision Matrix**:

| Component Failure | Degradation Strategy | Tier 1 Impact | Tier 2 Impact | Tier 3 Impact |
|------------------|---------------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| **Redis Cache Completely Down** | Fall back to database | Increased latency (50-200ms) | Functional | May be disabled |
| **OpenAI API Unavailable** | Fallback to Anthropic, then cached responses | None | Fallback AI model | Disabled |
| **MongoDB Secondary Down** | Continue on primary only | None | None | None |
| **MongoDB Primary Down (during failover)** | Brief write unavailability (10-30s) | Read-only mode | Read-only mode | Disabled |
| **S3 Upload Unavailable** | Queue uploads for retry | None | Queue for later | Disabled |
| **Auth0 Down** | JWT validation continues with cached keys | Existing sessions continue | New logins fail | Disabled |

**Degradation Scenarios and User Experience**:

**Scenario 1: Redis Cache Complete Failure**

```
Degradation Response:
- All cache operations fall back to database
- Application continues normal operation
- No features disabled
- Performance impact only

Technical Implementation:
try:
    data = redis_client.get(cache_key)
except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError):
    logger.warning("Cache unavailable, falling back to database")
    data = database.query(...)

User Impact:
- Increased response time: 5ms → 50-200ms
- All functionality remains available
- No visible error messages (transparent degradation)

User Notification: None (silent degradation)
Monitoring: CloudWatch alarm triggers, on-call engineer notified
```

**Scenario 2: LLM Provider Failure (OpenAI Unavailable)**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User Requests AI Generation] --> B{OpenAI Available?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use OpenAI GPT-4<br/>Normal Service]
    B -->|Circuit Open| D{Anthropic Available?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Use Anthropic Claude<br/>Display: Using backup AI]
    D -->|Circuit Open| F{Cached Response Exists?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Return Cached Similar Response<br/>Display: This is a cached response]
    F -->|No| H[Display Error Message<br/>AI temporarily unavailable]
    
    style C fill:#90EE90
    style E fill:#FFD700
    style G fill:#FFA500
    style H fill:#FF6B6B
```

**User Notifications**:
```
Tier 2 Degradation (Anthropic fallback):
Banner: "AI features running in backup mode. Response quality maintained."
Color: Yellow (warning)
Dismissible: Yes

Tier 3 Degradation (Cached response):
Banner: "This response is cached and may not reflect the latest information. AI features currently unavailable."
Color: Orange (caution)
Dismissible: No (important context)

Complete Failure:
Message: "AI features are temporarily unavailable. Please try again in a few minutes. Check our status page for updates."
Color: Red (error)
Link: https://status.6nove4.com
```

**Scenario 3: Database Primary Failure (During Failover)**

```
Degradation Response:
- Switch to read-only mode during election (10-30 seconds)
- Write operations return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
- Read operations continue from secondaries
- Retry-After header indicates retry timing

User Impact:
- Read operations: Continue normally (no impact)
- Write operations: "Service temporarily unavailable, please retry in 30 seconds"
- Auto-retry: Client automatically retries after 30 seconds

HTTP Response:
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": {
    "code": "SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE",
    "message": "Write operations temporarily unavailable during database maintenance. Please retry shortly.",
    "retry_after_seconds": 30
  }
}
```

**Scenario 4: File Upload Failure (S3 Unavailable)**

```
Degradation Response:
- Queue upload requests for background processing
- Return acknowledgment immediately
- Process uploads when S3 recovers
- Notify user of upload completion

User Experience:
1. User initiates file upload
2. Application detects S3 unavailability
3. Display message: "File uploads are queued due to temporary service issues. You'll be notified when your upload completes."
4. File stored temporarily in Redis or database (if small)
5. Background job retries upload every 5 minutes
6. Email notification or push notification when upload succeeds

Alternative: Disable upload UI entirely
Display: "File uploads temporarily unavailable. Please try again later."
```

**Service Health API**:

Public-facing health endpoint provides detailed service status:

```
GET /api/v1/health

Response (Normal):
{
  "status": "operational",
  "services": {
    "api": {"status": "operational", "latency_ms": 45},
    "database": {"status": "operational", "latency_ms": 15},

**Feature Flags for Graceful Degradation**:

Feature flags enable dynamic enabling/disabling of features without deployment:

from feature_flags import is_enabled

def generate_ai_response(prompt, user_id):

## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Overview and Technology Selection

#### 6.2.1.1 Database Technology Stack

The 6nove_4 system is architected with MongoDB 6.0+ as the primary database, deployed on MongoDB Atlas as a fully managed service. This architectural decision reflects the project's greenfield status and the need for schema flexibility during the initial development phases when data structures evolve rapidly based on emerging requirements and user feedback.

**Important Context**: This documentation describes the planned database architecture for a greenfield project currently in the planning phase. No implementation code currently exists in the repository, and all specifications represent intended architecture subject to validation during development.

MongoDB's document-oriented NoSQL architecture was selected over traditional relational databases based on several critical technical justifications. The document model's inherent schema flexibility enables the accommodation of evolving data structures without requiring complex migration scripts or downtime for schema alterations—a capability particularly valuable during the early stages of product development. The JSON-like BSON format aligns naturally with the application's JavaScript/TypeScript frontend and Python backend, eliminating impedance mismatch between application objects and database representations. MongoDB's horizontal scaling capabilities through replica sets and sharding provide a clear evolution path from initial deployment to enterprise scale without architectural redesign.

#### 6.2.1.2 Deployment Architecture

**MongoDB Atlas** serves as the recommended deployment platform, providing enterprise-grade managed database services with automatic operational management. Atlas eliminates operational overhead through fully managed replica set configuration, automatic backups with point-in-time recovery capabilities extending to 24-hour granularity, built-in monitoring with performance advisors that identify slow queries and recommend index optimizations, and global cluster capabilities enabling future multi-region deployment for geographic distribution and disaster recovery.

The Atlas free tier (M0 cluster with 512MB storage) supports initial development and prototyping, with seamless upgrading to production-grade clusters (M30 and above) as requirements grow. This deployment model significantly reduces time-to-market by eliminating database administration complexity while maintaining production-grade reliability and security.

**Alternative Deployment Options** were evaluated during architectural planning. Amazon DocumentDB provides MongoDB-compatible API (version 4.0 compatibility) with tight AWS integration but limited feature support compared to native MongoDB. Self-managed deployment on AWS EC2 or ECS offers maximum configuration control and potential cost optimization at scale but introduces substantial operational burden for backup management, monitoring infrastructure, security patch application, and high availability configuration. The Atlas managed service strikes an optimal balance for initial implementation, with transition to self-managed infrastructure remaining an option if cost optimization becomes critical at scale.

#### 6.2.1.3 Database Role in System Architecture

The Data Persistence Layer serves as the authoritative source of truth for all application state, integrating with multiple system components through well-defined interfaces. The Business Logic Layer interacts with MongoDB through the PyMongo driver, implementing the repository pattern to abstract database operations from business logic. The AI/ML Service Layer stores conversation history for context management, document content for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows, and optionally vector embeddings for semantic search. The Caching Layer implements cache-aside patterns where Redis serves as the primary cache, falling back to MongoDB on cache misses and populating the cache with query results for subsequent requests.

This architecture ensures that MongoDB remains the single source of truth while Redis optimizes read performance, reducing database query load by an anticipated 60-80% for read-heavy workloads and improving API response times from 50-200ms to under 5ms for cached data.

### 6.2.2 Schema Design and Data Models

#### 6.2.2.1 Data Modeling Principles

MongoDB's document-oriented model enables flexible schema design through strategic application of embedding and referencing patterns. The fundamental decision between embedding related data within a document versus referencing separate documents significantly impacts query performance, data consistency, and storage efficiency.

**Embedding Strategy** is applied when related data exhibits the following characteristics: data is consistently accessed together (reading a user profile always includes preferences), the relationship has bounded cardinality (a user has a limited, predictable number of addresses), the embedded data changes infrequently relative to the parent document, and atomicity is required for updates to both parent and embedded data. For example, user preferences are embedded within user documents since they are invariably accessed together, have limited size, and updates to preferences should be atomic with user profile updates.

**Referencing Strategy** is employed when data access patterns indicate: related data is frequently accessed independently (user information is queried without requiring conversation history), relationships have unbounded growth potential (a user may have thousands of conversations that would exceed document size limits), the same data is referenced from multiple parent documents (avoiding duplication), and independent scaling of related collections is beneficial. Conversations reference user IDs rather than embedding complete user objects, enabling efficient queries for either users or conversations without data duplication.

**Document Size Constraints** impose a practical limit of 16MB per MongoDB document, though best practices recommend keeping documents well below this threshold (typically under 1-2MB) to maintain query performance and avoid BSON parsing overhead. Large files exceeding 16MB utilize GridFS, MongoDB's specification for storing large files by dividing them into chunks stored across two collections.

**Denormalization Approach** strategically accepts controlled data duplication to optimize read performance. For instance, storing a user's name both in the users collection and denormalized within conversation documents enables displaying conversation participants without joining to the users collection. This trade-off exchanges some write complexity and storage overhead for significant read performance improvements—critical for user-facing queries where milliseconds matter.

#### 6.2.2.2 Core Data Collections

The database architecture organizes data into logically separated collections, each optimized for specific access patterns and consistency requirements. The following collections represent the illustrative core schema, subject to refinement during implementation as specific feature requirements emerge.

**users Collection** - User Identity and Profile Management:
```
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),           // Primary key
  user_id: "auth0|123456789",     // Auth0 identifier (unique, indexed)
  email: "user@example.com",       // Email address (unique, indexed)
  profile: {                       // Embedded profile data
    display_name: "John Doe",
    avatar_url: "https://cdn.../avatar.jpg",
    bio: "Product manager...",
    timezone: "America/New_York"
  },
  preferences: {                   // Embedded user preferences
    language: "en",
    theme: "dark",
    notifications: {
      email: true,
      push: true,
      frequency: "daily"
    }
  },
  roles: ["user", "beta_tester"],  // Authorization roles
  account_status: "active",        // Indexed for filtering
  created_at: ISODate("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"),
  updated_at: ISODate("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"),
  last_login_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T15:30:00Z")
}
```

This schema embeds profile and preferences as subdocuments since they are always accessed together and have bounded size. The email and user_id fields maintain unique indexes to support authentication workflows and prevent duplicate accounts.

**conversations Collection** - Chat History and LLM Interactions:
```
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  conversation_id: "conv_abc123",       // Application identifier (indexed)
  user_id: "auth0|123456789",           // Referenced user (indexed)
  title: "Product Roadmap Discussion",
  messages: [                            // Embedded message array
    {
      message_id: "msg_001",
      role: "user",                      // user | assistant | system
      content: "What features should we prioritize?",
      timestamp: ISODate("2024-01-20T10:00:00Z"),
      metadata: {
        model: null,
        tokens: null
      }
    },
    {
      message_id: "msg_002",
      role: "assistant",
      content: "Based on user feedback...",
      timestamp: ISODate("2024-01-20T10:00:05Z"),
      metadata: {
        model: "gpt-4",
        tokens: 150,
        latency_ms: 2500
      }
    }
  ],
  context: {                             // Conversation metadata
    total_messages: 2,
    total_tokens: 150,
    last_activity: ISODate("2024-01-20T10:00:05Z")
  },
  status: "active",                      // active | archived | deleted
  created_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T10:00:00Z"),
  updated_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T10:00:05Z")
}
```

Messages are embedded as an array within conversations since they are always accessed together and represent a logical unit. The array structure enables efficient chronological retrieval and atomic updates when appending new messages. For very long conversations exceeding practical document sizes, a windowing strategy archives older messages to a separate collection while maintaining recent message context.

**documents Collection** - Document Storage and Management:
```
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  document_id: "doc_xyz789",
  user_id: "auth0|123456789",          // Owner reference (indexed)
  title: "Q1 2024 Strategy",
  content: "...",                       // Full document text
  content_type: "text/markdown",
  metadata: {
    file_size: 45678,
    word_count: 2500,
    language: "en",
    tags: ["strategy", "planning", "2024"]
  },
  s3_reference: {                       // Optional S3 storage for large files
    bucket: "6nove4-documents-prod",
    key: "documents/auth0|123456789/doc_xyz789.md",
    version_id: "abc123"
  },
  embeddings: {                         // Optional vector embeddings
    model: "text-embedding-ada-002",
    vector: [0.123, -0.456, ...],      // 1536-dimensional vector
    generated_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T11:00:00Z")
  },
  permissions: {                        // Access control
    owner: "auth0|123456789",
    shared_with: ["auth0|987654321"],
    visibility: "private"               // private | shared | public
  },
  status: "active",
  created_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T11:00:00Z"),
  updated_at: ISODate("2024-01-20T12:30:00Z")
}
```

Documents store content directly for small to medium-sized files while optionally referencing S3 for larger files. Vector embeddings enable semantic search capabilities, storing the embedding model identifier for versioning and the dense vector representation for cosine similarity queries.

**configurations Collection** - Application Settings and Feature Flags:
```
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  config_key: "feature.ai_generation",   // Unique identifier (indexed)
  config_value: {
    enabled: true,
    providers: ["openai", "anthropic"],
    default_model: "gpt-4",
    fallback_model: "claude-3",

    }
  },
