#### 6.3.4.2 Auth0 Authentication Integration

Auth0 provides comprehensive authentication services, eliminating the need to build and maintain a secure authentication system in-house.

**Auth0 Capabilities Leveraged**:

- **Authentication Protocols**: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0
- **Social Login**: Pre-built integrations with Google, Facebook, GitHub, Microsoft
- **Multi-Factor Authentication**: SMS, email, authenticator apps, biometric
- **Security Features**: Breach password detection, bot detection, anomaly detection
- **User Management**: Profiles, roles, permissions, metadata management

**Integration Architecture**:

**Frontend to Auth0**: Client applications redirect users to Auth0-hosted login pages, eliminating the need to handle credentials directly and ensuring security best practices.

**Backend Token Validation**: Flask API validates JWT tokens by verifying signatures using Auth0's public keys (JWKS endpoint), with keys cached for 24 hours in Redis to reduce latency.

**Resilience Strategy**: JWKS caching enables JWT validation to continue even if Auth0 API is temporarily unreachable. Existing sessions remain functional while new logins fail gracefully with clear error messages.

#### 6.3.4.3 LLM Provider Integration (OpenAI / Anthropic)

The system implements a multi-provider fallback strategy for AI/ML capabilities, ensuring service continuity despite individual provider failures or rate limiting.

**Multi-Provider Fallback Chain**:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([AI Generation Request]) --> CheckCache{Similar Query<br/>in Cache?}
    
    CheckCache -->|Yes| ReturnCached[Return Cached Response<br/>Sub-millisecond latency]
    ReturnCached --> End1([Success])
    
    CheckCache -->|No| OpenAI{OpenAI<br/>Available?<br/>Circuit: Closed}
    
    OpenAI -->|Available| CallOpenAI[Call OpenAI GPT-4<br/>Primary Provider]
    CallOpenAI --> OpenAISuccess{Request<br/>Successful?}
    
    OpenAISuccess -->|Yes| CacheResponse[Cache Response<br/>Redis TTL: 1 hour]
    CacheResponse --> End2([Success])
    
    OpenAISuccess -->|No| OpenCircuit1[Open OpenAI<br/>Circuit Breaker]
    OpenCircuit1 --> Anthropic
    
    OpenAI -->|Circuit Open| Anthropic{Anthropic<br/>Available?<br/>Circuit: Closed}
    
    Anthropic -->|Available| CallAnthropic[Call Anthropic Claude<br/>Fallback Provider]
    CallAnthropic --> AnthropicSuccess{Request<br/>Successful?}
    
    AnthropicSuccess -->|Yes| CacheAnthropic[Cache Response]
    CacheAnthropic --> End3([Success])
    
    AnthropicSuccess -->|No| OpenCircuit2[Open Anthropic<br/>Circuit Breaker]
    OpenCircuit2 --> VectorSearch
    
    Anthropic -->|Circuit Open| VectorSearch{Cached Similar<br/>Response in Vector DB?}
    
    VectorSearch -->|Yes| ReturnSimilar[Return Similar Cached Response<br/>With Staleness Warning]
    ReturnSimilar --> End4([Degraded Success])
    
    VectorSearch -->|No| FailGracefully[Return Clear Error<br/>AI temporarily unavailable<br/>Retry guidance]
    FailGracefully --> End5([Failed])
    
    style Start fill:#90EE90
    style End1 fill:#90EE90
    style End2 fill:#90EE90
    style End3 fill:#FFD700
    style End4 fill:#FFA500
    style End5 fill:#FFB6C1
```

**Circuit Breaker Configuration by Provider**:

| Provider | Failure Threshold | Time Window | Open Duration | Half-Open Test Requests |
|----------|------------------|-------------|---------------|------------------------|
| **OpenAI API** | 5 failures | 60 seconds | 30 seconds | 5 requests |
| **Anthropic API** | 5 failures | 60 seconds | 30 seconds | 5 requests |

**Integration Details**:

**Prompt Engineering**: System constructs enhanced prompts combining system instructions, retrieved context from vector database, and user query.

**Context Window Management**: Automatic prompt truncation if combined content exceeds model limits (8K, 32K, 128K tokens depending on model).

**Token Usage Tracking**: Monitor token consumption for cost optimization, rate limiting enforcement, and billing purposes.

**Model Selection**: Dynamic routing between models based on query complexity, user tier, and cost constraints.

**Response Streaming**: Server-Sent Events deliver tokens in real-time as generated, reducing perceived latency from 15-30s to 1-2s.

**Result Caching**: Cache responses in Redis (1-hour TTL) and vector database (permanent with semantic search) to reduce API costs and improve response times for similar queries.

#### 6.3.4.4 AWS Service Integration

AWS provides comprehensive cloud infrastructure services supporting compute, storage, networking, security, and monitoring requirements.

**MongoDB Atlas Integration**:

**Deployment**: Fully managed MongoDB clusters on MongoDB Atlas (separate from AWS-managed DocumentDB for full feature compatibility).

**Configuration**:
- **Replica Set**: 3-node deployment (1 primary + 2 secondaries)
- **Write Concern**: `w: "majority"` for strong durability guarantees
- **Read Preference**: `primaryPreferred` for strong consistency with automatic failover
- **Automatic Failover**: 10-30 seconds total failover time when primary fails
- **Backup**: Continuous backup with point-in-time recovery (1-minute granularity, 24-hour retention)

**Redis ElastiCache Integration**:

**Deployment**: Cluster mode with automatic failover, multi-AZ deployment for high availability.

**Configuration**:
- **Failover Time**: < 60 seconds for automatic primary promotion
- **Persistence**: Optional AOF (Append-Only File) for data durability
- **Use Cases**: Session data, user profiles, API responses, LLM responses, rate limit counters

**Fallback Strategy**: Cache failures trigger graceful degradation where application falls back to MongoDB queries, maintaining functionality with increased latency (5ms → 50-200ms).

**S3 Object Storage Integration**:

**Pre-Signed URLs**: Enable direct client-to-S3 uploads, eliminating server passthrough and reducing bandwidth costs.

**Security**:
- **Time-Limited**: URLs expire after 5 minutes
- **Condition-Based**: Enforced file size and content-type restrictions
- **User-Scoped Paths**: Files stored with user-specific prefixes preventing unauthorized access

**Data Protection**:
- **Versioning**: Enabled for critical buckets protecting against accidental deletion
- **Cross-Region Replication**: Automatic replication to DR region (us-west-2)
- **Lifecycle Policies**: Automatic transition to cheaper storage classes (30 days → Infrequent Access, 90 days → Glacier Deep Archive)

**CloudFront CDN Integration**:

**Edge Caching**: Static assets cached at 450+ global edge locations.

**Performance**:
- **Cache TTL**: 24 hours for application bundles, 7 days for immutable assets
- **Latency Improvement**: 500ms → 20-50ms for international users
- **Cache Invalidation**: Versioned URLs enable aggressive caching without stale content concerns

**AWS Secrets Manager Integration**:

**Secret Storage**: API keys, database credentials, encryption keys stored encrypted with automatic multi-AZ replication.

**Automatic Rotation**: Database credentials rotated every 90 days with zero-downtime rotation procedures.

**Cross-Region Replication**: Secrets replicated to DR region for disaster recovery scenarios.

**AWS CloudWatch Integration**:

**Logging**: Application logs, API access logs, slow query logs aggregated for analysis.

**Metrics**: Custom metrics and dashboards for real-time monitoring.

**Alarms**: Threshold-based alerting for operational issues (high error rates, elevated latency, resource exhaustion).

**Log Retention**: 7 days in CloudWatch Logs, 7 years in S3 Glacier for compliance.

#### 6.3.4.5 API Gateway Configuration

**AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB)** serves as the API gateway providing Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancing, SSL/TLS termination, and health-based routing.

**ALB Configuration**:

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| **SSL/TLS Termination** | TLS 1.3 | Secure communication, offload encryption from containers |
| **Certificate Management** | AWS Certificate Manager | Automatic certificate renewal |
| **Load Balancing Algorithm** | Round-robin | Even distribution across healthy targets |
| **Sticky Sessions** | Disabled | Stateless design enables any-server-any-request |
| **Connection Draining** | 30 seconds | Graceful shutdown during deployments |
| **Idle Timeout** | 30 seconds | Close idle connections to free resources |
| **Deregistration Delay** | 30 seconds | Allow in-flight requests to complete |

**Health Check Configuration**:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant ALB as Application<br/>Load Balancer
    participant Container as Flask<br/>Container
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis
    
    Note over ALB,Cache: Health Check Every 30 Seconds
    
    ALB->>Container: GET /health
    Container->>DB: Test Connection<br/>(Simple Query)
    DB->>Container: Connection OK
    Container->>Cache: Test Connection<br/>(PING Command)
    Cache->>Container: PONG
    Container->>Container: Evaluate Health Status
    
    alt All Services Healthy
        Container->>ALB: 200 OK<br/>{"status": "healthy", "services": {...}}
        ALB->>ALB: Mark Target Healthy<br/>(After 2 consecutive successes)
    else Service Unhealthy
        Container->>ALB: 503 Service Unavailable<br/>{"status": "unhealthy", "services": {...}}
        ALB->>ALB: Mark Target Unhealthy<br/>(After 3 consecutive failures)
        ALB->>ALB: Stop Routing Traffic<br/>Trigger Container Replacement
    end
```

**Health Check Endpoint Response**:

```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "services": {
    "database": {
      "status": "connected",
      "latency_ms": 15
    },
    "cache": {
      "status": "connected",
      "latency_ms": 2
    },
    "external_apis": {
      "status": "operational"
    }
  },
  "version": "1.2.3"
}
```

**Traffic Routing Behavior**:

- **Healthy Target**: Receives traffic immediately, distributed round-robin across all healthy targets
- **Unhealthy Target**: Removed from rotation after 3 consecutive failures (90 seconds), no new connections routed
- **Recovery**: Target re-added to rotation after 2 consecutive successful health checks (60 seconds)
- **Zero-Downtime Deployment**: Rolling updates maintain service availability by launching new containers before terminating old ones

**Service Degradation Handling**:

When external services experience degradation or outages, the system implements graceful fallback strategies maintaining core functionality:

- **Auth0 Degradation**: JWT validation continues with cached JWKS keys, existing sessions remain functional, new logins fail with clear retry guidance
- **MongoDB Degradation**: Automatic replica set failover maintains availability, read-only mode during primary election (10-30 seconds)
- **Redis Degradation**: Transparent fallback to MongoDB queries, increased latency but full functionality
- **LLM Provider Degradation**: Multi-provider fallback chain (OpenAI → Anthropic → cached responses), clear user communication about degraded AI features
- **S3 Degradation**: Upload queuing for background retry, downloads served from CloudFront cache if available

### 6.3.5 Integration Resilience and Performance

#### 6.3.5.1 Circuit Breaker Pattern

Circuit breakers protect the system from cascading failures by failing fast when external services are unavailable, preventing resource exhaustion and reducing user-visible latency.

**Circuit Breaker State Machine**:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed: Initial State
    Closed --> Open: Failure Threshold Exceeded
    Open --> HalfOpen: Timeout Period Elapsed
    HalfOpen --> Closed: Test Requests Succeed
    HalfOpen --> Open: Test Requests Fail
    
    Closed: CLOSED STATE<br/>All requests proceed normally<br/>Track failure rate in time window<br/>Forward requests to external service
    
    Open: OPEN STATE<br/>All requests fail immediately<br/>Return cached data or fallback response<br/>No external service calls made<br/>User experiences fast failure (milliseconds)
    
    HalfOpen: HALF-OPEN STATE<br/>Limited test requests allowed<br/>Determine if service recovered<br/>Transition based on test results
```

**Circuit Breaker Benefits**:

- **Resource Protection**: Prevents thread exhaustion from requests waiting on unavailable services (30s timeout × 100 threads = entire pool blocked)
- **Improved User Experience**: Fast failure response (< 100ms) instead of slow timeout waiting (30+ seconds)
- **Cascade Prevention**: Failures in one external service don't cascade to system-wide outages
- **Automatic Recovery**: Circuit automatically closes when service recovers, resuming normal operation without manual intervention

#### 6.3.5.2 Integration Monitoring

**CloudWatch Metrics**:

Comprehensive monitoring tracks integration health and performance:

- **Request Rate**: Requests per second to each external service
- **Response Time Distribution**: P50, P95, P99 latency percentiles
- **Error Rate**: Errors by status code (4xx client errors, 5xx server errors)
- **Circuit Breaker State**: Track state transitions (closed → open → half-open → closed)
- **Rate Limit Violations**: Count and identify users hitting rate limits
- **External Service Latency**: Track third-party API response times

**CloudWatch Alarms**:

Automated alerting triggers operational response:

| Alarm | Threshold | Evaluation Period | Action |
|-------|-----------|------------------|--------|
| **High Error Rate** | > 5% of requests | 5 minutes | Page on-call engineer, investigate |
| **High Response Time** | P95 > 500ms | 10 minutes | Investigate performance degradation |
| **External Service Failures** | > 10 failures/minute | 2 minutes | Check service status, activate fallbacks |
| **Cache Unavailability** | No successful cache ops | 5 minutes | Investigate Redis cluster, validate fallback |
| **Database Connection Issues** | Connection pool exhaustion | 1 minute | Scale containers, investigate slow queries |
| **Circuit Breaker Open** | Circuit open for > 5 minutes | Immediate | Validate external service status, escalate |

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Security Architecture Overview

#### 6.4.1.1 Security Architecture Context

The 6nove_4 system implements a comprehensive security-first architecture designed to protect user data, ensure regulatory compliance, and maintain system integrity across all operational layers. The security design leverages industry-leading managed services including Auth0 for authentication, JWT-based authorization, AWS security services, and multi-layer data protection mechanisms to provide defense-in-depth protection against evolving security threats.

**Important Context**: This documentation describes the planned security architecture for a greenfield project currently in the planning phase. The repository contains only a placeholder README.md file, and no implementation code currently exists. All security specifications represent intended implementation approaches subject to validation and potential refinement during development based on security audits, penetration testing results, and evolving threat landscapes.

The security architecture implements zero-trust principles where explicit verification occurs at each layer, eliminating implicit trust relationships. Every request undergoes authentication verification, authorization checks validate permissions for specific operations, network segmentation isolates components by sensitivity, and comprehensive audit logging tracks all security-relevant events for forensic analysis and compliance reporting.

#### 6.4.1.2 Security Design Principles

The security architecture adheres to fundamental security principles informing all design decisions:

**Defense in Depth** - Multiple independent security layers ensure that compromise of a single layer does not expose the entire system. Network security controls restrict traffic flow, application-layer authentication verifies identity, authorization validates permissions, data encryption protects information at rest and in transit, and audit logging provides visibility into all security events.

**Least Privilege** - Users, services, and processes receive only the minimum permissions required to accomplish their designated functions. Database users operate with scoped permissions limited to necessary collections and operations, IAM roles grant service-specific permissions without overly broad access, JWT tokens embed only essential user context and permissions, and administrative access requires explicit elevation with audit trails.

**Secure by Default** - Security controls activate automatically without requiring explicit configuration, preventing security gaps from misconfigurations. Encryption at rest enables automatically for all databases and storage, HTTPS enforces by default with automatic certificate management, security headers apply to all API responses, authentication requirements protect all non-public endpoints, and rate limiting activates to prevent abuse without manual configuration.

**Fail Securely** - System failures default to secure states rather than exposing vulnerabilities. Authentication failures reject requests rather than granting access, authorization denials log security events for investigation, encryption failures prevent data access rather than serving unencrypted content, and circuit breakers fail closed when security services become unavailable.

**Audit and Accountability** - Comprehensive logging creates immutable records of all security-relevant events, supporting forensic investigation, compliance reporting, and threat detection. All authentication attempts log with outcomes, authorization failures trigger alerts for investigation, data access patterns enable anomaly detection, administrative actions maintain detailed audit trails, and compliance-related operations preserve records for regulatory retention periods.

### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

The system externalizes identity management to Auth0, a specialized identity platform providing enterprise-grade authentication services with minimal operational overhead. This architectural decision offloads the significant complexity of secure credential storage, multi-factor authentication implementation, breach password detection, and security vulnerability mitigation to a platform team with dedicated security expertise.

**Auth0 Platform Capabilities**:

Auth0 implements industry-standard authentication protocols including OAuth 2.0 for authorization delegation (RFC 6749), OpenID Connect (OIDC) for identity layer functionality providing standardized claims about authenticated users, and optionally SAML 2.0 for enterprise federation enabling single sign-on with corporate identity providers. The platform provides pre-built integrations with major social identity providers including Google, Facebook, GitHub, and Microsoft, eliminating custom integration development while maintaining consistent security controls.

**Identity Provider Architecture**:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Identity Sources"
        Database[Auth0 User Database<br/>Username/Password<br/>Hashed with bcrypt]
        Google[Google OAuth<br/>Social Login]

        GitHub[GitHub OAuth<br/>Developer Login]
    end
    
    subgraph "Auth0 Platform"
        AuthCore[Auth0 Core<br/>Identity Management<br/>Authentication Engine]
        MFA[Multi-Factor Auth<br/>SMS, Email, Authenticator<br/>Biometric]
        Rules[Auth0 Rules<br/>Custom Logic<br/>Claims Enrichment]
        Guardian[Auth0 Guardian<br/>Push Notifications<br/>Biometric Auth]
    end
    
    subgraph "Application Integration"
        Client[Client Applications<br/>Web/Mobile/Desktop]
        API[Flask API Gateway<br/>JWT Validation]
    end
    
    Database --> AuthCore
    Google --> AuthCore
    Microsoft --> AuthCore
    GitHub --> AuthCore
    
    AuthCore --> MFA
    MFA --> Guardian
    AuthCore --> Rules
    
    Client -->|OAuth 2.0 + PKCE| AuthCore

    Client -->|API Request + JWT| API

    style AuthCore fill:#87CEEB

    style API fill:#90EE90
```

Auth0 manages the complete user lifecycle including registration with email verification and password complexity enforcement, authentication with breach password detection preventing use of compromised credentials, profile management with extensible custom attributes, password reset through secure email-based workflows with time-limited tokens, account recovery with multi-factor recovery codes, and account linking enabling users to connect multiple identity providers to a single account.

**Security Certifications and Compliance**:

The Auth0 platform maintains rigorous third-party certifications validating security controls: SOC 2 Type II certification verifying controls for Security, Availability, and Confidentiality, ISO 27001 certification for information security management systems, GDPR compliance enabling European data sovereignty requirements, and CCPA compliance supporting California consumer privacy regulations. These certifications ensure that externalized authentication meets or exceeds the security standards achievable through in-house implementation while reducing audit scope and compliance burden.

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) provides defense against credential theft by requiring proof of identity beyond username and password. The system supports multiple MFA methods accommodating diverse user preferences and security requirements.

**Supported MFA Methods**:

| Method | Description | Security Level | User Experience |
|--------|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **SMS OTP** | Text message verification codes | Medium (vulnerable to SIM swapping) | High convenience, works on any phone |
| **Email OTP** | Email verification codes | Medium (email account compromise risk) | High convenience, no special device needed |
| **Authenticator Apps** | TOTP via Google Authenticator, Authy, etc. | High (offline token generation) | Moderate convenience, requires app installation |
| **Biometric** | Fingerprint, Face ID (device-supported) | High (device-bound credentials) | Excellent convenience on supported devices |

**MFA Enforcement Policies**:

MFA configuration operates per-user or per-role, enabling flexible security policies aligned with risk profiles. Administrative accounts require mandatory MFA preventing privilege escalation through compromised credentials. Standard users receive optional MFA with encouragement through UI prompts and security recommendations. Risk-based MFA triggers automatically detect suspicious patterns including unusual login locations geographic distance from typical locations, new or unrecognized devices without prior authentication history, impossible travel scenarios where login locations could not be physically reached in available time, and anomalous login times outside typical user activity patterns.

Auth0's anomaly detection engine analyzes login patterns across the entire platform, identifying potential account compromise indicators. When risk factors exceed configured thresholds, the system challenges users with MFA regardless of typical MFA requirements, providing adaptive security proportional to detected risk.

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

Session management maintains authentication state between the initial login and subsequent requests, enabling stateless API design while providing secure session tracking and automatic expiration.

**Redis-Based Session Storage**:

The system leverages Redis ElastiCache for distributed session storage, providing consistent session state across multiple application containers and geographic regions. Redis session storage offers sub-millisecond access latency compared to database-backed sessions reducing authentication overhead on every request, automatic expiration through built-in TTL support eliminating manual cleanup logic, atomic operations for concurrent session updates preventing race conditions, and multi-availability-zone replication ensuring session availability during infrastructure failures.

**Session Configuration and Lifecycle**:

```javascript
// Session structure in Redis
{
  "session:abc123def456": {
    "user_id": "auth0|123456789",
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "roles": ["user", "beta_tester"],
    "permissions": ["read:conversations", "write:conversations"],
    "last_activity": "2024-01-20T15:30:00Z",
    "device_info": {
      "device_id": "device_xyz789",
      "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0...",
      "ip_address": "203.0.113.42"
    },
    "created_at": "2024-01-20T14:00:00Z",
    "expires_at": "2024-01-20T15:30:00Z"
  }
}
```

Session duration implements a sliding window pattern where initial session creation establishes a 30-minute expiration, each authenticated request extends the expiration by an additional 30 minutes from the current time, and absolute maximum session duration prevents indefinite extension (typically 24 hours for standard users, 8 hours for administrative sessions). Explicit logout operations immediately delete the Redis session key, invalidating the session across all devices and preventing further use even if JWT access tokens remain valid but not yet expired.

**Concurrent Session Management**:

The architecture supports multiple concurrent sessions enabling users to authenticate from multiple devices simultaneously (desktop computer, mobile phone, tablet) without mutual interference. Each device maintains an independent session with separate session identifiers, enabling granular session management. Users can view active sessions through account settings, identifying devices by user agent, IP address, and last activity timestamp. Individual session revocation terminates specific device sessions without affecting other active sessions, supporting scenarios such as lost device reporting or suspicious activity detection.

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) implement the primary authorization mechanism, embedding user context and permissions directly within cryptographically signed tokens that APIs validate without database lookups.

**JWT Token Architecture**:

The system implements three distinct token types serving complementary purposes in the authentication and authorization flow:

**Access Tokens** - Short-lived JWT tokens (1-hour expiration) containing user identity and permissions, transmitted with every API request in the Authorization header. The token structure follows the standard JWT format with header specifying RS256 algorithm and token type, payload containing claims about the user including issuer, subject, audience, expiration, and custom claims for user_id, roles, and permissions, and signature generated using Auth0's private key enabling verification with the corresponding public key.

```json
{
  "header": {
    "alg": "RS256",
    "typ": "JWT",
    "kid": "key-identifier-123"
  },
  "payload": {
    "iss": "https://auth0-tenant.auth0.com/",
    "sub": "auth0|123456789",
    "aud": "api-audience-identifier",
    "exp": 1643645400,
    "iat": 1643641800,
    "scope": "openid profile email",
    "user_id": "auth0|123456789",
    "roles": ["user", "beta_tester"],
    "permissions": ["read:conversations", "write:conversations", "write:documents"]
  },
  "signature": "..."
}
```

**Refresh Tokens** - Long-lived opaque tokens (7-day expiration) enabling acquisition of new access tokens without re-authentication. Unlike JWTs, refresh tokens are random strings stored in Auth0's database, enabling revocation when compromise is detected. Refresh tokens store in HTTP-only cookies for web applications preventing JavaScript access and XSS attacks, or secure device storage for mobile applications using platform-specific secure storage mechanisms (iOS Keychain, Android KeyStore).

**ID Tokens** - Standard OpenID Connect tokens (1-hour expiration) containing user profile information. These tokens serve display purposes in client applications, providing user name, email, profile picture URL, and other identity attributes. ID tokens do not grant API access and should not be sent to backend APIs—access tokens serve that purpose exclusively.

**Token Validation Process**:

The API Gateway implements comprehensive JWT validation middleware executing on every authenticated endpoint:

1. **Token Extraction** - Parse the Authorization header expecting format `Bearer {token}`, rejecting requests with missing or malformed headers with HTTP 401 Unauthorized.

2. **Format Validation** - Verify JWT structure consists of three base64-encoded sections separated by periods (header.payload.signature), rejecting structurally invalid tokens before expensive cryptographic operations.

3. **Signature Verification** - Validate the RS256 signature using Auth0's public key retrieved from the JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) endpoint. The public key cryptographically verifies the token was signed by Auth0's private key and has not been tampered with.

4. **JWKS Caching Optimization** - Auth0 public keys cache in Redis for 24 hours significantly reducing validation latency from 50-100ms (JWKS endpoint request) to under 1ms (Redis cache retrieval). Cache invalidation occurs if signature verification fails with a cached key, automatically fetching fresh keys to handle Auth0 key rotation.

5. **Expiration Verification** - Compare the `exp` (expiration) claim against the current timestamp, rejecting expired tokens. Clock skew tolerance of 30 seconds accommodates minor time synchronization discrepancies between servers.

6. **Issuer Validation** - Confirm the `iss` (issuer) claim matches the configured Auth0 tenant URL, preventing token substitution attacks using JWTs from different issuers.

7. **Audience Validation** - Verify the `aud` (audience) claim matches the API's audience identifier, ensuring tokens intended for other APIs cannot be used to access this system.

8. **User Context Extraction** - Extract authentication context from validated claims including `user_id`, `roles`, and `permissions`, attaching this context to the request object for access by business logic layers.

9. **Request Forwarding** - Forward the authenticated request with attached user context to application business logic, where fine-grained authorization decisions occur based on resource ownership and permissions.

**Token Security Best Practices**:

The architecture implements security controls protecting tokens throughout their lifecycle: HTTPS-only transmission prevents interception over unsecured connections, short expiration times (1 hour for access tokens) limit exposure window if tokens are compromised, refresh token rotation issues new refresh tokens on each use invalidating the old token and preventing replay attacks, token revocation support through Auth0 Management API enables emergency token invalidation, HTTP-only cookies for web applications prevent JavaScript access eliminating XSS-based token theft, and PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for public clients (mobile apps, SPAs) prevents authorization code interception attacks.

#### 6.4.2.5 Password Policies

Strong password policies reduce the risk of credential-based attacks through enforcement of complexity requirements and detection of compromised passwords.

**Auth0-Enforced Password Requirements**:

Auth0 implements and enforces password policies configured through the dashboard:

- **Minimum Length**: 8 characters (configurable up to 128 characters), balancing security with usability
- **Complexity Requirements**: Enforced mix of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters preventing dictionary attacks
- **Breach Password Detection**: Automatic checking against databases of compromised passwords (Have I Been Pwned, security research datasets), rejecting passwords known to be compromised regardless of complexity
- **Password History**: Prevention of reusing the last N passwords (typically 5-10), preventing password cycling back to compromised credentials
- **Account Lockout**: Automatic account lock after N failed login attempts (typically 10 attempts within 15 minutes), preventing brute force attacks while accommodating legitimate user errors
- **Password Expiration**: Optional organizational policy requiring password changes every N days (typically 90 days for high-security environments), though current NIST guidelines recommend against forced expiration absent compromise indicators

**Password Storage Architecture**:

The system architecture never stores passwords within the application database—all password storage and verification occurs within Auth0's infrastructure. Auth0 utilizes industry-standard bcrypt hashing with automatically managed salt generation, computationally expensive hash calculations preventing rainbow table attacks, and adaptive work factor increases as computing power grows maintaining security over time. Application code never accesses plaintext passwords, eliminating password exposure risks from application vulnerabilities, database breaches affecting the application's database cannot expose passwords since they reside solely in Auth0, and password verification occurs exclusively through Auth0 API calls rather than direct hash comparisons.

**Password Reset Workflow**:

Auth0 provides self-service password reset functionality: users initiate password reset by entering their email address, Auth0 sends a time-limited password reset link (typically 1-hour expiration) to the verified email address, users click the link and enter a new password meeting complexity requirements, Auth0 validates the token and updates the password hash, and optionally mandates password change on first login for newly provisioned accounts ensuring default passwords don't persist.

### 6.4.3 Authorization System

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

Authorization decisions occur after successful authentication, implementing role-based access control (RBAC) where user roles and permissions embedded in JWT claims drive access decisions without database queries on every request.

**Multi-Layer Authorization Architecture**:

Authorization enforcement occurs at three distinct layers providing defense in depth:

**Layer 1: Authentication Middleware** - Executes on every API request before business logic invocation, validates JWT token authenticity and freshness, extracts user context including user_id, roles, and permissions from validated claims, attaches user context to request object for downstream access, and rejects requests with invalid, expired, or missing tokens returning HTTP 401 Unauthorized with clear error messages guiding client remediation.

**Layer 2: Route-Level Authorization** - Protects API endpoints based on required roles or permissions declared through decorators or middleware configuration. Before executing route handlers, the middleware checks whether the authenticated user's roles include required roles for the endpoint, verifies the user's permissions include required permissions for the operation, and rejects requests from users lacking sufficient authorization returning HTTP 403 Forbidden with details about missing permissions (in development environments) or generic denial messages (in production to prevent information disclosure).

```python
# Example route-level authorization decorator
@app.route('/api/v1/admin/users', methods=['GET'])
@require_authentication
@require_role('admin')
def list_all_users():
    # Only users with 'admin' role can access
    users = db.users.find({})
    return jsonify(list(users))

@app.route('/api/v1/conversations', methods=['POST'])
@require_authentication
@require_permission('write:conversations')
def create_conversation():
    # Requires specific permission
    user_context = get_user_context()
    conversation = create_new_conversation(user_context['user_id'], request.json)
    return jsonify(conversation), 201
```

**Layer 3: Resource-Level Authorization** - Validates user access to specific resource instances, implementing ownership checks and fine-grained permissions within business logic. This layer compares resource ownership with authenticated user identity, enforces sharing permissions for documents shared with specific users, validates time-based access restrictions (embargoed content, expired links), and checks cross-resource authorization such as whether user A can share document X with user B.

```python
# Example resource-level authorization
def get_conversation(conversation_id):
    user_context = get_user_context()
    conversation = db.conversations.find_one({'conversation_id': conversation_id})
    
    if not conversation:
        raise NotFoundError("Conversation not found")
    
    # Resource ownership check
    if conversation['user_id'] != user_context['user_id']:
        # Admin override
        if 'admin' not in user_context['roles']:
            raise ForbiddenError("Access denied to this conversation")
    
    return conversation
```

**Standard Role Definitions**:

The system defines a hierarchical role structure supporting future expansion:

- **user** - Standard authenticated user with basic permissions for personal resource management (conversations, documents, profile)
- **beta_tester** - Early access to beta features under development, enabling controlled feature rollout and feedback collection
- **moderator** - Content moderation capabilities for reviewing flagged content, managing reported users (future capability)
- **admin** - Full administrative access including user management, system configuration, and access to all resources regardless of ownership

Role membership stores in Auth0 and embeds in JWT claims, eliminating database lookups during authorization checks. Role modifications in Auth0 take effect on next token refresh (maximum 1 hour delay matching access token expiration).

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

Fine-grained permissions provide operation-level access control beyond coarse role assignments, enabling precise authorization policies.

**Permission Model**:

Permissions follow the format `action:resource` providing clear semantics: the action specifies the operation (read, write, delete, admin) and the resource identifies the target entity (profile, conversations, documents, users). Example permissions include:

- `read:profile` - View user profile information
- `write:profile` - Update user profile attributes
- `read:conversations` - List and view conversations
- `write:conversations` - Create and update conversations
- `delete:conversations` - Delete conversations
- `read:documents` - Access documents
- `write:documents` - Upload and modify documents
- `delete:documents` - Delete documents
- `admin:users` - Manage user accounts (admin only)

**Permission Assignment**:

Permissions assign to roles in Auth0 configuration, with roles then assigned to users. This indirection enables centralized permission management where modifying role permissions immediately affects all users with that role (on next token refresh), and role-based assignment simplifies user management compared to individual permission grants. Custom permission grants support edge cases where specific users require permissions outside their standard role.

**Permission Enforcement**:

Application code checks permissions at the point of access:

```python
def delete_document(document_id):
    user_context = get_user_context()
    
    # Permission check
    if 'delete:documents' not in user_context['permissions']:
        raise ForbiddenError("Insufficient permissions to delete documents")
    
    document = db.documents.find_one({'document_id': document_id})
    
    # Ownership check (even with delete permission)
    if document['user_id'] != user_context['user_id']:
        if 'admin' not in user_context['roles']:
            raise ForbiddenError("Can only delete own documents")
    
    db.documents.delete_one({'document_id': document_id})
    return {"status": "deleted", "document_id": document_id}
```

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

Resource-level authorization implements fine-grained access control over individual resource instances based on ownership, sharing permissions, and organizational hierarchy.

**Authorization Decision Matrix**:

| Resource | Action | Permission | Owner Check | Admin Override |
|----------|--------|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| User Profile | Read | `read:profile` | Own profile only | Yes |
| User Profile | Update | `write:profile` | Own profile only | Yes |
| Conversations | List | `read:conversations` | Own conversations | Yes |
| Conversations | Create | `write:conversations` | N/A | N/A |
| Conversations | Delete | `write:conversations` | Own conversations | Yes |
| Documents | Read | `read:documents` | Own + shared | Yes |
| Documents | Write | `write:documents` | Own documents | Yes |
| Documents | Delete | `write:documents` | Own documents | Yes |

**Document Sharing Authorization**:

Documents support sharing functionality enabling collaboration while maintaining security controls. Document owners can share documents with specific users granting read or write permissions, shared users inherit specified permissions (read-only or edit access), sharing permissions store in document metadata within the documents collection, and sharing audit trails maintain records of who shared what with whom and when.

```javascript
// Document schema with sharing permissions
{
  "document_id": "doc_xyz789",
  "user_id": "auth0|123456789",  // Owner
  "title": "Q1 Strategy",
  "permissions": {
    "owner": "auth0|123456789",
    "shared_with": [
      {
        "user_id": "auth0|987654321",
        "permission": "read",
        "shared_at": "2024-01-20T10:00:00Z",
        "shared_by": "auth0|123456789"
      },
      {
        "user_id": "auth0|111222333",
        "permission": "write",
        "shared_at": "2024-01-21T14:30:00Z",
        "shared_by": "auth0|123456789"
      }
    ],
    "visibility": "private"  // private | shared | public
  }
}
```

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

Security policy enforcement occurs at multiple system layers creating defense in depth where compromise of a single layer does not expose the entire system.

**Network Layer (AWS VPC & Security Groups)**:

Network-level access control restricts traffic flow between components based on AWS Security Groups acting as stateful firewalls. The Application Load Balancer accepts HTTPS traffic (port 443) only from the internet (0.0.0.0/0), application containers accept HTTP traffic (port 80) only from the ALB security group preventing direct internet access, MongoDB accepts connections (port 27017) only from application security group, Redis accepts connections (port 6379) only from application security group, and outbound traffic flows through NAT Gateways providing static IP addresses for external service IP whitelisting.

VPC Flow Logs capture all network traffic metadata enabling anomaly detection, suspicious connection pattern identification, and compliance audit trails. Logs export to CloudWatch Logs for analysis with 30-day retention in CloudWatch and 7-year retention in S3 Glacier for compliance.

**Application Layer (Flask Middleware)**:

Application middleware enforces security policies at the API level:

- **JWT Validation Middleware** - Executes on all authenticated endpoints, validates token authenticity and freshness, extracts user context, and attaches context to request object
- **Rate Limiting Middleware** - Enforces multi-tier rate limits (IP-based, user-based, endpoint-specific), prevents abuse and DoS attacks, and returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests when limits exceeded
- **Permission Checking Decorators** - Route-level authorization enforcement, validates required roles and permissions, and rejects unauthorized requests with 403 Forbidden
- **CORS Middleware** - Cross-origin resource sharing policy enforcement, allowlists trusted frontend domains, and restricts allowed methods and headers
- **Request Correlation** - Injects unique request ID for distributed tracing, enables request flow tracking across services, and facilitates debugging and audit trails

**Business Logic Layer**:

Application business logic implements fine-grained authorization:

- **Resource Ownership Validation** - Compares resource ownership with authenticated user identity
- **Fine-Grained Permission Checks** - Validates operation-specific permissions beyond route-level checks
- **Business Rule Enforcement** - Implements domain-specific authorization rules
- **Cross-Resource Authorization** - Validates complex authorization scenarios spanning multiple resources

**Data Layer (MongoDB & S3)**:

Data store access controls provide the final defense layer:

- **MongoDB User Roles** - Database users with least-privilege permissions (application_readwrite, application_readonly, backup_user)
- **Network Access Control** - IP whitelisting restricts connections to authorized sources
- **Encryption at Rest** - AES-256 encryption protects stored data
- **Audit Logging** - Database operations log for security monitoring

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

Comprehensive audit logging creates immutable records of security-relevant events supporting forensic investigation, compliance reporting, threat detection, and incident response.

**Audit Log Scope**:

Security audit logs capture:

- **Authentication Events** - Login attempts (success and failure), MFA challenges and outcomes, password reset requests, account lockouts, and session creation and termination
- **Authorization Failures** - Permission denied events with user identity, requested resource, required permission, and user's actual permissions
- **Resource Access** - Read/write/delete operations on sensitive resources, bulk operations affecting multiple resources, and data export requests
- **Administrative Actions** - User role changes, permission grants and revocations, configuration modifications, and feature flag changes
- **Security Events** - MFA enrollment and removal, password changes, suspicious activity detection, rate limit violations, and account security alerts
- **Compliance Events** - GDPR data deletion requests, data export requests, consent management, and data retention policy execution

**Audit Log Format**:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-20T15:30:45Z",
  "event_type": "authorization_failure",
  "event_id": "evt_abc123",
  "user": {
    "user_id": "auth0|123456789",
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "roles": ["user", "beta_tester"]
  },
  "resource": {
    "type": "conversation",
    "id": "conv_xyz789",
    "owner_id": "auth0|987654321"
  },
  "action": "DELETE",
  "required_permission": "write:conversations",
  "user_permissions": ["read:conversations"],
  "result": "DENIED",
  "reason": "Insufficient permissions and not resource owner",
  "metadata": {
    "request_id": "req_def456",
    "ip_address": "203.0.113.42",
    "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0...",
    "geo_location": "New York, US"
  }
}
```

**Audit Log Storage and Retention**:

Audit logs flow through multiple storage tiers balancing access performance with long-term retention:

- **Primary Storage**: CloudWatch Logs (30-day retention) - Real-time availability, searchable through CloudWatch Logs Insights, automated alerting on security patterns
- **Archive Storage**: S3 Glacier (7-year retention) - Compliance retention for regulatory requirements, immutable storage with object lock preventing tampering, cross-region replication for disaster recovery
- **Database Audit Events**: MongoDB audit logging captures database-level operations with structured log format, streams to CloudWatch for centralization, and retains for 1 year in MongoDB, 7 years in S3

**Audit Log Analysis**:

CloudWatch Logs Insights enables security event analysis through SQL-like queries:

```sql
-- Failed login attempts from single IP
fields @timestamp, user.email, metadata.ip_address
| filter event_type = "authentication_failure"
| stats count() by metadata.ip_address
| sort count desc
| limit 10

-- Authorization failures by user
fields @timestamp, user.email, resource.type, action, required_permission
| filter event_type = "authorization_failure"
| stats count() by user.email
| sort count desc

-- Administrative actions
fields @timestamp, user.email, event_type, resource.type, action
| filter event_type like "admin_"
| sort @timestamp desc
```

Automated CloudWatch Alarms trigger on security patterns: more than 10 failed login attempts from single IP in 5 minutes indicates brute force attack, authorization failures spike above baseline suggests privilege escalation attempts, unusual administrative actions outside business hours warrant investigation, and geographic anomalies where login location is impossible based on previous location and time difference indicate credential compromise.

### 6.4.4 Data Protection

#### 6.4.4.1 Encryption Standards

Data encryption protects information confidentiality at rest and in transit, ensuring unauthorized access to storage media or network traffic does not expose sensitive information.

**Encryption at Rest**:

All persistent data stores implement encryption at rest using industry-standard algorithms:

**MongoDB Atlas** - AES-256 encryption of all data files, indexes, journals, and backups using MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine encryption. Encryption operates transparently requiring no application code changes, keys manage through AWS Key Management Service with automatic rotation every 90 days, and encrypted backups ensure data remains protected throughout its lifecycle.

**AWS S3** - Server-side encryption with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3) or customer-managed keys in KMS (SSE-KMS). SSE-S3 provides default encryption for general-purpose storage with automatic key management, while SSE-KMS offers additional audit capabilities with CloudTrail logging of key usage. S3 object versioning protects against accidental deletion, and cross-region replication creates encrypted copies in disaster recovery regions.

**Redis ElastiCache** - Optional encryption at rest for AOF (Append-Only File) persistence. While in-memory data is inherently volatile, AOF persistence enables crash recovery, and encryption protects persisted snapshots. The trade-off involves 5-10% performance overhead for persistence encryption, which is acceptable for session data use cases.

**AWS Secrets Manager** - Automatic encryption of secrets (API keys, database credentials, encryption keys) using AWS KMS. Encryption occurs transparently with secrets never stored in plaintext, automatic rotation procedures supported, and access controlled through IAM policies.

**Encryption in Transit**:

All data moving between components travels over encrypted connections preventing interception:

**TLS 1.3 / TLS 1.2** - Client to ALB connections use TLS 1.3 (preferred) or TLS 1.2 (minimum) with strong cipher suites and forward secrecy. AWS Certificate Manager provides automatic certificate provisioning and renewal, certificates use 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit ECDSA keys, and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) headers enforce HTTPS usage.

**Application to Database** - MongoDB connections enforce TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. Redis connections optionally use TLS within the trusted VPC environment.

**Application to External APIs** - All external service integrations use HTTPS with certificate validation: Auth0 (JWT validation, user management), OpenAI and Anthropic (AI model inference), AWS services (S3, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch), and any future external integrations.

**Cipher Suite Configuration**:

Strong cipher suites with forward secrecy only:
- **Preferred**: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (TLS 1.3)
- **Preferred**: TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (TLS 1.3)
- **Supported**: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (TLS 1.2)
- **Supported**: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (TLS 1.2)
- **Disabled**: RC4, 3DES, MD5, SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1

#### 6.4.4.2 Key Management

AWS Key Management Service (KMS) centralizes encryption key management with automatic rotation, access control, and comprehensive audit logging.

**KMS Architecture**:

AWS KMS implements envelope encryption where Customer Master Keys (CMKs) encrypt Data Encryption Keys (DEKs), and DEKs encrypt actual data. CMKs remain within KMS hardware security modules never exposed in plaintext, while encrypted DEKs store alongside encrypted data. This architecture enables efficient key rotation where rotating a CMK only requires re-encrypting DEKs rather than re-encrypting all data.

**Key Rotation Policy**:

| Service | Key Type | Rotation Period | Rotation Process |
|---------|----------|-----------------|------------------|
| MongoDB Atlas | AWS KMS CMK | 90 days | Automatic, zero-downtime |
| S3 Buckets | SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS | Automatic (AWS-managed) or 90 days | Transparent |
| Secrets Manager | AWS KMS CMK | 90 days | Automatic with Lambda rotation function |
| Redis (optional) | AWS KMS CMK | 90 days | Requires AOF persistence |

**Access Control**:

KMS key policies restrict key usage to authorized services and roles:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "Enable IAM User Permissions",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:root"
      },
      "Action": "kms:*",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "Allow MongoDB Atlas to use the key",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/MongoDBAtlasEncryptionRole"
      },
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt",
        "kms:Encrypt",
        "kms:DescribeKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "Allow application to use the key for S3",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/ECSTaskExecutionRole"
      },
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt",
        "kms:GenerateDataKey"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Audit Logging**:

All KMS key usage logs to AWS CloudTrail enabling:
- Tracking who accessed which keys and when
- Detecting unauthorized key usage attempts
- Compliance reporting on encryption key management
- Forensic investigation following security incidents

CloudTrail logs capture operations including CreateKey, Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, EnableKeyRotation, and DisableKey, with immutable logs retained for 90 days in CloudTrail and 7 years in S3 Glacier.

#### 6.4.4.3 Data Masking Rules

Data masking protects sensitive information in non-production environments preventing exposure of production data in development and staging environments where security controls may be less rigorous.

**Data Sanitization Strategy**:

Before copying production databases to non-production environments, automated scripts mask personally identifiable information:

**Email Addresses** - Replace with test patterns: `test_<document_id>@staging.local`

**Names** - Replace with generic values: `Test User`, `Sample Customer`

**Phone Numbers** - Replace with valid but non-functional numbers: `555-0100` through `555-0199` (reserved for fictional use)

**Addresses** - Replace with generic locations: `123 Test Street, Test City, TS 12345`

**Message Content** - Redact or replace with lorem ipsum preventing exposure of business-sensitive communications

**Document Content** - Replace with placeholder text preventing intellectual property or confidential data exposure

**Field-Level Masking Implementation**:

```javascript
async function sanitizeProductionDataForStaging() {
  // Mask email addresses
  await db.users.updateMany(
    {},
    [{
      $set: {
        email: {
          $concat: ["test_", {$toString: "$_id"}, "@staging.local"]
        },
        "profile.display_name": "Test User",
        "profile.avatar_url": "/default-avatar.png",
        "profile.phone": "555-0100"
      }
    }]
  );
  
  // Redact message content
  await db.conversations.updateMany(
    {},
    [{
      $set: {
        messages: {
          $map: {
            input: "$messages",
            as: "msg",
            in: {
              message_id: "$$msg.message_id",
              role: "$$msg.role",
              content: "[REDACTED FOR STAGING]",
              timestamp: "$$msg.timestamp"
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }]
  );
  
  // Replace document content
  await db.documents.updateMany(
    {},
    {$set: {content: "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet..."}}
  );
}
```

**Masking Validation**:

Automated validation ensures masking completeness before non-production environment activation:
- Scan for email patterns matching production domains
- Search for production API keys or credentials
- Verify no unredacted message or document content
- Confirm all PII fields contain masked values
- Generate masking report for compliance verification

#### 6.4.4.4 Secure Communication

Network security controls implement defense-in-depth protection restricting traffic flow between components and external networks.

**VPC Network Architecture**:

AWS Virtual Private Cloud provides network isolation with public subnets hosting Application Load Balancer and NAT Gateway accepting inbound internet traffic and providing outbound internet access, and private subnets hosting application containers, MongoDB, and Redis with no direct internet accessibility. Inter-subnet routing occurs through VPC routing tables, and AWS PrivateLink enables private connectivity to AWS services without internet transit.

**Security Group Rules**:

Stateful firewall rules control traffic at the instance level:

**ALB Security Group**:
- Inbound: HTTPS (443) from 0.0.0.0/0 (internet)
- Outbound: HTTP (80) to application container security group

**Application Container Security Group**:
- Inbound: HTTP (80) from ALB security group only
- Outbound: MongoDB (27017) to database security group, Redis (6379) to cache security group, HTTPS (443) to 0.0.0.0/0 (external APIs)

**Database Security Group**:
- Inbound: MongoDB (27017) from application container security group
- Outbound: None

**Redis Security Group**:
- Inbound: Redis (6379) from application container security group
- Outbound: None

**Security Headers**:

All API responses include security headers protecting against common web vulnerabilities:

```
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data: https:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://auth0-tenant.auth0.com
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()
```

**CORS Configuration**:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing restricts which domains can access the API:

```python
CORS(app, resources={
    r"/api/*": {
        "origins": [
            "https://app.6nove4.com",
            "https://staging.6nove4.com"
        ],
        "methods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"],
        "allowed_headers": ["Content-Type", "Authorization"],
        "expose_headers": ["X-Total-Count", "X-RateLimit-Remaining"],
        "supports_credentials": True,
        "max_age": 3600
    }
})
```

#### 6.4.4.5 Compliance Controls

Regulatory compliance controls ensure the system meets legal requirements for data protection, privacy, and security.

**GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) Compliance**:

The European Union's GDPR establishes comprehensive data protection requirements:

**Right to Erasure (Right to be Forgotten)** - Users can request complete deletion of personal data within 30 days. The implementation processes deletion requests through a background job tracking progress and ensuring completion within regulatory timeframe.

```javascript
async function processGDPRDeletionRequest(userId) {
  // Create deletion job
  const job = await db.jobs.insertOne({
    job_type: "gdpr_deletion",
    user_id: userId,
    status: "queued",
    created_at: new Date(),
    compliance_deadline: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
  });
  
  // Delete user data across all systems
  await Promise.all([
    db.users.deleteOne({user_id: userId}),
    db.conversations.deleteMany({user_id: userId}),
    db.documents.updateMany(
      {user_id: userId},
      {$set: {user_id: "ANONYMIZED", owner_email: "deleted@anonymous.local"}}
    ),
    deleteS3Objects(`users/${userId}/`),
    redisClient.del(`user:${userId}:*`)
  ]);
  
  // Audit log (retained for compliance despite deletion)
  await db.audit_log.insertOne({
    event: "gdpr_erasure_completed",
    user_id: userId,
    timestamp: new Date(),
    retention_period: "7_years"
  });
}
```

**Right to Access** - Users can request a complete copy of their personal data in machine-readable format (JSON). The data export includes user profile, all conversations, all documents, account activity logs, and sharing permissions.

**Data Minimization** - Collect only data necessary for stated purposes, avoiding excessive data collection that increases privacy risks and compliance burden.

**Purpose Limitation** - Use personal data only for purposes disclosed to users at collection time, preventing undisclosed secondary uses.

**Privacy by Design** - Integrate data protection into system architecture from inception rather than retrofitting security controls, implementing encryption, access controls, and audit logging as fundamental design elements.

**Breach Notification** - Notify supervisory authorities within 72 hours of detected personal data breaches, with procedures documented in incident response runbooks.

**Data Retention Policies**:

| Data Type | Active Retention | Archive Retention | Deletion |
|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|----------|
| User Profiles | Until account deletion | N/A | 30 days after request |
| Conversations | 90 days | 7 years (S3 Glacier) | After 7 years |
| Audit Logs | 1 year (MongoDB) | 7 years (S3 Glacier) | After 7 years |
| Session Tokens | 30 minutes | N/A | Automatic (TTL) |
| Temporary Uploads | 24 hours | N/A | Automatic (TTL) |
| Background Jobs | 30 days | N/A | Automatic (TTL) |

**SOC 2 Compliance Considerations**:

System and Organization Controls (SOC 2) certification validates security controls through independent audits:

**Security** - Access controls, encryption, monitoring, and vulnerability management

**Availability** - 99.5% uptime target, multi-AZ deployment, automatic failover, disaster recovery procedures

**Processing Integrity** - Input validation, error handling, transaction controls, data consistency checks

**Confidentiality** - Encryption, access controls, data classification, secure transmission

**Privacy** - Data collection consent, purpose limitation, user rights support, data retention

**CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) Compliance**:

California's privacy law grants consumers rights over personal information:

**Right to Know** - Disclose personal information collected, purposes of collection, and third parties with whom data is shared

**Right to Delete** - Delete personal information (implemented through same GDPR deletion procedures)

**Right to Opt-Out** - Opt-out of data sale (not applicable - the system does not sell personal data to third parties)

**Right to Non-Discrimination** - Equal service regardless of privacy choices without discriminatory pricing or quality

### 6.4.5 Security Architecture Diagrams

#### 6.4.5.1 Authentication Flow Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client Application<br/>(Web/Mobile/Desktop)
    participant Auth0 as Auth0 Identity Provider<br/>OAuth 2.0 + OIDC
    participant ALB as AWS Application<br/>Load Balancer
    participant API as Flask API Gateway<br/>JWT Validation
    participant Redis as Redis Cache<br/>Session Storage
    participant Business as Business Logic Layer
    
    Note over User,Business: Initial Authentication (Authorization Code + PKCE)
    
    User->>Client: 1. Access Application
    Client->>Auth0: 2. Initiate OAuth 2.0 Flow<br/>Authorization Code + PKCE
    Auth0->>User: 3. Redirect to Auth0 Login UI
    User->>Auth0: 4. Enter Credentials<br/>(Username + Password)
    Auth0->>Auth0: 5. Validate Credentials
    
    alt MFA Enabled
        Auth0->>User: 5a. Request MFA Code<br/>(SMS/Email/Authenticator)
        User->>Auth0: 5b. Submit MFA Code
        Auth0->>Auth0: 5c. Validate MFA Code
    end
    
    Auth0->>Client: 6. Return Authorization Code
    Client->>Auth0: 7. Exchange Code for Tokens<br/>(with PKCE verifier)
    Auth0->>Client: 8. Return JWT Tokens<br/>(Access + Refresh + ID Token)
    Client->>Client: 9. Store Tokens Securely<br/>(Memory/Secure Storage)
    
    Note over User,Business: Subsequent API Requests (Authenticated)
    
    User->>Client: 10. Perform Action<br/>(e.g., Create Conversation)
    Client->>ALB: 11. HTTPS Request<br/>Authorization: Bearer {JWT}
    ALB->>API: 12. Route to Healthy Container
    
    API->>API: 13. Extract JWT from Header
    
    alt JWKS Cached
        API->>Redis: 14a. Check JWKS Cache<br/>(24-hour cache)
        Redis->>API: 14b. Return Cached Public Key
    else JWKS Not Cached
        API->>Auth0: 14c. Fetch JWKS Endpoint<br/>(Auth0 Public Keys)
        Auth0->>API: 14d. Return Public Keys
        API->>Redis: 14e. Cache JWKS<br/>(TTL: 24 hours)
    end
    
    API->>API: 15. Validate JWT Signature<br/>(RS256 with Auth0 Public Key)
    API->>API: 16. Verify Claims<br/>(exp, iss, aud)
    API->>API: 17. Extract User Context<br/>(user_id, roles, permissions)
    
    API->>Business: 18. Forward Authenticated Request<br/>(with user context)
    Business->>Business: 19. Process Business Logic
    Business->>API: 20. Return Response
    API->>ALB: 21. Return Response
    ALB->>Client: 22. HTTPS Response
    Client->>User: 23. Display Result
    
    Note over User,Business: Token Refresh (When Access Token Expires)
    
    Client->>Auth0: 24. Refresh Token Request<br/>(Refresh Token)
    Auth0->>Auth0: 25. Validate Refresh Token
    Auth0->>Client: 26. Return New Access Token<br/>(+ Optional New Refresh Token)
    Client->>Client: 27. Update Stored Tokens
```

#### 6.4.5.2 Authorization Flow Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([API Request with JWT]) --> Extract[Extract JWT from<br/>Authorization Header]
    
    Extract --> ValidateFormat{Valid JWT<br/>Format?}
    ValidateFormat -->|Invalid| Error401a[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid token format]
    ValidateFormat -->|Valid| CheckCache{JWKS Public Key<br/>in Redis Cache?}
    
    CheckCache -->|Cached| ValidateSignature
    CheckCache -->|Not Cached| FetchJWKS[Fetch JWKS from Auth0<br/>Cache in Redis 24h]
    FetchJWKS --> ValidateSignature[Validate JWT Signature<br/>RS256 Algorithm]
    
    ValidateSignature --> SignatureValid{Signature<br/>Valid?}
    SignatureValid -->|Invalid| Error401b[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid signature]
    SignatureValid -->|Valid| CheckExpiration{Token<br/>Expired?}
    
    CheckExpiration -->|Expired| Error401c[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Token expired]
    CheckExpiration -->|Valid| CheckIssuer{Issuer iss<br/>Matches Auth0?}
    
    CheckIssuer -->|Mismatch| Error401d[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid issuer]
    CheckIssuer -->|Match| CheckAudience{Audience aud<br/>Matches API?}
    
    CheckAudience -->|Mismatch| Error401e[Return 401 Unauthorized<br/>Invalid audience]
    CheckAudience -->|Match| ExtractContext[Extract User Context<br/>user_id, roles, permissions]
    
    ExtractContext --> RouteAuth{Route Requires<br/>Specific Role?}
    RouteAuth -->|Yes| CheckRole{User Has<br/>Required Role?}
    RouteAuth -->|No| ResourceAuth
    
    CheckRole -->|No| Error403a[Return 403 Forbidden<br/>Insufficient role]
    CheckRole -->|Yes| ResourceAuth{Resource Requires<br/>Permission?}
    
    ResourceAuth -->|Yes| CheckPermission{User Has<br/>Required Permission?}
    ResourceAuth -->|No| OwnershipCheck
    
    CheckPermission -->|No| Error403b[Return 403 Forbidden<br/>Insufficient permission]
    CheckPermission -->|Yes| OwnershipCheck{Resource Requires<br/>Ownership Check?}
    
    OwnershipCheck -->|Yes| IsOwner{User Owns<br/>Resource?}
    OwnershipCheck -->|No| ProcessRequest
    
    IsOwner -->|No| AdminOverride{User Has<br/>Admin Role?}
    IsOwner -->|Yes| ProcessRequest[Process Authorized Request]
    
    AdminOverride -->|No| Error403c[Return 403 Forbidden<br/>Not resource owner]
    AdminOverride -->|Yes| ProcessRequest
    
    ProcessRequest --> AuditLog[Log Authorization Event<br/>User, Resource, Action]
    AuditLog --> Success[Return 200 OK<br/>+ Response Data]
    
    style Start fill:#e1f5ff
    style Success fill:#d4f4dd
    style Error401a fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error401b fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error401c fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error401d fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error401e fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error403a fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error403b fill:#ffe1e1
    style Error403c fill:#ffe1e1
    style ProcessRequest fill:#fff4e1
    style AuditLog fill:#e8f4f8
```

| Layer | Control Type | Implementation | Purpose |
|-------|-------------|----------------|---------|
| Network | Firewall | VPC Security Groups | Restrict traffic to necessary ports/protocols |
| Network | Network Segmentation | Public/Private Subnets | Isolate resources by sensitivity |
| Network | DDoS Protection | AWS Shield | Protect against volumetric attacks |
| Network | Traffic Encryption | TLS 1.3 | Encrypt data in transit |
| Application | Authentication | Auth0 OAuth 2.0 + OIDC | Verify user identity |
| Application | Authorization | JWT-based RBAC | Control resource access |
| Application | Rate Limiting | Redis atomic counters | Prevent abuse and DoS |
| Application | Input Validation | Pydantic schemas | Prevent injection attacks |
| Application | Session Management | Redis with TTL | Secure stateless sessions |
| Data | Encryption at Rest | AES-256 (MongoDB, S3) | Protect stored data |
| Data | Encryption in Transit | TLS 1.2+ | Protect data movement |
| Data | Access Control | MongoDB user roles, IAM | Least privilege access |
| Data | Backup | Automated Atlas backups | Data availability and recovery |
| Data | Audit Logging | MongoDB audit, CloudWatch | Compliance and forensics |
| Monitoring | Security Alerts | CloudWatch Alarms | Detect anomalies |
| Monitoring | Log Aggregation | CloudWatch Logs | Centralized security events |
| Monitoring | Incident Response | PagerDuty, runbooks | Rapid response to incidents |
